patterns.title: The home page
patterns.question: The first page after sign-in has one job: tell the reader what needs doing now, in that order, before any figure. A home page typically holds a greeting, stat tiles, a setup section, a needs-attention list and a coming-up list. The disagreement is how much of that is above the fold, and whether the tiles lead or the work leads.

options.name: Work first, tiles second
options.rationale: The page opens on what needs doing, then the figures underneath. A returning manager reads the queue and stops; a curious one scrolls for the numbers.
options.cost: The tiles lose prominence, and a reader who came to check a number has to scroll. Costs one screen of vertical space.

options.name: Tiles first, work second
options.rationale: Figures give the reader a sense of scale in the first second, and the queue is read as a drill-down from them.
options.cost: Three large tiles push the needs-attention list below the fold, so the page reads as a report rather than a task list.

options.name: One queue, no tiles
options.rationale: The home page is nothing but the queue, ordered by consequence. Nothing to scroll past, and no figure to misread as the answer.
options.cost: The reader loses orientation entirely. Nothing says how big the day is, how much is coming, or whether anything is broken. The work-page shape calls for two to four tiles below the queue.

options.name: Grouped by area
options.rationale: The page is a set of per-area summaries, each linking into its own list. Home becomes a directory rather than a task list.
options.cost: A returning manager has to open an area before they can work, and nothing surfaces the one thing that is actually late. Better as a settings home than as a landing page.

options.name: Queue with an owner and an age
options.rationale: A triage shape. Each row carries who must act and how long it has waited, so several people can share the queue rather than duplicate the work.
options.cost: An owner and a clock are only honest if assignment is a real command. With no assignment, every row reads Alex and the columns are noise.

options.name: Guided first run
options.rationale: A new company gets a checklist before the queue exists, because a queue of nothing teaches nothing. The queue takes over once the checklist is done.
options.cost: Two different pages behind one route. The usual answer is a separate setup route plus a setup section, which is the same idea held in two places rather than one.

options.name: My work first, shared queue second
options.rationale: Linear's triage shape. What is assigned to Alex sits above what belongs to Acme Supply as a whole, so two people never decide the same refund twice. The shared queue stays visible, which keeps one person's morning from hiding the shared state.
options.cost: Assignment must be a real command with a real owner, or every row reads Alex and the split is decoration. Costs the tiles their place on short screens.

options.name: One next action, then the queue
options.rationale: Faster first action. The page names the single thing that costs most if it waits and puts its command at the top, so a busy reader acts in the first second without scanning. Everything else stays queued below in the same shape as the work-first page.
options.cost: Choosing the one next action is a judgment the application has to make and keep true; when it picks wrong, the real urgency sits one section down. Costs one section of vertical space above the queue.

compact.behaviour: The recommended option reflows: one column, header actions under the title, and a table scrolls inside its own region.

patterns.assessment: Work first, tiles second stays the pick: the manager reads the queue and stops, and the figures wait below for the curious. The Linear-style my-work split is the runner-up; prefer it once assignment is a real command and two people share one queue. Never ship the tiles-first order as the default: three stat tiles push the queue below the fold and the page reads as a report instead of a task list.

patterns.title: The list page
patterns.question: Find one record among many. The frame is fixed: header, views, search, filters, one table, pagination. The argument is almost entirely about which controls earn their place, because a search box on its own is not enough across 268 rows.

options.name: Search and a state filter only
options.rationale: Two controls for the two questions people actually ask: who is this, and what state is it in. Everything else is a view. This is the smallest honest addition to a bare list.
options.cost: A reader with 268 orders from 40 customers still cannot narrow to one customer. Acceptable while the search box already searches the customer name.

options.name: Views instead of filters
options.rationale: A segmented control across the top: All, Paid, Awaiting, Refunded, Disputed. One control instead of five, and the current choice is visible rather than hidden in a dropdown.
options.cost: Five segments plus a search box crowd one toolbar, and segments have no room for a count per state, so the reader cannot see where the work is before choosing.

options.name: Full filter row with chips
options.rationale: Search, customer, state, date range and channel, each as a control that stays visible. The applied set is restated as removable chips underneath, so the reader never guesses what narrowed the table.
options.cost: Four controls and a chip row is a lot of chrome above a table, and the chips duplicate the controls. Worth it once the list genuinely holds mixed records.

options.name: Saved views, opened from a menu
options.rationale: The states people return to are saved under names: Late payments, Disputed this week, Garcia orders. A dropdown holds them so the toolbar stays empty until asked.
options.cost: Nothing is discoverable on arrival, and every view needs its own storage. Good for power users, poor as a first-run surface.

options.name: Two lists on one page
options.rationale: Orders waiting for something sit above orders that need nothing. Two tables, so the working set is never mixed with the settled set.
options.cost: A list page holds one table, and a second table means a second page or a tab. Following it means two routes and two search states.

options.name: Dense filter bar with a result count
options.rationale: GitHub's issue-list shape. One filter bar states the query in words, a count says what matched, and a dense table sits under it. The reader sees what narrowed the list without opening a dropdown.
options.cost: A query syntax has to be learned, and typing a query is slower than pressing a segment for the two states people ask about daily. Best past a few hundred rows, noise below it.

options.name: Master and detail on one screen
options.rationale: The table on the left, the record on the right. Selecting a row fills the detail panel, so several orders can be compared in one sitting without losing the list.
options.cost: PatternFly's own guidance reserves this for comparing short lists of the same type, and says the detail pane needs a selected state and a close control. On a 1440 screen the table gets roughly 900 pixels, which is enough for five columns and not eight.

compact.behaviour: The recommended option reflows: one column, header actions under the title, and a table scrolls inside its own region.

patterns.assessment: Search plus one state filter stays the pick: two controls answer the two questions readers actually ask, and a bare list only needs the filter added. The GitHub-style dense filter bar is the runner-up; prefer it past a few hundred rows across many customers, where the query must be restated in words. Never ship two tables on one page: a list page holds one table, and a second table is a second route wearing a disguise.

patterns.title: The queue
patterns.question: Process items in batches. The queue is the one list page where selection is the interface, so the whole page has to answer: what does the checkbox select, and what happens to a thousand of them.

options.name: Select all on the page, banner for the rest
options.rationale: The header checkbox selects the 25 rows on screen. A banner then says All 25 on this page are selected. Select all 31, which makes the larger set an explicit second act rather than an invisible jump.
options.cost: Two clicks to act on everything, and the banner is one more thing on the page. Gmail's shape, and the clearest available answer to the select-all problem.

options.name: A checkbox on every row, no header checkbox
options.rationale: Selection is per order and never global, which is honest for money. The reader acts on five at a time and the page never implies it can act on all of them.
options.cost: The most common bulk job, refunding everything inside the window, becomes 31 clicks. A cap that protects money also removes the batch work the queue exists for.

options.name: Bulk bar that replaces the toolbar
options.rationale: While anything is selected, the toolbar is replaced by a bulk bar. The selection is the only thing the page offers, so the reader cannot act on a stale table.
options.cost: The layout shifts under the reader, and a search box they wanted to refine with disappears mid-decision. Widely used, and widely disliked for the jump.

options.name: Every row carries its own command
options.rationale: No selection at all. Each row has the one action that applies to it, with its own confirmation. The queue becomes a list of decisions rather than a list of things.
options.cost: No batch work at all, which is the whole point of a queue. Acceptable when the batch is rare and each decision needs different information.

options.name: Grouped by what the row is
options.rationale: The queue is grouped into priority tiers rather than one ordered list: money at risk, refunds closing, everything else. The reader takes the top group and stops if it is empty.
options.cost: Groups need a stated ordering and someone has to decide it. Atlassian's own advice is that several simple queues beat one complex one, which argues for separate routes rather than groups on one page.

options.name: Play mode, one decision per screen
options.rationale: Zendesk's play mode. The queue becomes one record at a time with Decide and Skip beside it and the next one already named. Each refund gets full attention, and the reader cannot half-read a row.
options.cost: One at a time is slow for thirty identical refunds, and the batch these queues exist for disappears. Prefer it when each decision needs different information, never for uniform work.

options.name: A table with a clock column
options.rationale: The queue sorted by the commitment clock, with three states: fine, closing, closed. This is Jira Service Management's shape, and it makes the ordering self-explanatory.
options.cost: The clock is only meaningful where something expires. A refunds table that holds the deadline but does not show it leaves the window invisible on the page.

compact.behaviour: The recommended option reflows: one column, header actions under the title, and a table scrolls inside its own region.

patterns.assessment: The Gmail-style page banner stays the pick: selecting the page and then explicitly selecting the rest is the clearest answer to the select-all problem, and money deserves the second click. The Zendesk-style play mode is the runner-up; prefer it when each decision needs different information and batch work is rare. Never ship the toolbar-replacing bulk bar: the layout jumps mid-decision and the search box vanishes just when the reader wants to refine it.

patterns.title: The record page
patterns.question: One record, and everything done to it. The frame carries a summary, at most three sections and an aside. The argument is about division: tabs against stacked sections, and what earns the aside.

options.name: Summary, sections, aside for history
options.rationale: What defines the record runs down the main column in at most three sections. History, which supports but does not define, goes in a narrower aside. This is the proven shape and the one Shopify's details template describes.
options.cost: Below roughly 1000 pixels the aside stacks under the sections, so the history lands after the actions. Acceptable; the order is right either way.

options.name: Four tabs over the same sections
options.rationale: When a record has more facets than three sections allow, tabs divide it. The active tab is in the URL, so a link carries it.
options.cost: The reader cannot see two facets at once, and the tab count grows with every new thing the back office adds. Carbon and GOV.UK both cap tabs at about six for this reason.

options.name: One page, headed sections, no tabs
options.rationale: GOV.UK names this as the alternative to tabs: keep everything on one page separated by headings, and let the reader scan down. No state to lose, nothing to remember.
options.cost: A record with six facets becomes a long page and the reader scrolls past the third one. The three-section ceiling is what keeps this honest.

options.name: Header carries the facts, sections carry the commands
options.rationale: The record's own values sit in the header area as a definition list, and the sections below hold only what can be done. The page separates what the record is from what it can do.
options.cost: A dense header pushes the commands below the fold on a phone, and it competes with the trail for vertical space.

options.name: Timeline as the page, record as the aside
options.rationale: For a record whose main interest is what happened to it, the history is the main column and the record's own values support it from the side.
options.cost: Wrong for most records. An order is mostly its facts; an audit trail or a collection record is mostly its history, and the shape has to follow which.

options.name: Editable properties in the rail
options.rationale: Linear's issue shape. The record reads down the main column while every editable property sits in the right rail, changed where it is shown. No Edit mode and no second page for one value.
options.cost: Every property needs its own save and its own failure state, so five quick edits are five round trips. Wrong where a change must be reviewed whole before anything is written.

options.name: Record with its own sub-navigation
options.rationale: Where a record genuinely has six or more facets, tabs become a side navigation of links, and the current one is marked. More room for labels, and it survives a phone.
options.cost: Takes horizontal space that a table would rather have, and a reader cannot see what is on the other pages at all.

compact.behaviour: The recommended option reflows: one column, header actions under the title, and a table scrolls inside its own region.

patterns.assessment: Summary with sections and history in the aside stays the pick: what defines the record runs down the main column while history supports it from the side. The Linear-style properties rail is the runner-up; prefer it when the aside must carry editable values rather than history. Never ship the facts-in-header variant: a dense header pushes every command below the fold on a phone and fights the trail for space.

patterns.title: The form page
patterns.question: Take one command's input. New-record pages are often inconsistent: one wraps its fields in a section with a left label column while another draws bare fields with no box and no Cancel. Both are this frame.

options.name: One section, one column of fields, Cancel beside Save
options.rationale: One command, one column, one place to submit and one to leave. The section is the only box, and the field labels sit above their controls so the column reads as a list of questions.
options.cost: A long form makes a long page. Grouping into several labelled blocks keeps it scannable, at the cost of a taller page.

options.name: Form section with the label in the left column
options.rationale: The labelled-block shape. Each block names itself on the left and holds its fields on the right, so several blocks read as a form with structure rather than a column of questions.
options.cost: The left column is about 150 pixels, which wraps the explanatory line to four words per line. The same content stacked would read better.

options.name: Stacked blocks with the title above
options.rationale: The same labelled blocks with the title above its fields rather than beside them. The label gets the full width, so the explanatory line reads at a normal measure.
options.cost: A longer page, and the reader loses the vertical alignment that made scanning between fields easy.

options.name: Two columns on a wide screen
options.rationale: Short fields sit side by side: price and compare-at price together, SKU and category together. One Save for the page rather than per block.
options.cost: A long amount or a long name does not fit half a column, so the layout forces some fields to be narrower than others. Two columns suit short fields on wide screens, as the editor page shows.

options.name: A stepper above one step's fields
options.rationale: A flow with more than three linear steps gets a stepper: The product, Then the price, Then publish. Each step validates before the next one opens.
options.cost: Carbon says a stepper is only for a linear flow of three or more steps, and not at all when the steps can be done in any order. Creating a product does not need three steps, so this is one step too many.

options.name: One question per screen
options.rationale: GOV.UK's one-thing-per-page shape. Each answer gets the whole screen, validates before the next opens, and the Back button is the browser's own. Nothing half-filled is lost to a section the reader skipped.
options.cost: Five screens for a form that fits one page feels slow to a returning reader, and the answers cannot be reviewed together until the final check. Reserve it for flows where each answer changes the next question.

options.name: Section per action, one Save at the foot
options.rationale: Each block is its own section with its own title and its own commands, and a single sticky foot carries one Save for the whole page. The reader sees the page's total work before committing any of it.
options.cost: One Save means a partial failure loses the lot, and a reader who wants to save the name and leave the price cannot. Two Saves on one screen is the worse version of this problem.

compact.behaviour: The recommended option reflows: one column, header actions under the title, and a table scrolls inside its own region.

patterns.assessment: One section, one column, Cancel beside Save stays the pick: a single command reads as a list of questions with one place to submit and one to leave. The GOV.UK one-question-per-screen flow is the runner-up; prefer it when each answer changes the next question and nothing may be skipped. Never ship the stepper for creating a product: three steps for work that fits one page is one step too many.

patterns.title: The report page
patterns.question: Read figures over one period. A statements page can put the period in the h1 and offer two outline buttons, August 2026 and October 2026, either side of it. Nothing says which is previous and which is next.

options.name: Chevron pair with the period as the heading
options.rationale: The period is the page heading, with an unambiguous chevron on each side to walk consecutive months and a dropdown to jump. A reader cannot mistake a chevron for a tab.
options.cost: Walking months one at a time is slow when comparing a quarter, which is why the dropdown stays.

options.name: Period tabs across the top
options.rationale: Months as a segmented control above the content, with the current one pressed. GOV.UK's tabs example is exactly this for comparison periods.
options.cost: Three or four months fit; a year does not, and Carbon warns tabs are wrong where the reader must compare across groups. Horizontal overflow on a phone.

options.name: Dropdown with presets beside a typeable range
options.rationale: A range control offering Last 30 days, This month, Last month, Custom, and a pair of typeable date fields. Nothing is hidden behind the calendar.
options.cost: Presets plus a range is two mechanisms on one control, and the preset that was used has to be shown afterwards or the reader loses track of the period.

options.name: The two buttons, labelled
options.rationale: Keep the two-button shape and make it legible: the pair reads Previous · next as one control around the period, which is the smallest change that removes the ambiguity.
options.cost: Still a month at a time, and the labels still compete with the heading for attention. Treats the symptom rather than the shape.

options.name: Report with the breakdown as tabs
options.rationale: The statement is the report; By warehouse, By channel and By tax rate are tabs beneath it, so the top of the page is always the same shape regardless of which breakdown is chosen.
options.cost: The reader loses the statement when they want a breakdown, and the tabs have to deep-link.

options.name: Cards with sparklines above the statement
options.rationale: Shopify's analytics shape. Three cards with sparklines name the trend before the statement names the total, so a dip is noticed before it is explained. The statement underneath keeps every euro accountable.
options.cost: Sparklines invite trend questions the monthly statement cannot answer, and three cards push the accountable total down. Prefer it mid-month; prefer the plain statement at settlement.

options.name: Report as a statement with no separate breakdown
options.rationale: One statement and nothing else, because a statement that adds up top to bottom is the whole report. A monthly settlement page is usually close to this already.
options.cost: Every question beyond the total needs a new page. Fine for a monthly settlement, wrong for a revenue question during the month.

compact.behaviour: The recommended option reflows: one column, header actions under the title, and a table scrolls inside its own region.

patterns.assessment: The chevron pair with the period as the heading stays the pick: a reader cannot mistake a chevron for a tab, and the dropdown still allows a jump across months. The Shopify-style cards with sparklines are the runner-up; prefer them mid-month when the question is trend rather than settlement. Never ship the two unlabelled month buttons: nothing said which was previous and which was next, and that was the ambiguity.

patterns.title: The settings home
patterns.question: Find one setting among many areas. A settings home can carry a whole tree: thirty routes under /settings, and the home has to carry all of it.

options.name: Grouped links, one line each
options.rationale: Each area is a link with a line saying what it holds, grouped into a handful of sections. The reader knows the area before they click and the page never grows a form.
options.cost: Nothing states which areas are incomplete, so a new starter has to open each one. The home page's setup section already does this job.

options.name: Cards with an icon and a state
options.rationale: Each area as a card with its icon, its purpose and, where it matters, its state: Payments connected, Payments not connected. The reader sees what is broken without opening anything.
options.cost: Cards are boxes, and the design contract says a section is the only box and never nests. A grid of bordered cards on the settings home is that rule broken by twenty boxes.

options.name: A list with a search box
options.rationale: One flat list of every setting with a search box over it. Thirty routes become one searchable index, and the reader types what they are looking for.
options.cost: The grouping is lost, so a reader who knows the area has to read it to find the area, and the search has to know every setting name a reader might use.

options.name: Grouped by how often it is changed
options.rationale: A Daily, Monthly and Once section. The page states that a monthly task goes in a menu and a once-only setup belongs in settings, which is the rule the page is applying to itself.
options.cost: The grouping is about frequency rather than about the thing, so a reader looking for 'where is the dock plan' has to remember which bucket it is in.

options.name: Incomplete areas first, everything else beneath
options.rationale: Anything not yet set sits at the top with the one command that fills it. The rest of the settings follow, so the page is also the setup checklist.
options.cost: The order changes as the reader completes setup, which makes the page feel unstable and makes a link to a settings area unreliable by position.

options.name: Left navigation with the area on the right
options.rationale: Stripe's settings shape. The areas live in a left navigation and the chosen area opens beside it, so thirty routes become one tree the reader scans without leaving the page. The current area is always marked.
options.cost: An area's incompleteness is invisible until it is opened, and a phone has no room for the tree, so the navigation must collapse into the same grouped links the pick already draws.

options.name: A checklist of what is left, then a plain index
options.rationale: The setup work and the reference work are separated: a checklist with verbs at the top, an index of every area underneath. The checklist disappears when it is done.
options.cost: Two structures on one page, and a reader who only wants the index scrolls past a checklist they have finished.

compact.behaviour: The recommended option reflows: one column, header actions under the title, and a table scrolls inside its own region.

patterns.assessment: Grouped links stay the pick: each area names what it holds, the page never grows a form, and thirty routes fit in a handful of sections. The Stripe-style left navigation is the runner-up; prefer it once areas gain enough depth to deserve their own tree. Never ship the frequency grouping: readers look for a thing, not for how often they change it.

patterns.title: The editor page
patterns.question: Edit what a customer sees, with a live preview beside the form. A storefront editor holds the look in a form and the result in a preview card beside it, and it must carry a Cancel and a dirty state: without them, leaving silently discards work.

options.name: Form left, live preview right, one Save
options.rationale: Every control writes straight into the preview, so the reader never saves to find out what a change looks like.
options.cost: The preview needs a phone toggle to be trusted for a storefront, and two thirds of a 1440 screen is a lot of preview for a few fields.

options.name: Preview as a device frame with a width toggle
options.rationale: The preview sits in a phone or desktop frame with an explicit toggle, because a storefront is judged at both widths and the form can hide half of it.
options.cost: The device frame costs horizontal room, so the form column narrows. A toggle means one width is never visible while the other is edited.

options.name: Preview above the form, full width
options.rationale: The preview is the point of the page, so it gets the top and the whole width, with the fields under it. Scrolling moves from the result to the inputs and back.
options.cost: Every field edit pushes the preview off the screen, which defeats a live preview. Only works if the preview is sticky or the field count is tiny.

options.name: Preview as a drawer pulled over the form
options.rationale: The form takes the whole page and the preview opens over it as a drawer, so the reader can check the result at either width without losing their place in the form.
options.cost: The preview is out of sight by default, and a drawer over a form is a layered context for something that is meant to be reassuring.

options.name: Tabs per facet with the preview always on the right
options.rationale: Branding, content and delivery are tabs; the preview does not move. Each tab is a short form, so the two columns never both get long.
options.cost: The preview shows a whole that the reader has only partly set. A tabbed editor grows a third tab here, so this is the next step rather than a change of kind.

options.name: Floating settings panel over a full-bleed preview
options.rationale: Webflow's shape. The preview takes the whole page and the settings float over it as a panel, so a cover image is judged at real size. Closing the panel is the same as stepping back from the work.
options.cost: The panel covers the preview it edits, and dragging it aside is fiddly on a laptop trackpad. Prefer it when the visual dominates, such as a cover; prefer side-by-side for fiddly fields.

options.name: Unsaved-changes bar pinned to the foot
options.rationale: An editor with no Cancel silently discards work on leave. A pinned bar naming what is unsaved and offering Save, Discard and Preview solves that without a dialog on every keystroke.
options.cost: A bar across the bottom of the page is a full-width band, which the tone rules reserve for deployment identity. It has to be neutral to stay inside the contract.

compact.behaviour: The recommended option reflows: one column, header actions under the title, and a table scrolls inside its own region.

patterns.assessment: Form left with a live preview right stays the pick: every control writes straight into the preview, so nobody saves to find out what a change looks like. The Webflow-style floating panel is the runner-up; prefer it when the visual dominates, such as a cover image judged at real size. Never ship the preview-above-the-form stack: every edit pushes the preview off screen, which defeats a live preview.

patterns.title: The outcome page
patterns.question: Where a flow ends: an order confirmed, a payment that failed, a link that expired. One state, one statement of what happened, one next step. Flows often end in a toast instead, which is why this frame is worth drawing.

options.name: One statement, one next step
options.rationale: What happened in the heading, what it means in one line, and exactly one primary action. A reader who came to find out whether it worked leaves in one glance.
options.cost: Saying nothing about what comes next makes the page a dead end unless the one action is right. Nothing else is offered, so a wrong guess is expensive.

options.name: Outcome with the record it changed
options.rationale: The same statement, then the record underneath so a reader who wants the full picture does not leave the page and lose the outcome.
options.cost: The page stops being an outcome and becomes a record page with an unusual header, which makes the flow's end indistinguishable from its middle.

options.name: Refusal outcome that names the fix
options.rationale: The same frame with the refusal tone, and the primary action is the one that resolves it: not 'Back', but the command that was refused.
options.cost: Every refusal needs a differently-worded fix, and one that does not have one has to fall back to explaining itself.

options.name: Outcome as a confirmation with a reference
options.rationale: For a flow that leaves the back office entirely, such as an invitation, the outcome carries a copyable reference and says where to go next.
options.cost: A reference is an identifier, and the design contract says an identifier on screen must be labelled and copyable rather than bare.

options.name: Outcome with a checklist of what is left
options.rationale: Where a command settles one thing and leaves three, the outcome page becomes the place that lists them, so the flow does not end with silent work outstanding.
options.cost: This stops being an outcome page and becomes a work page. The floorplan boundary blurs, and the one-glance property that makes an outcome page good is lost.

options.name: Confirmation band with the reference inside
options.rationale: GOV.UK's confirmation panel. A green band carries the outcome and the reference together, so the one thing to keep is the one thing that stands out. Everything below it is supporting detail.
options.cost: The band works for success and only success; a refusal in the same shape would read as approval. Reserve it for flows that leave a reference behind, never as a generic end screen.

options.name: Outcome as a toast with the record in place
options.rationale: No new page at all. The command succeeds, the record updates in place and a toast names what happened. The reader never loses their position.
options.cost: Carbon and Material both warn that a transient message must not be the only route to anything, and an outcome a reader may need to come back to needs to be a place, not a moment.

compact.behaviour: The recommended option reflows: one column, header actions under the title, and a table scrolls inside its own region.

patterns.assessment: One statement with one next step stays the pick: a reader who came to learn whether it worked leaves in one glance. The GOV.UK confirmation band is the runner-up; prefer it when the flow leaves a reference the reader must keep. Never ship the toast-only outcome for anything the reader may need to return to: a moment is not a place.

patterns.title: The live operations page
patterns.question: Dispatch day is happening: the docks are open, scanners are reading, and the warehouse lead needs the count at a glance. The argument is about what earns the glance: the total, the per-dock split, or only the exceptions.

options.name: The count, the docks, the exceptions
options.rationale: One number first, then the per-dock split, then only what needs a person. The warehouse lead reads the count in one glance and reaches the exceptions without scrolling past the day's log.
options.cost: Three structures on one page, and the exceptions sit below the docks on a phone. Acceptable; the order reads correctly either way.

options.name: Per-dock cards with a rate
options.rationale: Each dock carries its count, its share of the day and its last-hour rate, the way Datadog draws per-host cards. A slow dock is visible as a number, not as a feeling.
options.cost: Four cards with three figures each is twelve numbers before the exceptions. The warehouse lead gets diagnosis, not a glance.

options.name: Dispatches as a timeline
options.rationale: The day reads newest first: dispatches, double reads and connection drops in one place, the way PagerDuty draws an incident timeline. Nothing is grouped away from the reader.
options.cost: Six hundred dispatches do not fit a timeline, so the page shows the last five and a count of the rest. The count is the page; the timeline is decoration.

options.name: Exceptions only, quiet otherwise
options.rationale: The page promises silence: the count in the header, and below it only what needs a person. A warehouse lead who trusts the scanners reads one line and puts the phone away.
options.cost: When nothing needs anybody the page is nearly empty, and an empty page on a wall display reads as broken. It needs the count to prove it is alive.

options.name: Full-screen count for the wall display
options.rationale: A wall display carries one number and the exceptions count beside it. No navigation, no commands, nothing to misread from three metres away.
options.cost: A display is not a workplace: nothing can be opened, decided or closed from it. It answers how many, and every other question needs a phone.

options.name: Split: dispatches left, incidents right
options.rationale: The dispatch story and the incidents story sit side by side, the way GitHub draws a deploy beside its checks. Either column can be read without the other.
options.cost: Below a laptop the columns stack and the incidents land under the dispatch log. The stacking order has to put incidents first on a phone.

compact.behaviour: The recommended option reflows: one column, header actions under the title, and a table scrolls inside its own region.

patterns.assessment: The count with docks and exceptions stays the pick: the warehouse lead reads one number, then the per-dock split, then only what needs a person. The exceptions-only wall is the runner-up; prefer it on the wall display once the day is steady and the count is already known. Never ship the timeline as the main view: a list of six hundred dispatches is a log, not a page.

patterns.title: The calendar or schedule page
patterns.question: Ninety-three deliveries ahead need a shape that answers when, not what. The argument is density: a grid that shows the month against a list that shows the next delivery.

options.name: Month grid with deliveries marked
options.rationale: The month at a glance, with each delivery sitting on its date. Google Calendar's shape, and the only one where a clash between two deliveries is visible without opening either.
options.cost: Seven columns squeeze hard on a phone, and a date with three deliveries shows three clipped pills. The agenda is the honest phone shape.

options.name: Agenda grouped by day
options.rationale: Each day is a date chip with its deliveries beside it, the way Apple Calendar draws the list view. The reader scrolls time itself rather than paging through it.
options.cost: Empty days still take a row or the rhythm breaks, so a quiet month is mostly scrolling. The grid shows the quiet month better.

options.name: Week lanes per warehouse
options.rationale: Each warehouse gets a lane and each delivery a block on its days, the way Float draws allocations. A clash at one warehouse is a visible overlap, not a second page.
options.cost: Two warehouses fit; the third warehouse breaks the shape, and a phone has no room for lanes at all. Only honest for a company with few warehouses.

options.name: Upcoming list with a state filter
options.rationale: The schedule as a plain list page: search, one state filter, one table. Nothing to learn, and the same toolbar the orders page already teaches.
options.cost: A list answers what, not when: dates read as text and the shape of the month is invisible. Fine for ten deliveries, wrong for ninety-three.

options.name: Mini month beside the day
options.rationale: Outlook's shape: a small month for orientation, the chosen day in full beside it. The reader never loses the month while reading the delivery.
options.cost: Two structures need two selections that must agree, and on a phone the mini month stacks above the day it orients. Twice the page for one delivery.

options.name: Next 30 days as a week strip
options.rationale: Four weeks as four rows with their deliveries named inside, the way Airbnb draws payout weeks. The reader sees the rhythm of the month without learning a grid.
options.cost: Weeks are not months: a delivery on the 31st falls off the strip, and the strip must restate its own range every time it is read.

compact.behaviour: Seven columns do not fit a phone; the agenda list is the phone shape, with each day as a date chip beside its deliveries.

patterns.assessment: The month grid stays the pick: ninety-three deliveries ahead need density, and the grid shows the month the list cannot. The agenda list is the runner-up; prefer it on a phone, where seven columns become unreadable whichever way they are drawn. Never ship the week lanes as the default: two warehouses fit, and the third warehouse breaks the shape.

patterns.title: The onboarding or setup page
patterns.question: A new company has an account and nothing else. The argument is how much the page does: a checklist that waits, a wizard that leads, or a single page that states the three steps and gets out of the way.

options.name: Checklist with a progress bar
options.rationale: Three steps with a done, current and open marker, and a bar that says how far along the company is. Shopify's setup shape: the page waits, and each step opens its own command.
options.cost: A checklist can be ignored, and a reader who skips the payment step owns a back office that cannot take money. The home page's setup section has to repeat the warning.

options.name: Stepper wizard, one step open
options.rationale: One step open at a time with a stepper above it, the way Stripe draws onboarding. Each step validates before the next opens, so nothing half-filled is ever left behind.
options.cost: A wizard leads, which means it also blocks: the reader cannot add a product until the wizard is done. Wrong when the steps are independent.

options.name: Setup beside the guide
options.rationale: The steps on the left, what each step needs on the right, the way Notion draws setup beside its guide. The reader sees what a step costs before starting it.
options.cost: The guide duplicates the help text inside each step's own command, so two pages must agree about what the provider asks for. The copy drifts.

options.name: Start from a template
options.rationale: Starting from a template names what the first shipment is before anything else, and the template sets the lines to match. Everything stays editable after the choice.
options.cost: A template is a guess about the shipment, and a wrong guess sets lines nobody reads. Templates must stay visibly editable, never silently applied.

options.name: One page, one section per step
options.rationale: All three steps open on one page, each with its own Save, the way WordPress draws settings. The reader sees the total work before committing any of it.
options.cost: Three saves for a first run is three chances to leave half set up, and a reader who saves the name and leaves owns a back office that cannot take money.

options.name: Book help instead of reading
options.rationale: Setup as a conversation: the page offers a setup call beside the self-serve path, the way Shopify draws onboarding help. A reader who is stuck gets a person, not a longer page.
options.cost: A call is the most expensive control on the page, and it only helps in office hours. The self-serve path must still work alone at midnight.

compact.behaviour: The recommended option reflows: one column, header actions under the title, and a table scrolls inside its own region.

patterns.assessment: The checklist with a progress bar stays the pick: it states the three steps, shows which is done, and waits without leading. The stepper wizard is the runner-up; prefer it when a step cannot be skipped and the next depends on the last. Never ship the single page with a Save per section: three saves for a first run is three chances to leave half set up.

patterns.title: The error or not-found page
patterns.question: Something is missing, broken or refused. The argument is how much the page owns: a dead end with links back, or a working page that names the fix and offers it.

options.name: Centered not-found with links back
options.rationale: What happened, where to go, in one glance: the code, one line, and the two places the reader most likely wanted. GitHub's 404 shape, minus the joke.
options.cost: A dead end is still a dead end: the reader loses whatever they were doing. It must at least keep the navigation, so the way back is one click.

options.name: Inline error with a retry
options.rationale: The page keeps its frame and names what failed inside it, the way Vercel draws a failed deploy beside the project. The reader keeps their place and retries from it.
options.cost: A retry button promises the retry can work. Where the failure is permanent, the button is a lie told twice.

options.name: Full-page outage with the state named
options.rationale: When a provider is down, the page says which one, what still works and what does not. The status-page shape, as Stripe draws it: the failure is named, so the reader stops guessing.
options.cost: A full page for a partial failure hides what still works. Only honest when the failure truly blocks the page.

options.name: Permission refusal with the fix
options.rationale: A refusal worded from its code, with the one command that resolves it beside it. The page knows Jordan cannot refund and knows Sam Rivera can grant it, so it says both.
options.cost: Every refusal needs its own fix, and one without a fix falls back to explaining itself. The fix must be a command, never a longer paragraph.

options.name: Expired invitation with the next step
options.rationale: An expired link names its expiry and offers the re-invite beside it, the way Slack draws expired invites. The old link stays dead; the fix is one step, not a search.
options.cost: The page must know who the invitation was for after it expired, which means expired invitations are kept, not deleted. Retention with a reason.

options.name: Warehouse scanner is offline
options.rationale: The offline dock keeps scanning and says so: what is queued, when it last synced, and that nothing is lost. The page reports a state, not a failure.
options.cost: Offline confidence must be earned: the queued count has to be exact, or the first discrepancy teaches the warehouse to distrust the page.

compact.behaviour: The recommended option reflows: one column, header actions under the title, and a table scrolls inside its own region.

patterns.assessment: The centered not-found with links back stays the pick: it says what happened, says where to go, and does both in one glance. The permission refusal with the fix is the runner-up; prefer it whenever the page knows who can resolve it, because Back is not a fix. Never ship the inline error alone for a missing page: a retry button on a page that will never exist is a promise that cannot be kept.

patterns.title: The record drawer
patterns.question: Read a record without leaving the list. It exists so a reader can compare a row against what the row actually holds. The catch is width: a 420-pixel drawer inside a 1440 screen holds facts and nothing else.

options.name: Drawer beside the list, read-only
options.rationale: The list stays on screen and the drawer carries the record's facts and its few commands. The list context is the whole reason to use a drawer, so nothing covers it.
options.cost: A phone has no room for two columns, so the drawer becomes a full-screen page. The same route then has two layouts to verify.

options.name: Drawer over the list as an overlay
options.rationale: The drawer slides over the table with a scrim, giving the record more width than a column allows while still leaving the list identifiable behind it.
options.cost: Atlassian's panel guidance puts the panel beside the main area and only over it at 1024 and below. Overlaying at 1440 hides the row the reader is comparing against.

options.name: Row expands inline into a detail band
options.rationale: The record opens under its own row inside the table. Nothing is overlaid and nothing moves, so the comparison the reader came for is right there.
options.cost: A wide record cannot fit under a row without breaking the column grid, and NN/g reports that users do not clean up after themselves when they open several.

options.name: Drawer holding a small edit, list behind it
options.rationale: The drawer carries a record and a short edit beside it, which is the one case where editing in place beats leaving the list.
options.cost: Carbon says a modal is not for repeatable work, and this is repeatable work. The screen gets two nested sets of controls and one narrow column.

options.name: Drawer as a preview, closing back to the same row
options.rationale: A narrow drawer that shows only what the row cannot: the lines, the timeline, the last three things. The record link opens the full page for anything more.
options.cost: The reader has to know when the drawer is enough. One more place to judge, and the difference between it and the record page has to be obvious.

options.name: Drawer with timeline and reply box
options.rationale: Intercom's conversation shape. The drawer carries the timeline above and a reply box below, so reading and answering happen in the same place. The list behind stays the queue to return to.
options.cost: A reply box invites a hasty message from a narrow column, and a long timeline pushes the box out of reach. Prefer it for message-first work, never for records whose facts need the width.

options.name: Phone width, drawer becomes a full page
options.rationale: At 390 pixels there is no beside, so the drawer takes the whole screen with a Back control that returns to the list at the same scroll position.
options.cost: The list has to be kept alive behind the full-screen view, which is a navigation model rather than a layout. A real Back is the honest version of this.

compact.behaviour: At 390 pixels there is no beside: the drawer takes the whole screen with a Back control that returns to the list at the same scroll position.

patterns.assessment: The read-only drawer beside the list stays the pick: the list context is the whole reason to use a drawer, so nothing covers it. The inline detail band is the runner-up; prefer it when the record is four facts and the comparison must sit inside the table. Never ship the drawer holding an edit: repeatable work in a narrow overlay gives two nested control sets in one thin column.

patterns.title: Choosing the columns
patterns.question: A column is a fact a reader uses to choose a row. The question each time is what the reader sorts or scans by, and the default table answers with order number, customer, placed, state and paid, which covers choosing but not filtering. Placed is a secondary column, so it leaves below 768 pixels.

options.name: Five columns, nothing removable
options.rationale: The default set. Five columns is what fits 1440 without scrolling and covers the four questions: which order, who, when, what state, what money.
options.cost: Nothing can be dropped or added, so a team that wants the delivery as its own column or hides the email has no way to get there.

options.name: Six columns with a column chooser
options.rationale: Add the delivery as its own column and offer a chooser so each back-office user keeps the columns they use. TanStack's columnVisibility is a plain per-user map, so the state is cheap.
options.cost: The chooser is one more control, and a table where everyone sees different columns is harder to talk about in a support reply.

options.name: A chooser that shows the current set
options.rationale: The Columns control opens a list of every column with a checkbox, a drag handle and a Reset to default. The reader sees what they are looking at rather than picking from memory.
options.cost: Two panes, so the table is squeezed while the chooser is open. A popover narrow enough to fit beside the button avoids that.

options.name: Two lines per row, one column per fact group
options.rationale: Fold delivery into the order cell and customer into one cell, so the table is three columns wide and each row reads as two records of two lines.
options.cost: Sorting by delivery becomes impossible, because delivery is not a column. Carbon wants sorting in the headers, and a folded cell has nowhere to put an arrow.

options.name: Columns sized to their content
options.rationale: The money column is narrow and right-aligned, the customer column takes the slack, the date column is fixed. Each column is as wide as its values rather than an even split.
options.cost: A long customer name pushes its column wider on one row and narrower on the rest, because table layout is content-driven. Fixed widths are the only way to stop that.

options.name: One column per question, headers that name the question
options.rationale: Headers become the questions the reader asks: Who, Which delivery, When, State, How much. Each header is sortable, and the reader can name what they are looking at.
options.cost: Longer headers take width from the data, and 'How much was paid' is a question rather than a field name, which breaks the one-word-per-column feel.

options.name: Customer first, order code deferred to the record
options.rationale: Faster support triage. Support starts from who is asking, not from a code, so the customer and the delivery lead and the order code waits on the record where it is needed. The caller is identified in the first two cells.
options.cost: Two orders by one customer for one delivery read as near-identical rows until one is opened, because nothing on the row tells them apart. Costs the scannable identity the default order column gives.

options.name: A Columns popover listing every column
options.rationale: The Columns control opens a popover with every column, a checkbox each and Reset to default. The order column is always shown and says so. This is the shadcn/ui data-table view-options menu, and Linear's Display panel works the same way.
options.cost: The popover covers the table while it is open, and drag-to-reorder inside it is a second feature that most back-office users would never find.

options.name: Saved views carry their own columns
options.rationale: HubSpot and Linear tie a column set to a saved view. All orders keeps the default five, Finance swaps in method, paid and refunded, and Dispatch list shows customer, delivery and lines. Each role opens the table it needs, and a support reply can name the view.
options.cost: Views are a feature with its own lifecycle: who may create one, whether they are shared, and what happens when a column is retired. Too much for a first release.

compact.behaviour: The recommended option reflows: one column, header actions under the title, and a table scrolls inside its own region.

patterns.assessment: Keep the default five columns (a): they answer which order, who, when, what state and how much, and the delivery already rides under the order code. The runner-up is the Columns popover (h), worth adding once a sixth fact such as method or channel is asked for by more than one team. Saved views (i) are the right answer later, when finance and the warehouse want different tables. Never ship the question-shaped headers (f): they cost width and read as a form.

patterns.title: Sorting
patterns.question: The default orders table passes no sorting; it is newest first. Where a table passes sorting, each sortable header is drawn as a ghost button with an up-down arrow, and the sorted one with a solid up or down arrow. The sort lives in the URL, so a link carries it.

options.name: Arrow on the sorted column only
options.rationale: One arrow, on the column the table is sorted by, showing which way. Every other header is plain text that becomes a button on hover.
options.cost: Nothing tells a reader that the other headers sort at all until they hover, which is invisible on a touch screen.

options.name: Sort as a control above the table
options.rationale: The sort is one named control rather than six header affordances: Sort: newest first. Works on a touch screen and states itself in words.
options.cost: The reader has to find the control to change the order, and Carbon's own guidance is that sorting belongs in the headers.

options.name: Arrows on hover plus a reset
options.rationale: Unsortable headers carry a faint arrow on hover; the sorted one is dark. A Reset sort control appears only while a sort is applied, so the default state stays clean.
options.cost: The reset is a control that only sometimes exists, which is its own inconsistency. It is also invisible until a sort has been applied.

options.name: Multi-column sort, shown as a stack
options.rationale: When a reader sorts by delivery and then by date, the table says so in words rather than relying on two arrows. Useful once a table genuinely needs a secondary key.
options.cost: Almost no reader needs two keys, and the control is a menu of menus. Carbon treats sorting as one column at a time.

options.name: Sorting stated in the page description
options.rationale: The order is stated once, in words, under the heading, and the headers stay plain. A reader who wants a different order clicks a header.
options.cost: The statement goes stale the moment a reader sorts by clicking, so the page contradicts itself unless the description updates too.

options.name: Sort only the column that has choices
options.rationale: Only two headers are buttons: money and date. Order and state sort alphabetically, which almost nobody wants, so they are not buttons at all.
options.cost: Selective sorting breaks the expectation that every header is a control, and it hides a capability rather than offering it.

options.name: Every sortable header carries an arrow
options.rationale: Each sortable header is a ghost button with a faint up-down arrow, and the sorted one has a solid arrow. The shadcn/ui and TanStack table examples do the same, and so does Stripe.
options.cost: Five arrows is more ink in the header row, and a header that does not sort (Customer) looks inert beside its neighbours.

options.name: Headers on a desktop, a sort control on a phone
options.rationale: Stripe's dashboard sorts from the headers on a wide screen and its mobile list carries a Sort control instead, because a list of rows has no headers to click. The same URL parameter drives both.
options.cost: Two controls for one state, and only worth building once the table actually becomes a list on a phone.

compact.behaviour: Below 640 pixels the table becomes two-line rows and the headers leave with it, so a Sort control carries the same sort from the toolbar.

patterns.assessment: The pick is (g), every sortable header carries an arrow: it states that headers sort on touch screens too. The runner-up is (h), headers on a desktop with a Sort control on the phone list, which becomes necessary the moment the table turns into rows below 640 pixels. Never ship (d), multi-column sort: no back-office question needs two keys.

patterns.title: Filters
patterns.question: The default orders page has a search box and nothing else. Carbon's rule is that a closed filter control shows how many are applied and can clear them without reopening, and that several filter categories never go inside one dropdown.

options.name: One filter per category, visible
options.rationale: Delivery, state, date and channel each get their own control in one row. No menu holds more than one category, so a reader can see what is available without opening anything.
options.cost: Four controls plus a search box is a wide toolbar. Below about 700 pixels they have to wrap or collapse, which is where the complexity moves.

options.name: Applied filters restated as chips
options.rationale: The controls stay, and the row underneath restates what is applied with a remove control each. The chip row is the honest answer to 'what am I looking at', which the toolbar alone is not.
options.cost: The chips restate the controls, saying one thing twice on one page.

options.name: Filters with an applied count on the control
options.rationale: Each closed control carries a count badge, so the reader knows a filter is narrowing the table without opening anything. Carbon asks for exactly this minimum indicator.
options.cost: A count of one on a select is a badge that reads as decoration unless the reader knows what it means. It is only clear beside a label.

options.name: A filter panel beside the table
options.rationale: Filters in a panel down the left side, with every category open at once and nothing hidden. Carbon prefers this when there are more than three categories.
options.cost: A permanent panel takes about 190 pixels from the table on every page, and most visits apply no filter at all. The panel is a cost paid by everyone for the benefit of a few.

options.name: Filters in one dropdown
options.rationale: One Filters button holding every category, with the count on the button. Keeps the toolbar to two controls and leaves the table full width.
options.cost: Carbon states that multiple filter categories should never be put inside a menu. A reader cannot see that a date filter exists without opening it, and closing it hides the applied state again.

options.name: Views as tabs, filters as controls
options.rationale: The tabs carry the question the reader arrived with: All, Needs attention, Awaiting money. The filters below refine whichever tab is open.
options.cost: Two mechanisms over one table, and the reader has to work out whether to click a tab or a filter. HubSpot makes views do both jobs instead.

options.name: Every option carries its count before it is applied
options.rationale: Each filter option shows how many rows it matches given the other filters as set, so the reader sees a zero before choosing it rather than landing on an empty table. Fewer dead-end filterings instead of a better empty state afterwards.
options.cost: Each count is a read against the other filters, so opening one select costs several queries. Counts also go stale the moment another user acts, and a stale zero is worse than none.

options.name: Faceted filter buttons with counts
options.rationale: The shadcn/ui tasks example draws each category as a button that opens a checklist with a count per value. The reader sees the split before choosing, and several values in one category combine without one select per value.
options.cost: Counts per value are a read per category, and the popover covers the table while it is open. Worth it only where a category holds more than a few values.

options.name: Filter conditions as removable chips
options.rationale: Linear states each condition as a chip with its field, its operator and its value, and the chip removes itself. A compound filter reads as a sentence, and clearing one condition never touches the others.
options.cost: Chips wrap to several rows on a narrow screen, and building a condition needs a field menu, an operator menu and a value menu in sequence.

compact.behaviour: The recommended option reflows: one column, header actions under the title, and a table scrolls inside its own region.

patterns.assessment: The pick is (a), one visible control per category: a reader sees what can be filtered without opening anything, and each category keeps its own control. The runner-up is (h), faceted buttons with counts, once a category holds more than a few values and the reader needs to see the split before choosing. Never ship (e), every category inside one dropdown: it hides the applied state and contradicts the rule this item states.

patterns.title: Row density
patterns.question: Carbon defines five row heights, 24, 32, 40, 48 and 64 pixels, and requires the header, the toolbar and the pagination bar to match the row size. The default table runs at roughly 47 pixels per row, between md and lg.

options.name: 40 pixels, the default
options.rationale: Carbon's md default. Two lines of text fit and the row scans.
options.cost: Twenty-five rows is 1000 pixels, so a 268-row table is eleven screens. Fine for browsing, slow for counting.

options.name: 24 pixels, scannable
options.rationale: Carbon's xs. One line per row, so the eye can travel straight down a column. The right choice for a queue a back-office user works through rather than reads.
options.cost: One line means the delivery name and the customer's email have nowhere to go. Both have to be dropped or opened from the row.

options.name: 32 pixels, a working table
options.rationale: Carbon's sm. Enough for a badge and one line, which covers a working table where every row gets an action.
options.cost: A two-line cell such as order number over delivery name does not fit, so the delivery has to become a column or drop.

options.name: A density control the reader sets
options.rationale: Three densities offered as a small segmented control in the toolbar, persisted per user. Carbon treats density as a token, not a free choice, so three steps is the honest number.
options.cost: A third toolbar control for something most readers set once and never think about. And a screenshot test then has to hold three versions of every page.

options.name: Dense rows with a zebra pass
options.rationale: At 24 pixels the eye loses its place across a wide row, so Carbon's zebra modifier returns. Every second row takes the muted surface.
options.cost: Zebra on a two-line row is noisy, because the bands cut through the cell content rather than sitting behind it. It works at one line and not at two.

options.name: A record list instead of a table
options.rationale: One card-width block per record with two lines and its own commands on the right. It is what the phone layout wants.
options.cost: No columns, so no sorting and no comparison across a column. It trades every table capability for reading one record well.

options.name: Comfortable 48 px rows for a delivery list
options.rationale: Shopify Polaris draws its product lists at a comfortable height with a second line under the name, because deliveries are read one by one rather than scanned down a column. The load bar answers the only question the row exists for.
options.cost: Eight rows need a scroll where the compact table shows fourteen. Wrong for any queue a back-office user works through in order.

options.name: Compact rows with a header that stays
options.rationale: Linear's lists keep the header pinned while hundreds of compact rows scroll under it, so the column names survive the scroll. The right shape for a queue that is worked top to bottom without paging.
options.cost: A pinned header only pays off on a long list; on five rows it is chrome with no job. It also needs a fixed list height, which fights the page scroll.

compact.behaviour: Below 640 pixels the table becomes two-line record rows with the amount right; sorting and comparison down a column move to the desktop.

patterns.assessment: The pick is (a), 40 pixels: two lines fit, the row scans, and it matches the default size. The runner-up is (c), 32 pixels, for a working queue where every row is read once and acted on. Never ship (d), a density control the reader sets: most readers set it once, and a screenshot suite then holds three versions of every page. The phone answer is (f), a record list, covered in full by the phone-list item.

patterns.title: The bulk action bar
patterns.question: What appears once rows are selected. Shopify puts common bulk actions in a bar above the selected range; Material allows one action per snackbar and Carbon keeps an action-bearing toast on screen until it is dismissed.

options.name: A bar above the table naming the count
options.rationale: The bar states how many are selected and what that total is worth, then offers the commands. The count is the thing a reader checks before acting on money.
options.cost: The toolbar is still visible above the bar, so two rows of controls stack. Either the toolbar goes or the page gets taller.

options.name: The bar replaces the toolbar
options.rationale: While a selection exists the toolbar is replaced by the bulk bar. One set of controls at a time, and the page cannot be read as offering search while it is offering actions.
options.cost: The layout shifts under the reader mid-decision, and the search box they wanted to refine with is gone exactly when they are about to act.

options.name: Bar at the foot, above the pagination
options.rationale: The bar sits where the reader's eye already goes after ticking boxes, above the row count. The selection controls stay next to the count they describe.
options.cost: On a long table the foot is off screen while the checkboxes are not, so the reader has to scroll to find the action they just enabled.

options.name: Bar with the escalation, and money named
options.rationale: The bar carries both numbers: 25 on this page, 1,204 matching. It also names the money, because a refund bulk action on the wrong scope is the expensive mistake this page invites.
options.cost: A long bar with two numbers and three buttons. It only fits above about 900 pixels, so the phone needs its own version of the same warning.

options.name: Bar with a confirm before it commits
options.rationale: The bar's primary button opens a dialog naming the count and the money, because a bulk refund is exactly the action NN/g says to interrupt when it is rare and irreversible.
options.cost: Two steps for a batch the reader has just spent a minute selecting. Acceptable on money, wrong for anything reversible such as a bulk tag.

options.name: Bar with the action inline and an undo after
options.rationale: The bulk action runs with no confirmation and the bar becomes an undo toast. Carbon keeps an action-bearing toast until it is dismissed rather than letting a timer take the undo away.
options.cost: On money this is the option the evidence argues against: NN/g reports reflex clicking when confirmations are routine, and a refund is not the place to train that reflex.

options.name: A floating pill with the count and one menu
options.rationale: Notion and Linear float the selection bar over the content instead of pushing the table down: the count, the one or two common commands, and a menu for the rest. The table never shifts when the first box is ticked.
options.cost: The pill covers the bottom rows while it is up, and money wants its total stated, which a pill has no room for. Keep it for reversible work.

options.name: Bulk actions behind one dropdown
options.rationale: Stripe's dashboard keeps the bulk bar to a count and one Actions menu, drawn open here. Every command is named in one place, the bar stays narrow, and adding a fifth command costs no width.
options.cost: Two clicks to the common command instead of one, and nothing on the bar says that resending is what most back-office users reach for.

compact.behaviour: The recommended option reflows: one column, header actions under the title, and a table scrolls inside its own region.

patterns.assessment: The pick is (a), a bar above the table naming the count and the money: on a refunds page the total is the thing a reader checks before acting. The runner-up is (g), a floating pill, for reversible bulk work such as resending confirmations or tagging, where the bar must not push the table down. Never ship (c), the bar at the foot: on a long table the action sits off screen while the checkboxes that enabled it do not.

patterns.title: Pagination
patterns.question: The default page ends with 1 – 25 of 268 on the left and Page 1 of 11 with two chevrons on the right. The count and the page number say the same thing twice, and the reader cannot jump to a page.

options.name: Count left, numbered pages right
options.rationale: The default shape with numbered pages added and the redundant 'Page 1 of 11' removed. The reader can jump, and the count still says where they are.
options.cost: Seven page numbers plus two chevrons is a wide control, and it has to collapse on a phone. The count and the numbers still overlap slightly.

options.name: Count, page size and chevrons
options.rationale: Carbon's three parts: items per page, the current range and total, and the current page. The page size is the control most tables leave out and back-office users most want on a long list.
options.cost: Three controls in one bar. On a phone it becomes a row of three stacked lines, which pushes the table off screen.

options.name: First, previous, numbers, next, last
options.rationale: Five controls plus a window of numbers, so a reader on page 7 of 11 can reach either end in one click without scrolling the number strip.
options.cost: The widest pagination control there is, and the numbers still have to window or overflow. On a 268-row list it saves at most four clicks.

options.name: Count, chevrons, and jump to a page
options.rationale: Two chevrons and a small jump field. Fewest controls, and a reader who knows the page number types it rather than clicking eight times.
options.cost: The jump field is a fourth thing to learn, and typing 11 then Enter is slower than clicking for most readers.

options.name: Load more as a button at the foot
options.rationale: GOV.UK warns that infinite scroll breaks keyboard users, so loading is a button a reader presses. The count stays visible, so the total is never a surprise.
options.cost: A link to a specific page 9 is no longer available, which is the main reason Carbon and GOV.UK both land on pagination for admin lists.

options.name: No pagination, because the list is short
options.rationale: Under about fifty records the whole list fits and pagination only adds a control that cannot do anything useful.
options.cost: It cannot be a rule for the whole back office: orders reach thousands and deliveries reach hundreds, so the list page has to decide per query.

options.name: A compact pager: range plus two chevrons
options.rationale: Stripe's dashboard pager is the range and two chevrons, nothing else. It fits a phone without collapsing, and on a 268-row list most readers move one page at a time anyway.
options.cost: No jumping: reaching page 9 costs eight clicks. Only right where the reader rarely leaves the first pages.

options.name: No pager at all while everything fits
options.rationale: GitHub draws no pagination on a list that fits one page: no range, no chevrons, no control that cannot do anything. The table ends and the page ends with it.
options.cost: Nothing states the total, so a reader cannot tell 10 rows from a filter that hid the rest. Only right where the heading already names the count.

compact.behaviour: Below 640 pixels the numbered pages leave and the pager keeps the range with two chevrons.

patterns.assessment: The pick is (a), the count with numbered pages: the reader can jump, and the range still says where they are. The runner-up is (g), Stripe's compact pager, where width is tight and nobody jumps further than one page at a time. Never ship (d), the jump field: typing a page number then Enter is slower than clicking for almost every reader.

patterns.title: Row actions
patterns.question: NN/g's rule is that a row carries one or two inline actions, and more than that means either crowding or hiding behind hover, which is undiscoverable and inaccessible on touch. The default orders table has no row actions at all.

options.name: One inline action, the rest in a row menu
options.rationale: The first row command is drawn inline and everything else sits behind the row's overflow menu. It matches Polaris's instruction to put a row's other commands in its menu.
options.cost: The second command is invisible, and the overflow is a 32-pixel target that has to be found in every row.

options.name: The row is the only action
options.rationale: No commands on the row at all: clicking the order number opens the record, and every command lives there. The table is for finding, the record is for acting.
options.cost: A bulk job becomes one row at a time, so this shape fits finding, not acting.

options.name: Two inline actions, no menu
options.rationale: Two commands is NN/g's ceiling for inline placement. Anything beyond two becomes crowded, so this shape only works where a row genuinely has two.
options.cost: Two buttons plus a checkbox plus five columns is a wide row. At 24 pixels of density the buttons stop fitting and the row grows.

options.name: Row menu only
options.rationale: Every command sits behind the overflow. The row stays one link plus one dot, which keeps the table narrow enough for a phone.
options.cost: Nothing on the row says what can be done, so the reader has to open a menu to learn that anything can be done at all.

options.name: Hover reveals the action, always focusable
options.rationale: The row's action appears on hover so a quiet table stays quiet, and it stays in the tab order so a keyboard reader reaches it. This is the accessibility repair on the hover-only pattern.
options.cost: It still fails on touch, where there is no hover, and the two fixes together mean two renders of every row. Polaris and NN/g both warn about hover-only affordances.

options.name: One destructive command in the row, guarded
options.rationale: The row's second command is a removal, so it is drawn in the destructive tone and marked as the last item in the row menu rather than sitting inline next to a harmless one.
options.cost: A red word in every row is visual noise on a page where the reader is scanning for states, and Carbon warns that a tone with no action required should be plain text.

options.name: The row menu drawn open
options.rationale: The shadcn/ui dropdown menu on the row, drawn open: the harmless commands first, then a separator, then the destructive one last. The reader sees every command the row holds without guessing what the dots hide.
options.cost: An open menu covers the rows under it, so it only proves the menu's contents, not the table's reading. The menu must also flip sides near the table edge.

options.name: Open in a side preview, act from there
options.rationale: Shopify and Stripe open a row in a side panel that carries the record's facts and its commands together. Resending Maria Garcia's confirmation happens beside the order lines, so the reader checks what is sent before sending it.
options.cost: A panel over the list hides the rows it came from, and on a phone it is a full screen, which makes it a page by another name.

compact.behaviour: The recommended option reflows: one column, header actions under the title, and a table scrolls inside its own region.

patterns.assessment: The pick is (a), one inline command with the rest in the row menu: the common job is one click away and the row stays narrow. The runner-up is (h), a side preview, where acting needs the record's context, such as the lines before a resend. Never ship (e), hover-revealed actions: it fails on touch, and keeping a second focusable render of every row doubles the table for no gain.

patterns.title: The table's own states
patterns.question: Carbon makes three empty states distinct: no data yet, no results for a search and an error in place of the content. It also says an empty state replaces the table entirely, headers included, so a screen reader does not read six empty headers first.

options.name: No data yet, table replaced
options.rationale: Nothing has ever existed, so the table and its headers are gone and one positive sentence offers the command that creates the first record.
options.cost: The reader cannot see what a row will look like, so the columns are undiscoverable until there is data.

options.name: No results for a search, filters named
options.rationale: Something exists but nothing matches, so the copy names the term and the filters and offers to clear them. A different sentence from the no-data case, because a different thing happened.
options.cost: Two empty states means two pieces of copy per list page, both of which have to stay true as filters change.

options.name: Loading as skeletons at the real row height
options.rationale: Skeleton rows shaped like real rows at the real height, so nothing shifts when the data lands. Carbon asks for skeletons rather than a spinner over the body.
options.cost: Carbon also requires the header, the toolbar and the pagination to match the row size, which means a skeleton page has to get all four heights right or it jitters.

options.name: A failed read keeps the chrome
options.rationale: The table rendered before, so a refresh failed. Keeping the headers and showing the error in place tells the reader the data they can see is stale rather than current.
options.cost: Old rows under an error can be acted on by mistake, which is the opposite of what the message wants to prevent.

options.name: A failed first read drops the table
options.rationale: Nothing ever loaded, so there is no table to keep. Carbon's rule is that the empty state replaces the element it stands for, headers and footer included.
options.cost: The reader loses the column names, so a retry that succeeds looks like a different page rather than the page they were on.

options.name: Refreshing in place, with the last read stated
options.rationale: A queue reads itself on a timer. A quiet control says how often and when it last did, and offers to stop it.
