options.cost: A timer on a page holding money means the reader may act on a value that changes a second later. A statement of when it last read is the mitigation, not a fix.

options.name: No results with recent searches
options.rationale: Linear's search keeps the recent searches under a no-result state, so a mistyped term costs one click to repair instead of retyping. The recent terms are the reader's own, which makes them the most likely next query.
options.cost: Recent searches are stored state with their own lifecycle and their own privacy question. They also go stale as deliveries complete.

options.name: A slow read that says what it is doing
options.rationale: Vercel and PlanetScale name a slow read while it runs: what is loading, how long it has taken, and a way to stop waiting. A reader who knows the list holds 268 orders waits; a reader watching a blank box leaves.
options.cost: A progress note needs the total before the rows arrive, which is a second read. It also teaches the reader that some lists are slow, which invites the question why.

compact.behaviour: The recommended option reflows: one column, header actions under the title, and a table scrolls inside its own region.

patterns.assessment: The pick is (a) for the never-had-data case, paired with (b) for no-results and (c) for loading: three sentences for three different facts, each replacing the table it stands for. The runner-up is (h), a slow read that names what it is doing, for the nights the list takes seconds rather than milliseconds. Never ship a bare spinner over the table body instead of (c): rows that shift when the data lands move the row the reader already chose.

patterns.title: Status in a column
patterns.question: The messages list uses badges with tone. The default orders table renders bare words for the ordinary states and a badge only for the rest: Paid and Completed are muted text, everything else takes a badge. It shows two adjacent words, Paid and Completed, whose difference the page does not explain.

options.name: A badge for every state
options.rationale: Every state is a badge mapping a code to a word and a tone. The word is the signal; the tone repeats it.
options.cost: Carbon warns that more than five or six status indicators overwhelm the eye, and that a status needing no action should be plain text. A badge on all twenty-five rows is exactly that.

options.name: Plain text, and the label says which state
options.rationale: Plain words with no tone, because none of these states needs a decision. The header says State and the column holds one word, which keeps the interface quiet.
options.cost: A reader scanning for a problem has to read every word. With 268 rows that is slow, which is the case for badges.

options.name: Tone only on the states that block
options.rationale: States that need a decision get a tone; the rest are plain words. This satisfies the 'no action required, use plain text' rule and keeps the table readable. It is what the default orders table draws.
options.cost: The reader has to learn which states are toned, and a new state added later has to be classified before it is used.

options.name: Two states side by side, both named
options.rationale: The default table's actual problem fixed rather than hidden: payment state and order state are separate columns, so Paid and Completed stop looking like two names for one thing.
options.cost: A seventh column on a table that already carries five, for a distinction most readers do not need until something is wrong.

options.name: A dot beside the word
options.rationale: The word carries the meaning and a small dot carries the tone, so the column stays quiet and a scan still finds the one row that needs a decision.
options.cost: A dot beside a word is a third channel after word and badge, and it adds an element that has to be explained once. It is also below 3:1 against the row background unless the token is chosen for it.

options.name: The state as a progress of three steps
options.rationale: Where an order moves through a sequence, the column carries the sequence rather than the current step: placed, paid, packed, shipped. The reader sees both where it is and what is left.
options.cost: Four marks per row is heavy on a 268-row list, and it only works because the order lifecycle genuinely is linear. A state with branches cannot use it.

options.name: Status with the reason on a second line
options.rationale: Stripe's payments list pairs the state with its reason: Disputed with why the bank asked, Awaiting payment with how old the wait is. The word says what, the line says why, and the reader never opens a row to learn the reason.
options.cost: Two lines doubles the row height for every row, including the paid ones whose reason is nothing. Only right on a queue where most rows need a decision.

options.name: A stale wait takes a stronger tone
options.rationale: Zendesk and Intercom colour a waiting state by its age: an awaiting payment that is two hours old is neutral, at two days it turns caution. The tone answers how urgent the wait is, not just that there is one.
options.cost: The tone now depends on the clock, so the same row reads differently in the morning and the evening. A support reply that says 'the yellow one' goes stale within hours.

compact.behaviour: The recommended option reflows: one column, header actions under the title, and a table scrolls inside its own region.

patterns.assessment: The pick is (c), tone only on the states that block: Disputed and Awaiting payment take a badge because somebody has to act, and Paid and Completed stay plain words. It is also what the default table does. The runner-up is (g), the reason on a second line, for the disputes queue where the word alone never answers why. Never ship (f), the progress marks: four blocks per row on a 268-row list, for a lifecycle that branches.

patterns.title: The money column
patterns.question: Amounts are right-aligned and tabular in the default table. The open question is what the cell says beyond the number: the currency is implicit, and a EUR 0.00 row sits beside real amounts with nothing saying why.

options.name: Number only, right-aligned
options.rationale: The default shape. A column headed Paid is unambiguous about the currency, so repeating EUR on every row is noise.
options.cost: EUR 0.00 reads as an error rather than as a fact. Two of the eight default rows are zero, and neither says why.

options.name: Symbol and value, one column
options.rationale: The symbol sits in the cell rather than the word EUR, which is shorter and still unambiguous in a Dutch-language back office. The column header names it: Paid, EUR.
options.cost: A symbol alone fails WCAG 2.2 SC 1.4.1 if it is the only distinction, and a screen reader does not always read a symbol prefix. The currency belongs in the label as well.

options.name: A zero amount says why
options.rationale: EUR 0.00 is a real state, not an error, so the cell names it: Fully refunded. A bare zero reads as missing data, and the word says it is a fact.
options.cost: A word in a numeric column breaks the alignment. It has to be short enough not to push the column wide.

options.name: Two money columns: charged and refunded
options.rationale: Where refunds are common, the net matters more than the gross. A second column turns a negative into a fact rather than something the reader has to reconstruct.
options.cost: Two money columns on a five-column table is a lot of numbers, and most rows are identical in both, so the reader scans two equal columns to learn nothing.

options.name: Money as a share of the total
options.rationale: For a table read to answer 'what did this delivery take', the amount column is joined by a share. The reader gets proportion without a second table.
options.cost: A share is derived from the total, so it goes stale the moment the filter changes. One column of derived percentages is a small exception, not a pattern.

options.name: Amounts grouped by day
options.rationale: Rather than a derived percentage, the table is grouped by day with a subtotal per group, so the reader sees the shape of the money without a chart.
options.cost: Grouping removes the flat row order and makes the table a different component, so pagination and select-all both get harder to reason about.

options.name: A totals footer under the money
options.rationale: Shopify's reports end the money column with a totals row: what the page holds and, where a filter narrows it, what the filter holds. Finance reads the answer without exporting the list to add it up.
options.cost: A page total invites reading it as the whole answer when the filter holds eleven pages. The footer has to say which total it is or it misleads.

options.name: Refunded shown under the charged amount
options.rationale: Stripe's invoice lines keep one money column and put what went back on its second line: the charged amount, then what returned to the customer. One column stays scannable and the refund is still on the row.
options.cost: Two lines doubles the row height, and a part refund needs a third fact, the net, which has nowhere to go in this cell.

compact.behaviour: The recommended option reflows: one column, header actions under the title, and a table scrolls inside its own region.

patterns.assessment: The pick is (a), the number only: the header names the currency and repeating EUR on every row is noise. The runner-up is (h), the refunded part under the charged amount, on any queue where refunds are the work rather than the exception. Never ship (e), money as a share of the total: a derived percentage column answers a question no orders list is asked.

patterns.title: Exporting the list
patterns.question: A back-office user downloads the list when the work continues in another tool, prints it when the work happens where a screen cannot be trusted, and schedules it when the same question is asked every week. Download is for the accountant reconciling the Garcia Interiors restock in a spreadsheet, print is for the pickup counter holding a pickup sheet when the network drops, and a scheduled email is for finance wanting the Monday figures without opening the back office. The three differ only in when the reader needs the rows: once now, once on paper, or again and again without asking.

options.name: One Export button that downloads CSV
options.rationale: The default behavior. One button in the toolbar downloads exactly the rows in the current filter as CSV, so the accountant gets the Garcia Interiors restock orders with one click and no decisions.
options.cost: No choice of columns or format, so a reader who wants only order number and paid, or an Excel file, has to trim or convert it elsewhere.

options.name: Export dialog with columns and format
options.rationale: The Export button opens a dialog where the reader picks the format and the columns before anything downloads. The reader states what leaves the back office rather than trimming a fixed file afterwards.
options.cost: Two steps instead of one, and the dialog has to remember or reset its choices on the next visit, which the single button never has to decide.

options.name: Scheduled email export
options.rationale: The team sets a rhythm once and finance receives the orders without opening the back office. A Monday 07:00 email answers the weekly question before anyone asks it.
options.cost: A schedule is invisible state: nobody sees it on the orders page, so a stale recipient keeps receiving figures until someone remembers the schedule exists.

options.name: Print stylesheet with a Print button
options.rationale: The Print button opens the browser print path and the print stylesheet keeps only the rows: order, customer, placed, state and paid. The pickup counter gets a pickup sheet that works when the network does not.
options.cost: Paper freezes the list at print time, so an order paid after printing is missing and nothing on the sheet says how old it is except the printed date.

options.name: Per-row receipt download
options.rationale: Each row carries its own receipt, so answering one customer means downloading one file rather than exporting the whole list and cutting it down. Order 7K4Q2M for Maria Garcia downloads as its own EUR 125.00 receipt.
options.cost: A button on every row narrows the table and invites downloading receipts one by one for a job that wants the whole list, which is slower than one export.

options.name: Copy the list to the clipboard
options.rationale: One button copies the visible rows as tab-separated values, which paste straight into a spreadsheet. Nothing downloads, so there is no file to find, rename or delete afterwards.
options.cost: Only the visible page is copied, so pasting 25 rows when the filter holds 268 silently drops the rest unless the reader notices the pager.

options.name: A large export that runs in the background
options.rationale: Shopify's bulk operations prepare a large export while the reader keeps working, then email a download link. Past a few thousand rows a direct download times out, and a progress note beats a failed one.
options.cost: The file arrives later, so the reader cannot reconcile against it right away. The export also needs its own failure state when the job dies overnight.

options.name: Export history with repeat download
options.rationale: Stripe's dashboard keeps every export in a list with its rows, its date and who asked for it, and each one downloads again. The Monday figures are re-downloaded rather than re-built, and finance can see what left the back office.
options.cost: Stored files with customer data need their own retention and access rule. A history nobody prunes becomes a second database of personal data.

compact.behaviour: The recommended option reflows: one column, header actions under the title, and a table scrolls inside its own region.

patterns.assessment: The pick is (a), one Export button that downloads the filtered rows as CSV: the accountant's job costs one click and no decisions. The runner-up is (g), a background export, past a few thousand rows where a download would time out. Never ship (f) as the only export: copying the visible page silently drops every row past the pager.

patterns.title: Searching with highlighted matches
patterns.question: The default search box filters the table and says nothing about why a row matched. A term that matches the email but not the name leaves the reader guessing, and a term with forty matches gives no way to move between them.

options.name: Matches highlighted in the cells
options.rationale: GitHub's code search marks the matched text where it sits. The term stays visible in the box and every match glows in its cell, so the reader trusts the filter.
options.cost: Highlighting needs the match offsets from the server, not just the rows. A client-side guess highlights the wrong occurrence on long text.

options.name: Scoped search: this delivery or all deliveries
options.rationale: Shopify scopes a search to the current view or the whole store from one control beside the box. A reader inside the Garcia Interiors restock searches it first and widens only when nothing matches.
options.cost: A scope is invisible once set: a reader who narrowed to one delivery last week searches it again today and wonders where the rest went.

options.name: A match column naming where it matched
options.rationale: GitHub's issue search says which field matched when the term sits somewhere the row does not show. The column answers 'why is this row here' for matches in notes or metadata.
options.cost: A column spent stating what a highlight already shows, on every row, for every search. It only earns its width where rows match on hidden fields.

options.name: First match focused for the keyboard
options.rationale: Linear focuses the first result as the reader types, so Enter opens it without a click. Support answering a caller moves from term to record without touching the mouse.
options.cost: A focused row looks selected, and Enter opening it surprises a reader who meant to refine the term. The hint has to teach the key or it misfires.

options.name: Recent searches under the box
options.rationale: Vercel and Linear offer the reader's own recent terms under an empty search box. A term searched twice a day costs one click instead of fourteen keystrokes.
options.cost: Recent terms are stored per user with their own privacy question, and a term from a finished delivery lingers until it is cleared.

options.name: A searching indicator while the server answers
options.rationale: Stripe's dashboard says when a search is still running rather than showing yesterday's rows as if they matched. The reader waits instead of acting on a stale list.
options.cost: A visible search state needs debouncing and cancelling, or every keystroke queues a request and the indicator flickers.

compact.behaviour: The recommended option reflows: one column, header actions under the title, and a table scrolls inside its own region.

patterns.assessment: The pick is (a), matches highlighted in the cells: the reader sees why each row matched without opening it. The runner-up is (b), a scope control, once readers search across deliveries and need to say which one. Never ship (c), a match column, on its own: it spends a column stating what the highlight already shows.

patterns.title: Grouped rows
patterns.question: Some questions are asked per group, not per row: what did today take, what does each delivery hold. A flat table answers them only after an export, while a group header with its own subtotal answers them on the page.

options.name: Grouped by day with subtotals
options.rationale: Bank statements and Stripe payouts group money by day with a subtotal per group. The reader sees the shape of the takings and still opens any row.
options.cost: Grouping removes the flat row order, so pagination and select-all both get harder to reason about across group edges.

options.name: Grouped by delivery with collapse toggles
options.rationale: Linear's group-by puts a toggle on each group header, so a reader following one delivery collapses the rest. The header carries the count and the subtotal even while collapsed.
options.cost: Collapsed groups hide rows from find-in-page and from a reader who forgot they collapsed anything. The toggle state needs to survive a reload or it annoys.

options.name: Grouped by state
options.rationale: Linear groups issues by status so the blocked ones read as one block. Here the disputed and awaiting rows sit together at the top, which is the triage order support wants.
options.cost: States change under the reader: paying an order moves it to another group, which reads as the row vanishing. The list has to say where it went.

options.name: No grouping: a group column that sorts
options.rationale: Carbon keeps the table flat and lets the reader sort by the would-be group field instead. Nothing hides, paging stays simple, and the eye groups adjacent equal values on its own.
options.cost: No subtotals: the reader who wants today's takings sorts by date and adds the rows up by hand. Sorting is not grouping, it only looks like it.

options.name: Group headers that select the group
options.rationale: Outlook and Gmail let a reader tick a whole conversation from its header. Here one checkbox refunds the day's orders together, which is the batch the team actually runs.
options.cost: Selecting a group selects rows the reader may not have seen, including a disputed one that should never be batch-refunded. The confirm has to name them all.

options.name: Two levels: month, then day
options.rationale: Xero and bank statements nest day groups inside month groups for a year of rows. October holds its days, and the year reads as twelve subtotals before any row is shown.
options.cost: Two levels of headers for 268 rows is mostly chrome: the month header, the day header, then one row. Nesting pays off past thousands of rows, not hundreds.

compact.behaviour: The recommended option reflows: one column, header actions under the title, and a table scrolls inside its own region.

patterns.assessment: The pick is (a), grouped by day with subtotals: it answers what today took without a chart and without leaving the list. The runner-up is (b), grouped by delivery with collapse toggles, once the team holds enough deliveries that one day's rows stop fitting. Never ship (f), two group levels: month-then-day nesting turns the list into a tree that paging cannot cross.

patterns.title: Inline row expansion
patterns.question: Some rows hold a second level: an order holds its lines, its units, its history. Opening the record for each one costs a page load per row, while an expansion row under the row itself answers the question where it was asked.

options.name: Expand to the order lines
options.rationale: Stripe's invoice list expands a row to its lines: what was bought, at what price, adding to the row total. Support answers 'what did I pay for' without leaving the list.
options.cost: The detail row breaks the column rhythm, and sorting reorders parents while children follow, which confuses a reader who sorted by money.

options.name: Expand to the order timeline
options.rationale: Zendesk expands a record to its history: placed, paid, confirmation sent. The history sits under the row it belongs to, newest last, so the reader sees what happened in order.
options.cost: History grows without bound: a disputed order's expansion is a page of its own. It needs trimming to the last few entries with a link to the rest.

options.name: Expand to units and pickup state
options.rationale: A pickup list expands an order to its units with what is collected and where. The warehouse lead works the list at the counter instead of opening forty records.
options.cost: Pickup state changes by the second at busy times, so an expanded row goes stale while it is open. It needs the same refresh the pickup screen has.

options.name: One row open at a time
options.rationale: Carbon's accordion rule applied to the table: opening a row closes the last one. The list never grows past one detail, so the reader cannot lose their place in it.
options.cost: Comparing two orders means opening, memorizing, closing and opening. The rule trades comparison for tidiness.

options.name: An expand-all control above the table
options.rationale: GOV.UK's accordion pairs every toggle with a Show all control, so a reader checking every order's lines presses once instead of twenty-five times.
options.cost: Twenty expanded rows is a page nobody can scan, and each detail needs its own data, so Show all fires twenty-five reads at once.

options.name: No expansion: the row opens the record
options.rationale: The order number is a link and everything lives on the record page. One pattern for detail everywhere, and the list stays a list.
options.cost: Every question costs a page load and a back button. Checking three orders means six page loads where expansion needs none.

compact.behaviour: The recommended option reflows: one column, header actions under the title, and a table scrolls inside its own region.

patterns.assessment: The pick is (a), expansion to the order lines: it answers what the customer bought, which is the question asked from the list. The runner-up is (c), units with pickup state, on the pickup list where handover is the work. Never ship (e), expand-all: twenty expanded rows is a page nobody can scan, and the control exists to punish curiosity.

patterns.title: Pinned and resizing columns
patterns.question: A wide table scrolls, and a scrolling table loses its bearings: the order code leaves just when the money arrives. Pinning the identity column keeps the row named, and resizing lets the reader spend width where their own data needs it.

options.name: The order column pinned while the rest scroll
options.rationale: Shopify's orders index pins the order column and lets the other seven scroll under it. Nothing is folded, so every fact keeps its own scannable column.
options.cost: On a phone the reader sees the order code and one other column at a time. Pinning keeps the bearings, not the overview.

options.name: First and last pinned, actions always visible
options.rationale: Airtable pins the record name on the left and the row commands on the right, so both survive any scroll position. Acting never requires scrolling back.
options.cost: Two pinned columns on a phone leave no room for the middle at all. The pattern needs a wide screen to earn its keep.

options.name: Draggable widths with resize handles
options.rationale: Airtable and Retool put a handle on every header edge: drag it and the column follows. A reader with long delivery names spends width there instead of on the order code.
options.cost: Widths are per-user stored state that support cannot see, screenshots cannot hold, and a new column resets. A wide table of eight resizable columns is also eight ways to break the layout.

options.name: Pin any column from its header menu
options.rationale: Notion lets any column pin left from its header menu, drawn open here on Customer. The reader decides what their bearings are instead of the back office deciding for them.
options.cost: Pinning plus hiding plus sorting in one menu is three features wearing one trigger. Most readers find none of them.

options.name: No pinning: the table scrolls as one
options.rationale: Carbon's default: the table scrolls as one piece and every column leaves together. No sticky edges, no shadows, no special cases in the CSS.
options.cost: Halfway across, the money column arrives and the order code is gone. The reader scrolls back to check which row the amount belongs to.

options.name: Double-click a header edge to fit content
options.rationale: Google Sheets fits a column to its widest value on a double-click of the header edge. No dragging, no stored widths: the table answers the data it holds right now.
options.cost: Nobody discovers a double-click on a header edge without being told, and fitting to content reintroduces the page-2 shift that fixed widths prevent.

compact.behaviour: The recommended option reflows: one column, header actions under the title, and a table scrolls inside its own region.

patterns.assessment: The pick is (a), the order column pinned while the rest scroll: the row stays named at any scroll position, and it costs no control. The runner-up is (b), the actions pinned too, once rows carry inline commands that must stay reachable. Never ship (c), draggable widths, in a first release: per-user widths are stored state that support cannot see and screenshots cannot hold.

patterns.title: Deliveries as a grid
patterns.question: Deliveries are few and dated: the company runs a handful a week and asks how each one is doing. A table answers with rows of numbers, while a card answers with the run itself: its date, its warehouse, and how full it is.

options.name: Delivery cards with a load bar
options.rationale: Each delivery is a card with its date, its warehouse and how full it is. Four deliveries a week read as four runs, not as four rows of a table.
options.cost: Cards stop scanning past a dozen deliveries: no column to sort, no state to scan down. The pattern fits a handful, not a hundred.

options.name: A table with a load progress column
options.rationale: Shopify's product list keeps the table and adds an inventory bar per row. The deliveries stay sortable and comparable, and the bar still answers how full each one is.
options.cost: A bar in a table row is a chart without an axis: 80 percent of 40 pallets and 53 percent of 60 pallets read as two bars of different lengths for different totals.

options.name: A date-led list with month dividers
options.rationale: Google Calendar's schedule view leads with the date and groups by month. A planner reads October, then December, then March, each run under its own day.
options.cost: Dates lead and states follow, so finding the one draft means reading every month. The view answers when, not what needs work.

options.name: A month calendar with delivery chips
options.rationale: Google Calendar draws the month as a grid and each delivery as a chip on its day. Clashes show as two chips on one square, which no list makes visible.
options.cost: Four deliveries on thirty squares is mostly empty grid, and nothing on a chip says how full the run is. The calendar answers scheduling, not loading.

options.name: Compact rows with a status word
options.rationale: Linear's project list is one quiet row per project: name, owner, status, date. A team holding forty runs scans states down one column instead of opening forty cards.
options.cost: Quiet rows hide the load: nothing says how full a run is until it is opened. The list answers state, not loading.

options.name: A table/grid toggle the reader sets
options.rationale: Notion lets the reader switch a view between table and board without leaving the page. Finance keeps the table, the warehouse lead keeps the cards, and both read the same deliveries.
options.cost: Two views of one list is two layouts to build, two to test, and a toggle whose state must survive reloads and shared links.

compact.behaviour: The recommended option reflows: one column, header actions under the title, and a table scrolls inside its own region.

patterns.assessment: The pick is (a), delivery cards with a load bar: four deliveries read better as four cards than as four rows, and the bar answers the only question the list exists for. The runner-up is (c), a date-led list, once the year holds dozens of runs and cards stop fitting. Never ship (d), the month calendar: it answers when, which the deliveries list is never asked.

patterns.title: The list on a phone
patterns.question: At 390 pixels the five-column table cannot survive: the columns either crush or scroll. Every option here answers the same question, what the orders list becomes on a phone, and each one keeps a different capability: reading, sorting, acting, or comparing.

options.name: Two-line rows with money right
options.rationale: Stripe's mobile list and Polaris condensed rows read as order over customer on the left, money over state on the right. Everything fits 390 pixels with nothing scrolling sideways.
options.cost: No headers, so no sorting and no comparison down a column. Sorting moves to a control, and comparing moves to the desktop.

options.name: Stacked records with labelled cells
options.rationale: GOV.UK's responsive tables stack each row into labelled values on a narrow screen. Nothing is dropped and nothing needs discovering: every fact keeps its name.
options.cost: One order fills the screen, so six orders is six screens of scrolling. Thorough, and too long to scan.

options.name: A scroll container with a sticky first column
options.rationale: Shopify's mobile tables keep every column and scroll sideways under a pinned first column. Nothing is redesigned for the phone: the table is the table, with its bearings kept.
options.cost: Sideways scrolling hides four of five columns at any moment, and comparing two columns means scrolling between them. The phone shows a window, not the list.

options.name: Priority columns only
options.rationale: Financial tables keep customer, state and money on a narrow screen and drop the rest. Three columns fit 390 pixels without scrolling, and opening the row recovers the dropped facts.
options.cost: The order code, the placed time and the delivery all leave. Support identifying a caller by code finds the one column they need is gone.

options.name: A card per order with its actions
options.rationale: Mobile order apps draw each order as a card with its own Resend button. The phone is for acting on one order, not for comparing twenty, so each card carries its command.
options.cost: Cards are tall: three orders fill the screen where rows fit six. A queue worked top to bottom becomes twice the scrolling.

options.name: Search and chips above one-line rows
options.rationale: Gmail's mobile list leads with search and a chip row, then one line per message. Finding beats browsing on a phone, so the list spends its width on the query, not the columns.
options.cost: One line per order holds the customer or the code, never both with the money. The row identifies just enough to be opened, nothing more.

compact.behaviour: Below 640 pixels the table becomes two-line rows with the amount right; sorting moves to a Sort control.

patterns.assessment: The pick is (a), two-line rows with money right: it reads well at 390 pixels, keeps the order code, the customer and the amount, and pairs with a Sort control where sorting matters. The runner-up is (c), a scroll container with a sticky first column, for the rare phone task that needs every column. Never ship (f), search hiding the list: a list that starts empty teaches the reader there is nothing to see.

patterns.title: The record header
patterns.question: One record, stated at the top. Polaris's rule is precise: always a title, always a breadcrumb when there is a parent, exactly one primary action, with everything else secondary beside it. The order page follows all three; the product page puts a destructive action where the primary should be.

options.name: Title, state, breadcrumb, one primary action
options.rationale: The order header, and the shape Polaris describes. The state badge sits beside the title so the record's state is read before anything else.
options.cost: Two actions of the same weight beside the primary, and the destructive one is in the same visual group as a harmless one unless the tone separates them.

options.name: Title and state only, no description
options.rationale: The heading and its state, and nothing between them and the content. The trail already says where the record is, so the description repeats it.
options.cost: A record with a long name or a subtle state loses the one line that says which delivery this order belongs to, which is the most-asked question.

options.name: State as a badge under the title
options.rationale: The state on its own line under the heading rather than inline with it, which lets a long record name wrap without dragging the badge down with it.
options.cost: Two lines where one would do, and the badge is below the fold on a long title. Polaris puts the state in the title metadata slot, which is the inline arrangement.

options.name: Destructive action in its own place, separated
options.rationale: The product header puts Discontinue immediately beside Pause sales, both in the header. Separating the destructive one into a row menu or a lower group keeps the primary slot for the reversible command.
options.cost: A destructive action behind a menu is three clicks from a misclick, which is the other failure. Tone plus position is the usual answer, and neither is complete alone.

options.name: Facts in the header, commands beside them
options.rationale: The record's own values sit in the header as a definition list, so a reader never scrolls to learn what they are looking at. The commands stack beside it.
options.cost: A tall header pushes the content below the fold on a phone, and a four-fact list competes with the trail for the same vertical space.

options.name: No title, because the trail is the title
options.rationale: The breadcrumb names the record and the page opens straight into its sections. The largest possible use of the space goes to the content.
options.cost: Fails WCAG 2.4.8 Location in spirit and reads as a bare panel. Every page carries exactly one h1, which automated checks enforce, so this fails that check.

options.name: Title, state, and who saved it last
options.rationale: Fewer overwrite conflicts. Support and finance share an order, so the header says who touched it last and when before anyone acts on it. A reader who sees Priya Shah saved at 09:34 asks before saving over her.
options.cost: One more line in the header on every record, and it is only honest if the data tracks the last writer. On records nobody shares it is noise.

options.name: One primary, the rest in an overflow menu
options.rationale: Stripe draws one primary action on a charge and folds the rest behind an overflow menu, so the header stays one line however many commands a record gains. Resend, refund and export all fit without a second row of buttons.
options.cost: Secondary commands are a click further away, and a reader cannot tell what the menu holds without opening it. The menu also needs its items ordered by frequency, which is a judgment per record.

options.name: The primary follows the state
options.rationale: Shopify changes the order page's primary action with the order's state, so the next step is always the button. An unpaid order offers Record a payment; a paid one offers Message customer; a disputed one offers Answer the bank.
options.cost: The primary moves meaning between visits, so a reader who learned its place has to read its label every time. Every state needs its own chosen next step, which is a decision per record type.

compact.behaviour: The recommended option reflows: one column, header actions under the title, and a table scrolls inside its own region.

patterns.assessment: Keep the title, state, breadcrumb and one primary action: it is the Polaris shape and the state beside the title answers the first question on every record. The runner-up is the overflow-menu option, which is the better choice once a record carries four or more commands. Prefer the state-driven primary on records with a clear next step, such as an unpaid order. Never ship the title-less option: it fails the check for exactly one h1 per page.

patterns.title: Tabs on a record
patterns.question: Records hold at most three sections, and more facets become tabs. The product page carries four: Pricing, Availability, Returns, Details. Carbon and GOV.UK both cap tabs at about six and require the tab state in the URL.

options.name: Four tabs with the active one in the URL
options.rationale: Four facets in tabs, which is inside the six every cited system allows. GOV.UK also asks for a heading inside each panel repeating the tab label, which the Details tab does.
options.cost: A reader cannot see two facets at once, and GOV.UK says tabs are the wrong choice when comparing across facets is the job.

options.name: Three tabs, the fourth becomes a page
options.rationale: Hold the ceiling at three facets in tabs and push the fourth to its own route. Every cited system treats six as the ceiling; holding to three is the same discipline applied earlier.
options.cost: One more navigation step for the reader who wants details, and a fourth page in a system that already counts its routes in the hundreds.

options.name: Tabs with counts
options.rationale: Each tab carries the number of things in it, so a reader knows whether a facet is worth opening before opening it. Four tabs where one holds three and another holds none.
options.cost: Counts on tabs are a claim that has to stay true, and a count of 0 invites a click that leads to an empty state.

options.name: Tabs with icons as well as words
options.rationale: An icon per tab so the row is scannable without reading, with the words still present for anyone who does not recognise the icons.
options.cost: Carbon's tab guidance is explicit that icons are not permitted in tab labels. Two channels for one thing, and a second set of icons to design and maintain.

options.name: Scrollable tabs with a fade at the edge
options.rationale: Where a record genuinely needs six facets, the row scrolls horizontally with a fade at the edge so the reader knows there is more. Useful on a phone, where four tabs wrap.
options.cost: A hidden seventh tab is a hidden feature, and a horizontal scroll on a page hides content from anyone who never swipes.

options.name: Tabs below the summary, not below the header
options.rationale: The summary stays visible above the tab row, so a reader always knows which record they are on and what state it is in, whichever facet is open.
options.cost: The tab row moves down the page, so it is less prominent, and the summary has to be short or the tabs fall below the fold.

options.name: Facets in a side rail instead of tabs
options.rationale: GitHub draws repository settings as a side rail of links rather than a tab row, which holds a dozen facets without scrolling and keeps the panel wide enough for a form. The current facet reads as selected in the rail, and each facet keeps its own URL.
options.cost: The rail takes about 200 px from every facet at desktop width, and on a phone it has to become a select or stack above the panel, which is a second arrangement to keep true.

options.name: A select on a phone, tabs on a wide screen
options.rationale: Polaris collapses its tab row into a select on narrow screens, so four facets fit a 390 px viewport without scrolling or wrapping. The control names the current facet and opens the same panels the tabs open.
options.cost: Two controls for one choice, so the tab state and the select state have to stay in agreement. A reader on a phone also cannot see the other facets without opening the control.

compact.behaviour: Below the md breakpoint the tab row becomes a select naming the current facet; the panels stay the same.

patterns.assessment: Keep the four tabs with the active one in the URL: four is inside every cited ceiling and the repeat of the label as a panel heading answers GOV.UK. The runner-up is the side-rail option, which is the better choice past five facets or where one facet is a long form. Prefer the counts option only where a facet can be empty and the count saves a wasted click. Never ship the icon tabs: Carbon forbids icons in tab labels and the icons add a second channel for one meaning.

patterns.title: The summary
patterns.question: The section at the top of a record that answers 'what am I looking at' without scrolling. It states the record's identity: a summary that states supporting information, such as the customer's details, answers the wrong question.

options.name: Facts about the record itself
options.rationale: The summary holds the facts that define this record: its date, its place, its state, what it holds. Everything else is a section below it.
options.cost: Repeats what the header already says, since the header carries the title and state. Saying a thing twice is what the design contract forbids.

options.name: One line of key values, no heading
options.rationale: A single row of label and value pairs with no Section around it, because a summary is not a block of content, it is a restatement of the heading.
options.cost: Breaks the rule that a Section is the only box, because the values would float on the canvas with nothing holding them together visually.

options.name: Money summary as a statement
options.rationale: Where the record is a settlement, the summary is a statement: what came in, what went out, what is left. It adds up top to bottom, which is what the reader came for.
options.cost: Wrong for a record with no money, and a statement is longer than a summary ought to be, so it pushes the sections down.

options.name: Summary with a figure and a sub-line each
options.rationale: Each fact carries a figure and a quieter line under it, as a figure row with a sub-line. A count beside its unit, a money figure beside what it is.
options.cost: A figure and a sub-line per fact needs three columns or a very wide row, and the sub-lines repeat the label's meaning in more words.

options.name: Summary with a progress bar for the one number that matters
options.rationale: One number, 'pallets left', carries a bar and a count. Everything else is plain text, because one figure is worth watching and four are not.
options.cost: Choosing which number matters is a judgment the data has to support, and a bar on a capacity figure implies a ratio that stops mattering once loading is over.

options.name: No summary, straight to sections
options.rationale: The header already states the record and its state, so the summary is dropped. Every fact appears once, in the section it belongs to.
options.cost: The reader scrolls to learn what the record is. For a long record that is a real cost, and the record-page shape reserves a summary slot for exactly this reason.

options.name: Facts plus copyable identifiers
options.rationale: Stripe puts a copy button beside every identifier on a charge, because support reads a reference out on the phone or pastes it into a dispute. The human facts stay plain text; the order number, payment reference and customer email copy with one click.
options.cost: A copy button per row is visual noise on a record nobody quotes, and each button needs its copied confirmation, which is a small behaviour per row.

options.name: Four tiles instead of a section
options.rationale: Vercel opens a project on four stat tiles, because four figures side by side compare at a glance where a fact list reads line by line. Loaded, left, money so far and days to dispatch are the four the company checks each morning.
options.cost: Tiles carry figures, not sentences, so anything that needs a qualifier does not fit. A tile row also answers nothing about who or where, so the facts still need a home below it.

compact.behaviour: The recommended option reflows: one column, header actions under the title, and a table scrolls inside its own region.

patterns.assessment: Keep the facts about the record itself: the delivery summary states when, where and how full, which is the identity of the record rather than its support. The runner-up is the copyable-identifiers option, which is the better choice on records a reader quotes elsewhere, such as an order read out on the phone. Prefer the progress-bar summary only for the one figure the company watches daily. Never ship the heading-less value row: values with no section break the rule that a section is the only box.

patterns.title: The aside
patterns.question: The record page has an aside slot for what supports the record rather than describing it. The order page puts its history there, which is the right use; the parcel page puts nothing there at all.

options.name: History in the aside, sections in the main column
options.rationale: History supports the order without describing it, and it reads top to bottom beside the facts. On a wide screen it is a narrow column; below that it stacks under the sections.
options.cost: Below about 1000 pixels the aside stacks under everything, so the history a reader most wants lands after the sections they came to use.

options.name: Aside for what needs a decision
options.rationale: The aside holds the things that need the reader: a pending decision, a clock, a mismatch. History moves into a tab, because a list of past activity is rarely the reason to open a record.
options.cost: The aside becomes a work panel, which changes what the page is. An order with nothing pending has an empty aside, which is its own awkward state.

options.name: No aside, sections fill the width
options.rationale: The main column takes everything. Sections side by side where there are two that fit.
options.cost: A two-line fact list stretched across 1200 pixels is a very long measure for a name and an email, and the history loses its association with the record.

options.name: Aside sticky, main column scrolls
options.rationale: The aside stays in place while the sections scroll, so a decision in the aside is always reachable from anywhere on a long record.
options.cost: A sticky aside on a phone is a stacked block that no longer sticks, so the behaviour has two shapes and one of them is untested in practice.

options.name: Aside for related records
options.rationale: The aside holds what relates to this record but is not part of it: the delivery it ships with, the other lines on it, the messages it has had.
options.cost: Related records are what a reader navigates to, so putting them in the narrowest column makes them the least likely to be found.

options.name: Aside collapses to a section on narrow screens
options.rationale: The same content, ordered so the aside's sections come first in the DOM. A reader on a phone reads history before the lines list rather than after it.
options.cost: Two different orders for one record, so a screenshot test holds two arrangements. The DOM order and the visual order disagree, which is also an accessibility question.

options.name: People and labels in the aside, history below
options.rationale: Linear puts assignee, state, labels and dates in the issue sidebar, because a record a team hands between shifts needs its ownership beside its facts. Alex Morgan sees at a glance that this order waits for Priya Shah under the label refund-check, and the history still reads below the handover.
options.cost: Ownership fields need data that tracks them, and on records one person owns end to end they repeat what the team already knows. The aside also grows long once labels, dates and watchers all claim a row.

options.name: Related records and history share the aside
options.rationale: HubSpot draws associated records and the activity timeline in one right rail, so the aside answers both who this record touches and what happened to it. The delivery, the other order from this customer and the messages sit above a short history with a link to the rest.
options.cost: Two different jobs in one column, so neither gets the width it wants. Related records compete with history for the top of the aside, and the loser sits below the fold on a short viewport.

compact.behaviour: Below the md breakpoint the aside stacks as sections under the header, with history first.

patterns.assessment: Give the pick to history in the aside: history supports the order without describing it, which is exactly what the aside slot is for. The runner-up is the decision panel, which is the better choice on records that wait for someone, such as a dispute with a deadline. Prefer the people-and-labels aside on records a team hands between shifts. Never ship the empty aside state by accident: an order with nothing pending and no history reads as a rendering fault.

patterns.title: The record timeline
patterns.question: What happened to one record. The evidence is consistent: newest first, always a timestamp, always a byline, because the question the reader has is who did this and when. Sublabels matter more than labels for attribution.

options.name: Newest first with actor and timestamp
options.rationale: Newest first, each entry a plain-verb title with a byline and a timestamp, one deep link at most: the shape Maersk and Paste both describe.
options.cost: A long history has to be paginated or collapsed. Maersk collapses descriptions behind a toggle, which this does not.

options.name: A table instead of a timeline
options.rationale: When the history is the record rather than context, a table is denser and sortable: when, who, what, with an amount column when money moved.
options.cost: Gives up the shape of a sequence for a grid of facts. A reader asking 'what happened in order' has to read down a table, which is slower than a timeline.

options.name: Grouped by day with a date label
options.rationale: Where entries cluster, a date heading above each group saves repeating the date on every line and makes the shape of the day obvious.
options.cost: More markup for the same information, and a reader scanning for one entry has to look under the right date heading.

options.name: Collapsed descriptions behind a toggle
options.rationale: Maersk's approach: title and byline always, description behind a show-details toggle. Keeps a fifty-entry history to fifty lines.
options.cost: The description is where the evidence lives for a dispute, so hiding it by default hides what a support reader came for.

options.name: Grouped by actor, for an audit question
options.rationale: When the question is 'who touched this', the timeline is grouped by person. Each person carries their own list, newest first within it.
options.cost: Destroys chronological order, which is the order a timeline exists to give. A person touching a record five times over a month reads as one entry.

options.name: Timeline with a 'what changed' diff on each entry
options.rationale: Each entry names what it changed, so the history answers what the record looks like now as well as how it got here. This is what an audit register carries.
options.cost: A diff needs the before and after, so it has to be reconstructed at read time rather than read from the entry that recorded the change.

options.name: Filtered by kind and actor
options.rationale: GitHub lets a reader filter an issue timeline to comments, commits or references, because a long record mixes kinds and the reader usually wants one. The filters sit above the timeline and the count beside each says what choosing it keeps.
options.cost: A filtered timeline hides entries without saying which, so a reader can miss the one line that mattered. The filter state also needs a reset that is always visible, or the hiding looks like absence.

options.name: Entries and internal notes in one feed
options.rationale: Zendesk draws notes and entries in one order feed, newest last, because support reads what the team said beside what the system did. A note Jordan Lee wrote at 11:18 sits between the resend it explains and the payment it followed.
options.cost: Notes and entries compete for the same line height, so the feed grows long faster than either would alone. A reader who wants only the system's facts has to skip the team's words, and there is no filter on this option.

compact.behaviour: The recommended option reflows: one column, header actions under the title, and a table scrolls inside its own region.

patterns.assessment: Keep the newest-first timeline with actor and timestamp: it is the shape Maersk and Paste both describe and it answers who and when on every line. The runner-up is the filtered timeline, which is the better choice once a record carries dozens of entries across kinds. Prefer the day-grouped option for dispatch records, where entries cluster on one morning. Never ship the actor-grouped timeline as the main history: it destroys the chronological order a timeline exists to give.

patterns.title: Records related to this one
patterns.question: An order belongs to a delivery, a customer and a channel; a delivery belongs to a warehouse and a schedule. The order record states the delivery in prose in its description rather than linking to it.

options.name: Each relation is a link with its state
options.rationale: The delivery, the customer and the channel appear as links carrying their own state, so a reader can jump and knows what they will find. Nothing here is prose.
options.cost: Three links is a small nav of its own, and it competes with the record's own commands for the reader's attention.

options.name: A breadcrumb as the relation chain
options.rationale: The trail itself is the relation chain: delivery, then order. Nothing repeats it, which is the design contract's strongest single rule.
options.cost: The trail cannot carry state, so a reader cannot tell a scheduled delivery from a finished one without opening it.

options.name: A section of other orders on the same delivery
options.rationale: The related record is the other orders, as a short list with the money beside each. Answers 'who else is on this delivery' without leaving.
options.cost: Anywhere between one and two hundred rows, which is a table with a limit rather than a section. The money page already splits it by delivery for this reason.

options.name: A cross-reference line, not a section
options.rationale: One line under the heading naming the parent record as a link. The smallest possible way to say where this record belongs, and nothing more.
options.cost: Invisible to anyone who does not read descriptions, and it cannot carry the parent's state, so the reader has to open it to learn whether it is still live.

options.name: A count that links to the filtered list
options.rationale: '2 parcels on this order' links to the parcels list filtered to this order, so the relation is navigable in both directions and the count is never stale.
options.cost: A link whose text is a number reads as a figure, not a destination, unless the hover and the visited colour make it clear. WCAG 2.4.4 wants the purpose to be clear from the link text.

options.name: The parent as a card above the record's own sections
options.rationale: The parent record opens in a card at the top with its own state and its commands, so a reader acting on the child can act on the parent without navigating.
options.cost: A box inside the page above the sections, which is the nesting the design contract forbids, and it makes the child look secondary when it is the page.

options.name: Links with a preview of the parent
options.rationale: Notion shows a preview of a linked page on hover, because the reader usually wants one fact from the parent rather than the parent itself. The delivery row expands to its date, place and state inline, so a reader checking a parcel learns the dispatch window without navigating.
options.cost: A preview is a second rendering of the parent to keep true, and only one row can be open at a time before the section doubles in height. It also answers nothing about children, which still need the list.

options.name: Children as an editable table
options.rationale: Airtable draws linked records as rows that can be added and removed in place, because the relation itself is the work. The variants of a product gain a row each with their price and stock count, and the section holds the Add control rather than sending the reader elsewhere.
options.cost: Editing inside a section blurs reading and writing: every row needs its own validation and refusal states. It also fits only children with few columns; a wide child still wants its own page.

compact.behaviour: The recommended option reflows: one column, header actions under the title, and a table scrolls inside its own region.

patterns.assessment: Ship the link-with-state list: each relation is a link carrying its own state, so a reader can jump and knows what they will find. The runner-up is the preview-card option, which is the better choice where the parent's facts decide the next step, such as a parcel read against its delivery. Prefer the filtered-list counts on records whose children number in the hundreds. Never ship the bare cross-reference line: it cannot carry the parent's state and it hides in the description.

patterns.title: A record the reader may not act on
patterns.question: A refused state exists, and the guidance says a page a role cannot use shows it with the reason and the grant that helps. The question is whether that is a whole page or a part of one.

options.name: The commands are refused, the record is not
options.rationale: Warehouse staff can read an order and cannot refund it. The page shows everything and refuses only the commands, naming the grant that would allow each one. This is an explained action: a disabled button with its reason beside it.
options.cost: A page full of refused commands is a page that looks broken to someone who does not know what their role is.

options.name: The whole page is refused
options.rationale: The record itself is out of the reader's reach, not just its commands. A refused state replaces the page body and names the grant.
options.cost: Nothing is shown, so a warehouse lead cannot read a customer's name to answer a question at the counter. That is a real cost on the surface where names matter most.

options.name: A banner above the page, the record still readable
options.rationale: A page-level notice says what this role may not do on this page, once, and the sections below stay readable. The reader is told rather than blocked.
options.cost: A full-width band on a page about other work breaks the rule that tone marks content, not chrome, so this has to be a neutral notice, not a caution one.

options.name: The command is absent, not refused
options.rationale: A command the role does not have is not drawn at all. The guidance is that a tab or link appears only for a viewer who may open its page, extended to buttons.
options.cost: Nothing tells the reader the capability exists elsewhere, so they cannot find out who can do it. On a page of four commands, three of them missing looks like a broken deployment.

options.name: Personal data withheld field by field
options.rationale: The order stays readable and only the customer's personal data is withheld, each field saying so where the value would be. The server never sends the value, so nothing is merely hidden. The header offers the one step that would change it.
options.cost: Every personal field needs a withheld form, and a reader sees that a value exists without seeing it. A caution alert on top of that repeats what the fields already say.

options.name: A role switcher rather than a refusal
options.rationale: The development persona menu already lets a staff member act as somebody else. A record the role cannot use offers the role that can, in one click, for a deployment being demonstrated.
options.cost: Only honest where acting as somebody is a real capability. On a production deployment with one real account it is a security hole with a nice button on it.

options.name: Ask for access from the refused command
options.rationale: Google Drive turns a refusal into a request: the reader asks, an owner decides, and the decision arrives as a message. A warehouse lead who needs to resend the confirmation asks from the refusal itself instead of finding an owner in a corridor.
options.cost: Every request needs an owner who answers it, and a queue of access requests is a new surface to build and watch. On records where access is never granted it promises a decision that never comes.

options.name: A read-only ribbon naming what the role can do
options.rationale: Figma tells a view-only reader exactly that, in a ribbon above the canvas, and lists what the role can still do. The ribbon here says the warehouse role reads orders and scans parcels, so the reader knows their reach before they reach past it.
options.cost: A ribbon on every page a role cannot fully use is a ribbon on most pages for the narrowest roles. It also states the role's reach in words the data has to keep true per page.

compact.behaviour: The recommended option reflows: one column, header actions under the title, and a table scrolls inside its own region.

patterns.assessment: Keep the refused commands on a readable record: warehouse staff can read an order and cannot refund it, and each refusal names the grant that would allow it. The runner-up is the ask-for-access option, which is the better choice where access is routinely granted, such as a seasonal worker joining support. Prefer the field-withheld option only where the values themselves are restricted, such as customer personal data under a warehouse role. Never ship the role switcher on production: acting as somebody is a development capability, and the button would be a security hole with a label on it.

patterns.title: Who changed the record
patterns.question: One order or one delivery is touched by several people before the week is over: the customer corrects an email, the manager answers, finance adds a note. When the customer disputes what happened, the company answers from the record itself, naming who did what and when. The audit trail is that answer, read beside the facts it explains rather than in a log elsewhere.

options.name: History as a tab on the record
options.rationale: The audit sits beside Details and Payment as one more facet, so the record keeps one route and the tab state stays in the URL the way record tabs do. A reader checking a claim opens History without losing the order.
options.cost: The trail is hidden until its tab opens, and facts cannot be compared against the trail without switching back and forth.

options.name: History in a side panel beside the summary
options.rationale: Facts and history read side by side, so Alex Morgan sees the email and who corrected it in one glance. Nothing is behind a tab.
options.cost: Each column is half the width, so long entries wrap, and on a narrow screen the panel stacks below the facts it explains.

options.name: Full-page audit log with filters
options.rationale: Every change on one scrolling page with actor and kind filters, which suits a long-lived delivery whose trail outgrows a tab. Filters answer whose changes these are without reading them all.
options.cost: The trail leaves the record it explains, so the reader holds the facts in memory, and the filters need data support for actor and kind.

options.name: Last change line with an expander
options.rationale: One line answers the common question, who touched this last, and the expander reveals the rest without a new route. The record stays short.
options.cost: Older changes stay hidden behind a click, and the expander state is not shareable, so two people cannot point at the same open trail.

options.name: Money movements only
options.rationale: Finance sees only the movements of money, each tied to its amount, without the operational edits around them. The lines add up top to bottom.
options.cost: The edits that explain the money are missing, so a corrected email before a resend reads as a gap, and there are two histories to keep true.

options.name: Exportable trail for disputes
options.rationale: The trail downloads exactly as it reads, with actor and time on every line, so Priya Shah can attach it to a dispute reply. What the screen states and what the file carries are one thing.
options.cost: The download freezes wording that a later correction invalidates, and the file format becomes a contract the data has to keep stable.

options.name: Per-field history beside the facts
options.rationale: Google Sheets shows the edit history of one cell, because a dispute is usually about one value rather than the whole record. Each fact carries its own changed-by line, so the email row says Maria Garcia corrected it at 10:51 without opening a trail.
options.cost: Every fact doubles in height, so a long summary becomes a long read. Fields that never change carry a line saying so, which is honest but heavy.

options.name: Two versions side by side
options.rationale: Wikipedia compares two revisions column to column with the changed lines marked, because a dispute names a moment and asks what changed then. The order as Maria placed it sits beside the order as it reads now, and only the email row is marked.
options.cost: Two columns halve the width each version gets, so long values wrap or clip on a phone. Picking the two moments to compare is also a control of its own, with its own state.

compact.behaviour: The recommended option reflows: one column, header actions under the title, and a table scrolls inside its own region.

patterns.assessment: Ship the history tab on the record: it keeps one route, the tab state stays in the URL, and a reader checking a claim opens History without losing the order. The runner-up is the per-field history, which is the better choice where one value is disputed, such as the email the confirmation went to. Prefer the full-page log only for long-lived records whose trail outgrows a tab. Never ship the money-only trail as the audit: the edits that explain the money are missing and there are two histories to keep true.

patterns.title: Notes on a record
patterns.question: Support and finance think on the record, not beside it: why the confirmation was resent, what the customer was told, what still waits. A note is staff writing with a byline and a time, and the reader must always know whether the customer can see it.

options.name: A notes section with the composer on top
options.rationale: Shopify draws order notes as a timeline with the composer at the top, newest first. The writer sees what was already said before adding to it, and every note carries its writer and time.
options.cost: The composer takes the top of the section even when nobody writes, and a long note history pushes the record's own sections down the page.

options.name: Notes mixed into the timeline
options.rationale: Zendesk draws agent notes inside the order feed, because what the team wrote explains what the system did next. The resend at 11:20 reads directly under the note that caused it.
options.cost: Notes and system entries compete for attention in one feed, so a reader who wants only the facts has to skip the team's words. Long notes also stretch a feed meant for short lines.

options.name: Internal or customer-visible, chosen per note
options.rationale: Zendesk splits its composer into internal note and public reply, because staff write both from the same record and the wrong scope is a real failure. The scope toggle sits on the composer and every note keeps its marker.
options.cost: Two scopes double the reading of every note, and a customer-visible note needs the message pipeline behind it rather than a plain save. The toggle is also one more control to misread in a hurry.

options.name: Resolved notes collapse away
options.rationale: Google Docs resolves a comment thread once its question is answered, because an open list grows until nobody reads it. The collection question resolves once the resend lands, leaving only what still waits.
options.cost: Resolving hides the reasoning a later dispute may need, so the resolved list has to stay one click away and stay readable. Somebody also has to do the resolving, which is a habit to build.

options.name: Notes in the aside
options.rationale: Linear keeps comments in the issue's main column and properties in the rail; this option reverses it for records whose facts are the work. Notes sit beside the order so they never push the money down, and the composer stays one line until it opens.
options.cost: A 260 px column is narrow for a paragraph, so notes wrap early and long threads scroll inside a short box. Notes also lose the prominence they need on a support-heavy record.

options.name: No notes yet
options.rationale: Notion draws an empty discussion as an invitation rather than a blank box, because a record nobody has annotated is the common case. The empty state says what notes are for and offers the first one.
options.cost: An empty section takes vertical space on every quiet record to say there is nothing to read. Hiding the section until the first note would save the space but hide the capability.

compact.behaviour: The recommended option reflows: one column, header actions under the title, and a table scrolls inside its own region.

patterns.assessment: Ship the notes section with the composer on top: it matches how Shopify draws order notes, the newest note reads first, and internal scope is the default that cannot leak. The runner-up is the internal-or-customer composer, which is the better choice on records where staff routinely write to the customer from the same box. Prefer resolved-notes only once note volume makes open ones hard to find. Never ship notes without a scope marker: a reader who cannot tell internal from customer-visible will eventually write the wrong one.

patterns.title: Attachments on a record
patterns.question: A dispute needs its evidence, a delivery needs its packing list, a product needs its photos. An attachment is a file the company put on the record, with who added it and when, and the reader must know what each file is before opening it.

options.name: A file list with a drop zone
options.rationale: Linear draws issue attachments as rows with a drop zone beneath, because the list answers what is here and the zone answers how to add. Each row carries the file kind, who added it, when, and the size.
options.cost: Rows give every file equal weight, so a ten-file record reads long. Large files also need an upload state per row, which this option does not draw.

options.name: Compact rows for many files
options.rationale: GitHub lists release assets as compact rows, because a record with a dozen files has to stay scannable. Name, size and a download action fit one line each; who added it moves to the file's own page.
options.cost: Who and when leave the row, so the reader cannot tell a fresh upload from a stale one without opening it. Compact rows also hide the file kind behind the name alone.

options.name: Evidence grouped by what it proves
options.rationale: Stripe asks for dispute evidence by category, because the bank checks kinds rather than files: the receipt, the terms, the proof of fulfilment. Each group says whether it is filled, so Priya Shah sees what is still missing before she answers.
options.cost: The categories belong to card disputes, so the shape fits nothing else without renaming. A file that proves two things also has to sit in two groups or one group has to stay empty.

options.name: The drop zone is the section
options.rationale: Dropbox draws an empty folder as one large drop target, because adding is the only job and the target should be unmissable. The section states what belongs here and takes the file anywhere it lands.
options.cost: Once files exist the large zone wastes the space the list wants, so the shape has to change after the first upload. It also says nothing about what is already there.

options.name: Images as thumbnails, documents as rows
options.rationale: Zendesk draws attached images as thumbnails and documents as rows, because a reader checks a photo by looking and a contract by opening. The thumbnails answer at a glance; the rows answer on click.
options.cost: Two shapes in one section, so the section needs a rule for what is an image and what is not. Thumbnails also cost a render per file that rows never pay.

options.name: No files, and what belongs here
options.rationale: Figma tells an empty project what to put in it, because an empty box without guidance reads as a fault. The section names the kinds that belong on a dispute and offers the upload in the same breath.
options.cost: Guidance text per record type is content to write and keep true. A generic empty state would fit everywhere and help nowhere, which is the worse trade.

compact.behaviour: The recommended option reflows: one column, header actions under the title, and a table scrolls inside its own region.

patterns.assessment: Ship the file list with a drop zone: each row names the file, its kind, who added it and its size, and the drop zone invites the next one. The runner-up is the evidence-grouped option, which is the better choice on a dispute, where the bank asks for kinds rather than files. Prefer thumbnails only where images dominate, such as product photos. Never ship the drop-zone-only section: a record whose files hide behind an upload control reads as empty.

patterns.title: A property list with copy
patterns.question: Support reads a reference out on the phone and pastes an identifier into a dispute. A property list is labelled values where the identifiers copy with one click, and the reader must know the copy landed.

options.name: Every identifier copies
options.rationale: Stripe puts a copy button beside every identifier on a charge, because support quotes references all day. Order number, payment reference, customer email and parcel codes each copy with one click; human facts stay plain.
options.cost: A button per row is noise on records nobody quotes, and each button needs its copied confirmation to be honest. The list also grows long once every identifier claims a row.

options.name: Copy appears on hover only
options.rationale: GitHub shows the copy button on a file path only on hover, because a quiet row reads better and the control appears where the pointer already is. The list stays a clean two columns until the reader reaches for a value.
options.cost: Touch screens have no hover, so on a phone the button never appears and the pattern fails where warehouse staff work. Keyboard readers also have to tab into a row to find a control they cannot see.

options.name: Identifiers grouped in one card
options.rationale: Vercel groups a deployment's identifiers in one card apart from its facts, because identifiers are quoted together: the id, the reference and the address leave in one message. One card holds all three with their copy buttons.
options.cost: The identifiers leave the facts they belong to, so the reader jumps between the summary and the card to connect a value with its meaning. A second card is also a second heading for the same record.

options.name: Copied confirmation in place
options.rationale: Railway confirms a copy inside the row that was copied, because a toast at the edge of the screen is easy to miss while reading a reference aloud. The button turns into a check beside the value for two seconds.
options.cost: The row changes shape for two seconds, which shifts the rows below it unless the confirmation holds the button's width. It also confirms only the click, not that the paste landed where it should.

options.name: Long values truncate with expand
options.rationale: Sentry truncates long identifiers to one line with an expander, because a receipt URL or a full address would otherwise push the copy button off the row. The row stays one line; the full value opens on demand and still copies whole.
options.cost: A truncated value cannot be checked by eye until it expands, so a reader comparing two long codes opens both. The expander is also one more control per long row.

options.name: Stacked on a phone
options.rationale: Polaris stacks a description list on narrow screens, because three columns cannot fit 390 px. The label sits above its value and the copy button stays beside the value, so the thumb reaches it without scrolling sideways.
options.cost: A five-row list becomes five blocks, so the section doubles in height on the smallest screen. Labels above values also read slower than labels beside them.

compact.behaviour: Below the sm breakpoint each row stacks: the label above its value, the copy button beside the value.

patterns.assessment: Ship the always-visible copy button per identifier: it matches how Stripe draws charge details, and support reaches for it without hunting. The runner-up is the in-place confirmation option, which is the better choice once miscopied references cause real mistakes. Prefer hover-only copy nowhere: touch screens have no hover and the button would never appear. Never ship a property list whose long values clip without a way to expand them.

patterns.title: The record header on a phone
patterns.question: Warehouse staff read records on a phone at the dock, 390 px wide, one hand free. The header must state which record, what state, and the one step that matters without scrolling sideways or hiding the title.

options.name: Stacked title, full-width primary, the rest in a menu
options.rationale: shadcn dashboard pages stack the header actions under the title below the sm breakpoint, with the primary first and full width. The title and state read first; the thumb finds one large button; rarer commands wait behind the menu.
options.cost: The header grows tall on the smallest screen, so the content starts lower. Secondary commands also hide behind a tap that a hurried reader may not try.

options.name: A sticky action bar at the foot
options.rationale: Shopify pins the order actions to the foot of a phone screen, because the thumb is already there and the step stays reachable mid-scroll. Message and Resend stay pinned while the facts scroll above them.
options.cost: The bar covers content at the foot of every scroll position, so the last section needs padding it would not otherwise need. It also pins two actions that may not be the two this record needs.

options.name: Back chevron and state in the bar
