options.rationale: iOS puts the way back in the navigation bar, because a phone reader arrives from a list and returns to it. The bar carries the chevron and the order number; the page opens straight into the state and the summary.
options.cost: The bar is shared chrome, so a record-specific bar is a second bar to keep true. The breadcrumb also leaves the page, which breaks the trail contract every other page keeps.

options.name: The description folds behind the title
options.rationale: GitHub mobile folds long issue context behind the title, because the title and state are the wayfinding and the rest is detail. One tap opens customer, delivery and placed; until then the header is two lines.
options.cost: The delivery name hides behind a tap on exactly the record type where which-delivery is the most-asked question. A folded header also looks unfinished to a reader who never unfolds it.

options.name: One scrolling row of actions
options.rationale: Material design scrolls a row of action chips under the title, because every action stays visible as a word rather than hiding in a menu. Message, Resend, Refund and Export all fit one swipeable row.
options.cost: A sideways scroll inside a vertical page hides anything past the edge until swiped. Equal chips also give the destructive action the same weight as a harmless one.

options.name: No actions in the header at all
options.rationale: GOV.UK keeps small screens to one purpose per page, so commands live in the sections they belong to rather than crowding the header. The header states the record; Resend sits with the parcels and Refund sits with the money.
options.cost: The most-used command is a scroll away instead of a tap away, and a reader who learned the desktop header finds nothing where the buttons were. Every section also needs its own command row.

compact.behaviour: This item is the compact behaviour: title and state first, a full-width primary under them, rarer commands in a menu.

patterns.assessment: Ship the stacked title with a full-width primary and the rest in a menu: it keeps the desktop order, title then actions, and the primary stays reachable by thumb. The runner-up is the sticky foot bar, which is the better choice on records where the step is taken mid-scroll, such as scanning at the dock. Prefer the scrolling action row only where every action is equally likely. Never ship actions that need sideways scrolling to be discovered: a hidden Refund at the dock is a queue that stops moving.

patterns.title: Moving between records
patterns.question: Support works a queue, not a record: the next order in the list, the next dispute waiting for an answer. Moving on must be one step that keeps the list order, so the reader never returns to the list just to open its neighbour.

options.name: Chevrons beside the breadcrumb
options.rationale: Gmail puts newer and older arrows above a message, because triage is neighbour to neighbour and the list order is the queue. The position reads between the chevrons, so the reader knows where they are.
options.cost: Chevrons move one step at a time, so jumping ten records ahead is ten clicks. They also need the list order behind them, which fails when the record was opened from a search.

options.name: Chevrons in the header with keyboard hints
options.rationale: Gmail teaches j and k beside its arrows, because a triage reader moves faster without the pointer. The header holds previous and next with their keys, and the position reads beside them.
options.cost: Keyboard hints help nobody on a phone, where warehouse staff do this work. The header also gains two buttons that compete with the record's own commands.

options.name: Back to the list, then in again
options.rationale: Polaris moves between products through the list, because the list holds the search and the filters that define the queue. The record carries one way back; the next record opens from the list with its context intact.
options.cost: Two steps per record instead of one, and the list has to hold its scroll and filters across the round trip or the reader loses their place. Triage of fifty orders becomes a hundred navigations.

options.name: A list drawer beside the record
options.rationale: Intercom draws the queue beside the conversation, because triage reads the list and the record together. The drawer lists the queue's orders with their state and money; the record reads to its right.
options.cost: The drawer takes a third of the width at desktop and the whole width on a phone, where it has to become a sheet. It also duplicates the orders list page, so two lists of orders have to stay true.

options.name: Jump to a record by searching
options.rationale: Linear jumps to any issue from its command menu, because a reader who knows the number should not walk the queue to reach it. The order number, customer name or email lands on the record in one step.
options.cost: Search answers only the record the reader already knows, so it never helps triage an unknown queue. It also needs the menu everywhere, which is a frame behaviour rather than a record pattern.

options.name: No movement: each record opens from the list
options.rationale: Some consoles deliberately offer no neighbour step, because the list is the queue and the record is the work. The reader finishes an order, closes it, and the list shows what is next. Nothing on the record can carry a stale position.
options.cost: Every record costs a full round trip through the list, which is slow triage and loses the reader's scroll each time. It is honest but it is the slowest honest option.

compact.behaviour: The recommended option reflows: one column, header actions under the title, and a table scrolls inside its own region.

patterns.assessment: Ship the chevrons beside the breadcrumb: they match how Gmail moves between messages, they keep the list order, and they cost almost no space. The runner-up is the jump-by-search option, which is the better choice once the reader knows the next record's number rather than its neighbour. Prefer the list drawer on triage queues where the reader skims many records. Never ship movement without a position: chevrons that never say 4 of 268 leave the reader lost in the queue.

patterns.title: The order record, whole
patterns.question: The order is the record support opens most: Maria Garcia's SO-1042, EUR 125.00 for two lamps, a delivery fee and a cable tray. It must state its lines, its payments and its refunds in one reading, with the money adding up and every refund drawn against the payment it reverses.

options.name: Summary, three sections, history in the aside
options.rationale: A summary of the order with the customer, the lines and the money beside a history aside. Each facet of SO-1042 has one home and the money adds up top to bottom in its own section.
options.cost: Three sections is a ceiling, so the fourth facet waits for a tab or a second page. The aside also stacks below everything under 900 px, which buries the history on a phone.

options.name: One facet per tab
options.rationale: Shopify draws an order as tabs for timeline, lines and payments, because an order with messages, notes and refunds outgrows three sections. The customer summary stays above the tabs so the record is always identified.
options.cost: Lines and payments can no longer be read together, so checking a refund against its line means switching tabs. The tab state also has to live in the URL to stay shareable.

options.name: One long page, everything in order
options.rationale: Stripe draws a charge as one scrolling page, because support reads top to bottom and prints the page for the file. Customer, lines, payments, refunds and history follow in the order the questions are asked.
options.cost: A long page buries the later sections, so refunds sit below the fold on every order. There is also no shortcut to one facet: the reader scrolls past everything above it.

options.name: Money first
options.rationale: Xero opens an invoice on its money, because finance asks what moved before asking who moved it. Payments and refunds sit directly under the header with the statement adding up, and the customer and lines follow below.
options.cost: Support reads the customer first, so money-first puts their answer second on every call. The money section also repeats the lines it totals, which is the same figure stated twice.

options.name: Customer first
options.rationale: Zendesk opens a case on the requester, because support answers a person rather than a record. The customer card leads with name, contact and order history, and the lines and money read as that customer's story below it.
options.cost: The record's own identity waits behind the customer's, so an order-first reader scrolls past a card they did not open. Customer history on the order also duplicates the customer page.

options.name: The order on a phone
options.rationale: Shopify stacks an order on mobile in the order the questions are asked at the counter: state and customer first, then parcels, then money. One column, full-width primary, nothing beside anything else.
options.cost: Stacking puts the money last, so a refund at the counter is a long scroll away. The history also drops to the foot, where nobody on a phone reads it.

compact.behaviour: On a phone the order stacks in the order the questions are asked at the counter: state and customer first, then parcels, then money.

patterns.assessment: Ship the record-page shape with summary, three sections and history in the aside: it keeps customer, lines and money each in their own section. The runner-up is the money-first layout, which is the better choice for finance readers reconciling payments against refunds. Prefer the tabbed layout only once an order's facets outgrow three sections. Never ship the phone layout as the desktop page: stacked sections at 1440 px waste two thirds of the width.

patterns.title: A money field
patterns.question: The back office holds prices, fees, refunds and settlement figures, and not one of them is the software's to choose. The field is where that rule meets a keyboard. The evidence says: text input with an inputmode, the currency named in the label, and a symbol prefix that is aria-hidden.

options.name: Text input, currency in the label, symbol inside
options.rationale: The HMRC pattern: an aria-hidden prefix inside the field and the currency named in the label, so a screen reader hears the currency even though it does not read the symbol. Not a number input, because GDS rejected type="number" outright.
options.cost: The user can type the symbol into the field, so validation has to accept it rather than refuse it. Two decimal places maximum, per the HMRC pattern.

options.name: Currency as a separate select
options.rationale: The amount and the currency are two inputs, so a company selling in several currencies changes one select rather than retyping an amount.
options.cost: No design system in this set publishes a currency select beside an amount, and the company invoices in one currency. A select for a closed set of one is a control that cannot do anything.

options.name: Amount with a unit suffix, for a count
options.rationale: GOV.UK's suffix pattern, where the unit is a word rather than a symbol: 'per unit', 'per order', 'per pallet'. Reads better than a symbol where the unit is not money.
options.cost: The suffix takes horizontal room in a narrow field, and it cannot carry a currency. Money and a unit would need two suffixes, which no pattern here supports.

options.name: Money with an error that says what to do
options.rationale: The same field in its refused state. The message is GOV.UK's own template, which is why it reads as a specific instruction rather than a rejection.
options.cost: The three states cannot be seen at once, so a reviewer has to be told which one a mock shows. Each mock here is one state.

options.name: Amount with a stepper
options.rationale: A plus and a minus either side of the value, for the case where one amount is overwhelmingly the common one and small deviations are the exception.
options.cost: NN/g and Carbon both warn against a stepper for a price, because a continuous value cannot be reached by stepping and 1.50 units cannot be expressed. Wrong control for this field.

options.name: Money as a read-only fact with an edit command
options.rationale: Once a charge has been priced, it is shown as a figure with one command to change it. The value is never retyped, so a mistyped price cannot become a second record.
options.cost: Editing moves to a second surface for a field the user touches often, and a charge already priced is a versioned fact rather than a field.

options.name: Price with the customer-facing total restated
options.rationale: Clearer money. The user types what the unit costs and reads what the customer pays on the same screen before saving. The EUR 50.00 all-in figure stops the fee from surprising either side at checkout.
options.cost: The restated total must update as the user types, which a static mock cannot show. Costs one line under every price field, even where the fee is zero.

options.name: Gross price with the net and tax restated
options.rationale: Stripe Dashboard restates every gross amount as net plus tax under the field, so the user prices what the customer pays and reads what the company keeps.
options.cost: The restated lines must update as the user types, and the rates come from configuration keyed by date, so a price from January restates with January rates. Costs two lines per field even where the user never looks twice.

options.name: Preset price chips for the common price points
options.rationale: Square and Shopify POS put the common amounts one tap away: most units land on a round price, and typing 45.00 ninety times a year is ninety chances to type 54.00. The field stays for the odd price.
options.cost: The presets are company data that must be learned or configured, and a stale set pushes the user toward last year prices. Five chips plus a field is also wider than a field alone on a phone.

compact.behaviour: The recommended option reflows: one column, header actions under the title, and a table scrolls inside its own region.

patterns.assessment: The HMRC prefix with the currency in the label stays the pick: it reads in both themes, it names the currency to a screen reader, and it refuses nothing the user can type. The customer-total restatement is the runner-up and belongs on every price the customer sees, because it stops the fee from surprising either side. Never ship the stepper: a continuous price cannot be reached by stepping, and 1.50 units cannot be expressed.

patterns.title: Choosing a record
patterns.question: The rule is that a reference to another record is chosen from a picker showing names; nobody types an identifier. The failure to avoid is a select reading 'Choose a warehouse' beside a field holding 'WH-0C893968A2' as if it were a value to type.

options.name: Searchable picker showing names
options.rationale: A search over names, showing nothing else. NN/g's time-zone research is the reason it searches: 44% of first searches were by city and search beat scrolling every time.
options.cost: A picker hides how many records exist, and a user who knows the warehouse is in 'Zaandam' still has to search rather than scan. Needs an empty-result state that offers creating one.

options.name: Picker with the record's facts beside its name
options.rationale: Each option carries the one fact that tells two similar records apart: capacity for a warehouse, date for a delivery, state for a price tier. Two depots both called Rotterdam are told apart by what they hold.
options.cost: A wider list, and the extra column is only useful for records that share a name. For a record set where names are already unique it is noise.

options.name: A select of names
options.rationale: A plain select listing names. Fewer moving parts than a picker, and it works with the keyboard out of the box.
options.cost: GOV.UK's own guidance is to reduce the option count before reaching for a select, because research finds them hard to use, and it forbids pre-selecting an option. A 40-warehouse select is the case that guidance is about.

options.name: A picker whose options are typed
options.rationale: The user types part of a name and the list narrows, but they must choose from the list. APG warns that list autocomplete with automatic selection silently adopts the first suggestion, which stores the wrong record.
options.cost: The field must not commit on blur or on Enter alone, or a mistyped prefix books the wrong warehouse. That is an implementation rule the mock cannot show.

options.name: A read-only reference showing what is linked
options.rationale: On a record rather than a form, the relation is shown as a fact with a command to change it, so the reader sees what is linked without opening a picker.
options.cost: Two steps to change a relation, and on a page with several relations it is several such facts. It belongs on a record page, not on a create form.

options.name: A picker that also creates
options.rationale: The list ends with the command to make the missing record, so a user who needs a new warehouse is never sent away to make one and come back.
options.cost: The field now opens a second surface, and a dialog must never open another dialog. Creating a warehouse has to be a page, which means losing the form's contents.

options.name: Recent records above the search
options.rationale: Linear opens every picker on the records the person touched last: the warehouse for the next delivery is almost always the warehouse of the last one. Recent first turns the common case into one tap and leaves search for the rest.
options.cost: Recent is per person, so two users see two orders and a screenshot never matches twice. It also needs an empty state for the first delivery, where nothing is recent yet.

options.name: Results grouped by state with counts
options.rationale: GitHub command palette groups results under a heading with a count, so a list of thirty reads as three lists of ten. Grouping tiers by state keeps a closed tier from being copied by mistake.
options.cost: The groups are one more opinion about the records, and a group the picker invents has to stay in sync with the states the records actually hold. Costs a heading row per group on a phone.

compact.behaviour: The recommended option reflows: one column, header actions under the title, and a table scrolls inside its own region.

patterns.assessment: The searchable picker over names stays the pick: nobody types an identifier, and search beats scrolling for every list longer than a screen. The picker with one distinguishing fact per row is the runner-up for records that share a name. Never ship a bare identifier field: a code such as WH-0C893968A2 is not a value a person can type or check.

patterns.title: A date and time field
patterns.question: A common failure is the browser's native type="date", which draws as dd/mm/yyyy --:-- with a native picker icon and is visibly not the application's own control. GDS rejected type="date" for browser implementation problems.

options.name: Three text inputs with a format hint
options.rationale: GOV.UK's own answer to a date: three fields, numeric inputmode, autocomplete tokens, and a hint reading 'For example, 31 3 1980'. Every browser renders it the same.
options.cost: Three fields for one value, and a user entering 94 dates a year types 282 numbers. This is the most accessible answer and the slowest one.

options.name: One text field with a calendar that opens beside it
options.rationale: One field the user types into, with a calendar beside it for the ones who would rather click. APG's combobox date-picker pattern is exactly this, and Carbon's rule is that there must always be a way to type.
options.cost: A calendar is a grid of 42 cells to build, translate and test in two languages. It is the most code in the form package for one field.

options.name: Date and time on one row, the time zone named once
options.rationale: Date and time sit side by side as two fields, with the time zone stated once above them rather than repeated under each. Fewer repetitions of the same fact.
options.cost: On a narrow screen two fields plus the row wraps to three lines, and a time zone that is stated once has to be read before the second field rather than next to it.

options.name: Relative dates for the near future, absolute for the far
options.rationale: A dispatch plan is written in relative language: 'dispatch at 08:00', 'loading 4 hours before'. One field takes a duration and the page works out the clock time from the delivery date.
options.cost: An absolute time has to be derivable and shown, or the user has to hold it in their head. And a relative field cannot express 'dispatch at 08:00 unless the driver is late'.

options.name: A duration field for a length of time
options.rationale: For loading, a timeout or a hold, the user knows 'four hours', not '04:00'. One field for the number and a unit beside it, per NN/g's rule that the step and the unit be explicit.
options.cost: Two fields where one number would do, and it cannot express '2h30'. A single field parsing both needs error wording for every way a duration can be wrong.

options.name: The date refused, with the date that was wrong
options.rationale: The same field refused, with GOV.UK's error wording: name the field and say what to do. It says what was entered and what is wrong, so the user does not have to remember what they typed.
options.cost: The message repeats the value, which makes it longer than the field. A message that fits above the input and not inside it.

options.name: Preset chips for the usual dispatch times
options.rationale: Calendly puts the usual lengths above a custom field because most meetings are thirty minutes; dispatch times cluster the same way around 08:00. Two presets plus Custom covers the week without typing.
options.cost: The presets are company data that goes stale when the season changes, and a preset that names a date has to be regenerated every week. A stale chip offers last month mornings.

options.name: Start and end as one range with a length readout
options.rationale: Airbnb and Linear ask for a range as one control with the length read back, because a start without an end is not a value the page can use. The readout catches the overnight mistake before the submit does.
options.cost: Two values in one field need one error message that names both, and a screen reader meets a composite where it expected a field. The labels have to be wired with care.

compact.behaviour: The recommended option reflows: one column, header actions under the title, and a table scrolls inside its own region.

patterns.assessment: One typed field with a calendar beside it stays the pick: there is always a way to type, and the calendar serves the users who would rather click. The three GDS inputs are the runner-up where accessibility review demands them, at the cost of the slowest entry in the form. Never ship the native date input: it draws the browser chrome instead of the application control and renders differently everywhere.

patterns.title: A text field and its states
patterns.question: Every text field has to draw seven states, and GOV.UK is blunt about two of them: the label is always visible and above the input, and a placeholder is never the label because it vanishes on first keystroke.

options.name: Label above, help under, six states on one page
options.rationale: The component reference page for the field: default, filled, focused, error, disabled and readonly. Showing them together is how a reviewer checks one control rather than six screenshots.
options.cost: Six instances of one field is a style guide, not a screen. It never appears in the product; it exists so the states cannot drift apart.

options.name: Label above, placeholder as a hint
options.rationale: The label names the field and the placeholder shows an example. Both present, which is GOV.UK's actual recommendation once a hint is genuinely needed.
options.cost: Two sets of words per field, so a form with five fields carries ten lines before the first value. The hint has to earn its place every time.

options.name: Placeholder as the label
options.rationale: The search field with no label: the only description of what the search covers is a placeholder reading 'Order number, name or email'.
options.cost: Fails GOV.UK's guidance on three counts at once: it vanishes on first keystroke, not every screen reader reads it, and its default colour often misses 1.4.3 contrast.

options.name: Character count under a long-answer field
options.rationale: Where a field has a hard limit, the remaining count sits under it. GOV.UK says count characters only where its own research shows it nets positive.
options.cost: GOV.UK's validation guidance permits live counting only as its own exception, precisely because it validates before the field is finished. On a policy text it is worth it; on a name it is not.

options.name: A textarea with the customer's words preserved
options.rationale: Long answers are shown with the typist's own line breaks. A policy pasted from a document keeps its paragraphs instead of reflowing into one block.
options.cost: Uncontrolled line breaks in stored text are a rendering hazard on a customer page, where the width differs from the editor's. It has to be normalised somewhere.

options.name: A field that grows as the answer does
options.rationale: The textarea expands with its content up to a limit, so an incident report is not a 74-pixel window with a scrollbar inside it.
options.cost: A growing field pushes everything below it down as the reader types, which moves the button they are about to press. Most implementations stop growing at about six lines.

options.name: Inline confirmation of a good value
options.rationale: Stripe Checkout and Vercel confirm a valid value where it was typed, with a tick and a quiet line, instead of waiting for the submit. Confirming Standard early saves the user a round trip for the name they wanted.
options.cost: GOV.UK permits live validation only as a narrow exception, because it judges a field before it is finished. The check must wait for a pause in typing, or it nags.

options.name: Floating labels that shrink when filled
options.rationale: Material Design answers the placeholder problem by floating the label above the value once the field fills, so the label never vanishes. It keeps the compact look the placeholder promised without breaking it.
options.cost: The empty state still reads as a placeholder, with its small text and low contrast, and a floated label at 10.5 px is smaller than any label the back office otherwise draws. GOV.UK keeps the label above and full size for that reason.

compact.behaviour: The recommended option reflows: one column, header actions under the title, and a table scrolls inside its own region.

patterns.assessment: The six-state reference page stays the pick, because it is the only option that pins every state one field must draw. Inline validation that confirms a good value is the runner-up for create forms, where it saves a refused submit. Never ship the placeholder as the label: it vanishes on first keystroke, and its colour misses contrast.

patterns.title: Choosing one of a few options
patterns.question: A closed set. GOV.UK's rules are that a select is a last resort, that radios beat it, and that nothing is pre-selected in a question though it is allowed in settings. The naming field below is a radio list with three well-worded options.

options.name: A radio list with a description per option
options.rationale: Each option carries a sentence saying what it means for the customer, which is the only way a person can choose between 'The customer name' and 'Every recipient named'.
options.cost: Three options at 22 pixels each is a tall block, and it does not scale to twelve options, which a permission picker does need.

options.name: A segmented control for two or three
options.rationale: Where the choice is between two or three values that are all visible at once, a segmented control shows every option rather than hiding them behind a menu.
options.cost: Labels have to fit, so 'A blank product' and 'A template' both had to be shortened. The control grows with its longest label.

options.name: Plan cards for a priced choice
options.rationale: For a choice between priced options, each card names the option, its price and its period, and the one the company holds says so in words rather than only by a ring.
options.cost: Cards are boxes, and the layout contract says a Section is the only box and never nests. Three plan cards inside a section break that rule three times.

options.name: Cards with a radio inside each
options.rationale: The plan cards, with the choice made by a real radio so the tab order and the arrow keys work as a form control rather than as a set of buttons.
options.cost: Two nested controls in one card. The whole card has to forward the click to the radio, and the radio still has to be reachable by Tab.

options.name: A select, in a settings page where nothing is pre-selected
options.rationale: GOV.UK allows a pre-selection in settings and nowhere else. Where the value has no default and the options are many, a select with a real empty first option is the least-bad shape.
options.cost: The empty option is a placeholder, and the layout contract says not to show one. A select whose first choice is a blank that must be replaced is two states, not one.

options.name: A multi-select as a list of checkboxes
options.rationale: GOV.UK states it directly: do not use select multiple, because of its history of poor usability and assistive support. Checkboxes in a list, or a dedicated picker where the options are many.
options.cost: Twenty checkboxes is a wall. Above about eight, the picker needs a search and a summary of what is chosen, which is a component rather than a field.

options.name: A listbox with a checkmark and descriptions
options.rationale: Apple HIG and Radix UI draw a choice with descriptions as a listbox: one button showing the current value, a checkmark on it in the list, and full keyboard support. It carries the same sentences as the radio list in the height of one field.
options.cost: The options hide behind a button, so a reader compares them only by opening the list. A radio list shows all three at once; this one shows one and promises two more.

options.name: A binary question as two plain buttons
options.rationale: Typeform asks a yes-or-no question as two large buttons with the consequence under each, because a binary choice deserves no menu and no dropdown. Both answers stay visible with their cost attached.
options.cost: Two cards for one bit is the heaviest binary control on this page, and it answers only questions with two honest answers. A third option or a conditional follow-up breaks the shape.

compact.behaviour: The recommended option reflows: one column, header actions under the title, and a table scrolls inside its own region.

patterns.assessment: The radio list with a description per option stays the pick: each choice carries the sentence that lets a person choose between names that sound alike. The segmented control is the runner-up for two or three short values with no descriptions. Never ship the native multi-select: GOV.UK rules it out for its usability and assistive record, and a checkbox list replaces it.

patterns.title: A switch or a checkbox
patterns.question: The storefront editor holds a toggle for the platform credit line. A back office holds many settings where a switch fits, so this item is about which control the setting deserves and what the label has to say.

options.name: A switch with the label and its consequence
options.rationale: The label says what is on and the line under it says what turning it off does, so the choice is reversible and stated.
options.cost: A switch has no pressed state on first paint, so a reader cannot tell what is currently on without looking twice. And it carries no visible text.

options.name: A checkbox where the off state is the default
options.rationale: A checkbox rather than a switch, because the default is off and the action is to tick something. GOV.UK's wording is to phrase it as what ticking does, not as what the box is.
options.cost: A checkbox and a switch look nearly identical here, and readers conflate them. The difference has to be carried by the label's phrasing.

options.name: A checkbox with the consequence under it, no state carried
options.rationale: Every setting as a checkbox with a consequence line. One control for the whole page, so nothing about the shape depends on whether the value happens to be on.
options.cost: A reviewer cannot see at a glance which are on without reading the boxes. On a settings page with eight such settings that matters.

options.name: Two options where the difference is the money
options.rationale: Settlement frequency is a choice between two money outcomes, so it gets radio cards with the amount and the date on each, not a switch that hides the difference.
options.cost: Cards for a two-way choice is heavy, and the amounts are derived figures that have to be computed per company to stay honest.

options.name: A switch that is refused, with the reason
options.rationale: A setting the role cannot change, switched off and refused, with the reason in visible text. This is the explained-action pattern applied to a control rather than a button.
options.cost: A disabled switch with no value is a dead pixel to a reader who does not notice the reason. The reason has to sit directly under it, not at the foot of the section.

options.name: A switch with the number it would change
options.rationale: Where flipping the setting changes an amount, the amount is on the same line. The user reads the consequence before flipping rather than after.
options.cost: A derived figure beside a control has to be current, which means a read that the switch itself depends on. It also puts a number on a page that was otherwise free of them.

options.name: Instant apply with an undo toast
options.rationale: Linear and Google Material apply a low-risk switch at once and offer Undo in a toast, so there is no Save to forget and no dialog to dismiss. The toast names what changed, which a silent apply never does.
options.cost: Every flip is an audited command the moment it happens, with no review step before it. It fits display settings; it does not fit money, access, or anything a toast cannot undo.

options.name: A three-way choice as a segmented control
options.rationale: Slack draws a three-way notification choice as a segmented control, because the values are short, ordered, and all worth seeing at once. No menu hides the middle option the user actually wants.
options.cost: Three labels have to fit the control, so the wording shortens until it almost stops meaning anything. A fourth option or a per-option description breaks the shape back into radios.

compact.behaviour: The recommended option reflows: one column, header actions under the title, and a table scrolls inside its own region.

patterns.assessment: The switch with its consequence stated stays the pick: the label says what is on and the line under it says what turning it off does. The instant-apply switch with an undo toast is the runner-up for low-risk settings a user flips often. Never ship a switch whose label names the control instead of the outcome; a reader must not open documentation to learn what on means.

patterns.title: An upload field
patterns.question: The storefront editor holds a Logo and a Banner image drop zone with the file type and size in words under it. The data-imports area needs a CSV upload, which is a different shape: wrong file, wrong columns and wrong rows are all refusals.

options.name: A drop zone that states what it accepts
options.rationale: The accepted types and the size limit in a sentence under the zone, so nobody discovers the limit by being refused.
options.cost: A drop zone invites a click anywhere, and a user who drops a file on the page outside the zone gets nothing at all. No affordance says where the zone is.

options.name: The file already chosen, with what it will do
options.rationale: After the choice, the row carries the file, its size and the consequence of saving: the old logo is replaced, and customers see the new one within a minute.
options.cost: A file that has been uploaded but not saved is a resource that exists and is not referenced. It needs a cleanup, or the storage fills with orphans.

options.name: A CSV upload that states its columns first
options.rationale: For an import, the field states what it needs before anything is uploaded: the four column names, and a link to a template. The upload cannot be wrong about a format nobody told it.
options.cost: Stating four columns above the zone is a paragraph of prose, and the layout contract keeps prose out of components. It belongs on the page beside the field, not inside it.

options.name: The upload refused, naming the row that failed
options.rationale: The file is refused for a reason the user can act on: row 412 has no email. A refusal that names a row is worth more than one that says 'invalid file'.
options.cost: Naming one row out of 2,000 needs the whole file read before answering, so the upload is not instant and the user waits without knowing why.

options.name: An image field with the dimensions stated
options.rationale: For a picture that must be a particular shape, the dimensions are part of the requirement, not a nicety. The field says '1600 by 700 pixels reads best' and refuses a wrong shape.
options.cost: The layout contract says the layout decides a stored image's box, not the image's own dimensions. A field that demands a ratio re-decides that per field.

options.name: An import that reports what it made
options.rationale: After an import, the page says what happened: how many rows became what, how many were refused and why. The user can undo it while nothing has been paid out.
options.cost: A real import is a command whose effect spans many records, which the architecture reserves for a named exception. The report has to be a real read, not a summary of the session.

options.name: One progress row per file
options.rationale: Dropbox and Google Drive report each file on its own row with its own bar and its own cancel, because two files never finish together. One bar for all would lie about both.
options.cost: A row per file is a list the page must manage: cancel one, remove one, retry one. For a single logo it is heavier than the one zone it replaces.

options.name: Drop anywhere on the section
options.rationale: GitHub and Notion accept a drop anywhere on the editing surface and highlight the target while the file hovers, so the user never aims at a small box. The over state is the affordance the plain zone lacks.
options.cost: A page that accepts drops everywhere must also refuse them precisely: a CSV over the logo box needs a refusal, not a silent nothing. Every surface needs its own accepted list.

compact.behaviour: The recommended option reflows: one column, header actions under the title, and a table scrolls inside its own region.

patterns.assessment: The drop zone that states its types and size limit stays the pick: nobody should discover the limit by being refused. The per-file progress tray is the runner-up for imports of several files, where one bar per file beats one bar for all. Never ship a CSV upload with no stated columns: a file refused for a format nobody told it is a refusal the application caused.

patterns.title: Reporting a refused submit
patterns.question: GOV.UK requires an error summary on every validation failure, including a single error, headed 'There is a problem', carrying role="alert", taking focus, and linking to each errored field. WCAG 3.3.1 and 3.3.3 are the criteria underneath.

options.name: A summary above the form, plus a message on each field
options.rationale: The GOV.UK pattern in full: the summary first, receiving focus, each entry linking to its field, and the same wording repeated on the field so it reads the same out of context.
options.cost: The wording now exists in two places per error, so it has to be generated once and used twice. Hand-written copies drift, and the drift is invisible.

options.name: Messages on the fields only
options.rationale: Each field carries its own message and nothing else. The reader sees the error where they have to fix it.
options.cost: On a long form the first error may be below the fold, so the reader submits, sees nothing change and concludes the button is broken. G139 exists precisely to jump to the errors.

options.name: A summary in a dialog above the form
options.rationale: The summary arrives as a dialog over the form, which cannot be scrolled past and cannot be missed, so the reader cannot submit again unaware.
options.cost: A dialog over a form breaks focus rules: a dialog never opens another layer, and a form is not a dialog. It also hides the form the reader has to fix.

options.name: A summary as a banner above the page, not the form
options.rationale: The summary sits at the top of the page, above the heading, as GOV.UK specifies: below the back link and breadcrumb, above the h1, taking focus.
options.cost: Above the heading it is easy to miss on a long page, and it pushes the heading below the fold on a phone. GOV.UK accepts that because the page title also gets an 'Error: ' prefix for screen readers.

options.name: The refused field only, with no summary at all
options.rationale: The one field the command refused carries a message; everything else is untouched. The smallest response to a single refusal, which is what most refusals are.
options.cost: This common behaviour satisfies WCAG 3.3.1 but not 3.3.3, because 'Invalid date' names no field and says nothing about what to do.

options.name: The refused command, with what to do instead
options.rationale: When a refusal is about the command rather than a field, it goes above the form as an alert with the code's sentence and, where the application can help, why it was refused and what resolves it.
options.cost: The refusal is not attached to anything the reader can click, so it explains rather than navigates. Useful for a business rule, useless for a typo.

options.name: Validation on leaving each field
options.rationale: Shopify Polaris and Stripe check a field on blur and mark it good or wrong where it sits, so the user fixes one field and moves on. By the submit there is nothing left to refuse.
options.cost: A complement to the summary, never a replacement: with three errors and no summary the reader still cannot see them all at once. And a check on blur fires while the form is half filled.

options.name: One question per screen with a progress marker
options.rationale: TurboTax and Typeform ask one question per screen with nowhere else for an error to hide: the refusal sits under the only field on the page. A guided flow cannot submit with a field unseen.
options.cost: Four screens for four fields is the slowest form in this category, and a user who knows all four answers resents the pacing. It fits a first delivery; it does not fit the fortieth.

compact.behaviour: The recommended option reflows: one column, header actions under the title, and a table scrolls inside its own region.

patterns.assessment: The GOV.UK summary with focus plus per-field messages stays the pick: it satisfies WCAG 3.3.1 and 3.3.3, and the links carry the reader to each field. Inline validation on blur is the runner-up as a complement, never a replacement: it confirms good values early but cannot orient a reader facing three errors. Never ship the dialog summary: it hides the form the reader must fix.

patterns.title: Work that is not saved
patterns.question: A common failure is an editor with no Cancel and no dirty state: nothing tells a reader that what they typed is unsaved, and nothing stops them leaving it.

options.name: A visible unsaved marker beside the Save
options.rationale: The moment a field changes, the Save button carries the word 'Save changes' and a note says what changed. The reader never has to remember whether they typed anything.
options.cost: A note naming one changed field is a derived fact about the form's state, which has to come from the form rather than the route. And a Save that changes its own label moves under the reader's cursor.

options.name: Leave-with-a-question when there is something to lose
options.rationale: Cloudcape's rule is to confirm only when there is real data at risk and to be consistent about it, so the same dialog appears for a Cancel, a breadcrumb and a navigation away.
options.cost: Every page with a form needs the same guard, and the browser's own beforeunload prompt cannot be worded, so the custom one and the native one both appear on a browser Back.

options.name: Autosave, with a saved marker
options.rationale: The form saves itself every few seconds and a quiet marker says 'Saved 4 seconds ago'. Nothing is ever lost and no dialog is ever needed.
options.cost: Autosave makes each save a command against money and access, which means an audit entry per keystroke batch. A past decision must stay reconstructable, and a trail of keystroke batches is not one a reviewer can read.

options.name: A draft, saved and left on the server
options.rationale: The form's state is a draft the server holds. Leaving the page leaves the draft, and returning to it offers to carry on. GOV.UK asks for this where a long form may be completed over more than one sitting.
options.cost: A draft is a second version of the record with its own name and its own rules about when it expires. It is a new aggregate, not a field on the form.

options.name: Saved silently, with the command in the page header
options.rationale: For a settings page where each change is independent, each section saves itself on its own Save and the header carries nothing. A reader who changes two areas can save each.
options.cost: Two Saves on one screen is the case where a reader edits one form and saves the other. The rule has to be one Save per page or one per section, never a mix.

options.name: A read-only form because the state forbids it
options.rationale: Once the sale has opened, the price is a versioned fact and the field is read-only rather than a field with a save. Changing it is a different command with its own consequences.
options.cost: A read-only field with no command leaves the reader stuck, unless the command to change it is stated. The explained-action pattern exists for exactly this case.

options.name: A save bar pinned to the top while dirty
options.rationale: Shopify Polaris pins a contextual save bar to the top of a dirty form, so Save and Discard never scroll out of reach on a long settings page. The bar appears with the first keystroke and leaves with the save.
options.cost: A pinned bar covers content on a phone and follows the reader past sections it has nothing to do with. It also needs the same dirty tracking as the marker, so it adds no new information, only reach.

options.name: Per-field revert to the saved value
options.rationale: Webflow and Figma mark each changed field with a dot and offer Revert beside it, so the user keeps one change and drops another without retyping. The old value sits under the field as the honest fallback.
options.cost: A dot plus a revert button per field is two more elements on every row of a long form, and a reader who wants to keep everything still needs the page-level Save. It pays off only where partial saves are common.

compact.behaviour: The recommended option reflows: one column, header actions under the title, and a table scrolls inside its own region.

patterns.assessment: The visible unsaved marker beside Save stays the pick: the reader never has to remember whether they typed anything. The sticky save bar is the runner-up for long settings pages where the form actions scroll out of view. Never ship silent autosave on money or access: each save would be an audited command, and an audit entry per keystroke batch is not a trail a reviewer can read.

patterns.title: Picking a period
patterns.question: A user closing the month or reporting on it starts by choosing the window: the settlement run, the week after the launch opened, the month the delivery falls in. Two typed dates answer every window but make the user type both edges every time, so the field pairs typed dates with the presets the user reaches for and states what each edge includes.

options.name: Two date inputs with presets
options.rationale: The presets fill both fields and the user adjusts either edge by typing, so the common windows cost one tap and the rare ones stay possible. The control that fills the fields and the fields that hold them are one unit.
options.cost: Two controls describe one value, so the preset must visibly become Custom the moment either date is edited, or the row claims a window it no longer holds.

options.name: Preset segmented control: 7, 30, 90 days
options.rationale: One tap and no typing for the three windows a settlement check almost always wants. The resolved dates are shown back under the control so the preset is a promise the user can read.
options.cost: No preset reaches a launch-anchored window like the launch to the delivery, so a custom range still needs a second control beside this one.

options.name: Month picker
options.rationale: Settlement and tax reporting run by calendar month, so picking March 2026 in one control beats typing the first and the last day of the month by hand.
options.cost: A window that crosses a month edge, like the fortnight around the delivery, cannot be expressed. Whole months are the only shape this control draws.

options.name: Open-start rolling window
options.rationale: Everything since the launch opened needs only an end date, because the start is the opening and never moves. One field where two would ask a question the user cannot answer differently.
options.cost: An open start silently includes old test orders, so the resolved start must be shown back under the field. Without it the user cannot tell what the window holds.

options.name: Refusal when the end precedes the start
options.rationale: An end before the start is refused where it was typed, in the GOV.UK template: the message names the field and says what to do, and the summary above it says the same in one line.
options.cost: One more state to draw and to test, and the refusal must wait until both fields hold a date, or it fires while the user is still typing the second one.

options.name: Timezone-safe inclusive day boundaries
options.rationale: Each edge is a whole day in Europe/Amsterdam, so an order placed at 22:41 on the delivery day falls inside the window that ends on that day. The boundary sentence is part of the control, not documentation beside it.
options.cost: The sentence must be read to work, and a user thinking in UTC sees different instants. Stating the zone once keeps it from being repeated under each field.

options.name: A calendar with the range painted
options.rationale: Airbnb and Google Flights paint the chosen range across the calendar, so the user sees the window instead of reading two dates. The endpoints stay readable as dates under the control.
options.cost: A painted month shows one month, and the settlement window usually spans two. Two months side by side is the honest control, and it does not fit a phone.

options.name: Delivery-anchored presets
options.rationale: Mixpanel and Amplitude anchor ranges to the milestones the business runs on, because last-30-days drifts while the launch stays fixed. The preset resolves to typed dates the user can still adjust.
options.cost: Anchors multiply: launch, dispatch, close, settlement runs. Three anchors fit a control; six need a picker of their own, and the window stops being one tap.

compact.behaviour: One month is shown; the second month of the window follows below it.

patterns.assessment: Two typed dates with presets stays the pick: one tap for the common windows, typing for the rare ones, and both edges always visible. The two-month painted calendar is the runner-up for reporting screens where the window itself is the question. Never ship presets alone with no typed fallback: no preset reaches the launch-to-delivery window the settlement check wants.

patterns.title: A slug or URL field with a preview
patterns.question: Every product and every storefront lives at an address the company chooses. The slug is the short part typed in; the address is what the customer reads, links and prints.

options.name: Slug with the live address under it
options.rationale: Contentful and Shopify show the full address under the slug field and update it as the user types, so the short value is never saved unseen. The copy command beside it is how the address leaves the back office.
options.cost: The address must update as the user types, which a static mock cannot show. It also states the host the platform gives, which the user cannot change on this screen.

options.name: The address as a fact with a change command
options.rationale: GitHub shows a repository address as a fact and puts Rename behind a command, because an address in use is depended upon. The 30-day redirect is what makes the change survivable.
options.cost: Two steps to change a value, and the redirect has to be a real behaviour, not a sentence. A redirect nobody builds is a promise the page breaks.

options.name: Transliterated from the name with an edit toggle
options.rationale: WordPress builds the permalink from the title and lets the user edit it, because the name and the slug agree nine times in ten. Typing both by hand is the same words twice.
options.cost: The generated value must transliterate Dutch diacritics the way the user expects, and a renamed product must not silently re-slug. Generation runs once at creation, never again.

options.name: Availability check with alternatives offered
options.rationale: Namecheap answers a taken domain with free alternatives, because a refusal without a next step sends the user back to guessing. The alternatives keep the shape of what was wanted.
options.cost: The alternatives must be checked live, one by one, or the list offers addresses that fail the same way. Three checks per keystroke pause is a read the page has to budget for.

options.name: The slug refused with the rule that refused it
options.rationale: The GOV.UK error template applied to a slug: the summary first, then the field, with the message naming what was entered and what to do. The rule is stated once and enforced the same way.
options.cost: The message repeats the value, which makes it longer than the field. It also has to name every offending character class, not just the first it found.

options.name: Custom domain with its DNS instructions
options.rationale: Vercel and Webflow pair a domain field with the exact DNS record it needs, because the field alone is half the task. The record is stated as values to copy, not as prose to interpret.
options.cost: Verification is a read against DNS the back office does not control, so the badge can only say what the last check found and when. A stale badge claims a state the world has left.

compact.behaviour: The recommended option reflows: one column, header actions under the title, and a table scrolls inside its own region.

patterns.assessment: The slug with its live address under it is the pick: the user types the short part and reads the full address before saving. The transliteration from the name is the runner-up for creation, where typing the same words twice is pure overhead. Never ship an address that cannot be read before it is saved.

patterns.title: A capacity field
patterns.question: The Amsterdam warehouse holds 10,000 units, and every price tier draws from the same shelves. The capacity field is where a user divides the stock without selling it twice.

options.name: A number with the warehouse ceiling restated
options.rationale: The warehouse total sits beside every quantity field, because a tier allocation means nothing without the stock it draws from. The bar shows how full the stock is at a glance.
options.cost: The restated ceiling must update when another tier changes, or two screens state two stocks. It is a read of the whole product behind one field.

options.name: The split across types with what is left
options.rationale: Inventory draws as one row per tier with sold against cap, because the question is the stock, not the row. The leftover line is what the user came to read.
options.cost: A row per tier is a table wearing a list costume, and at twelve tiers it needs the table back. Editing still jumps to one tier at a time.

options.name: A stepper for a small count
options.rationale: Apple HIG reserves the stepper for small counts adjusted by one, which a 24-unit sample list is. Tapping plus twice beats selecting 24 and typing 26.
options.cost: A stepper for 9,600 units would be tapped 9,600 times, so it fits only counts under fifty. The field must still take a typed value for the jump from 4 to 40.

options.name: A percentage held back from sale
options.rationale: Holds are a percentage of the stock kept for the trade counter, restated as units so the user reads both. A percentage survives a stock change; a count does not.
options.cost: Two numbers describe one hold, and they round differently: 5% of 10,000 is 500 until the stock becomes 9,999. The units win and the percentage follows.

options.name: The capacity refused with the overage named
options.rationale: The refusal worded on screen, with the field carrying the same message: GOV.UK names the field and says what to do, and the numbers supply the overage. The user reads the overage, not just the rule.
options.cost: The message must recompute the overage for every value, and a value that breaks two rules needs two messages. One refusal per field keeps it readable.

options.name: Sold as a read-only fact beside an editable cap
options.rationale: Stripe draws an available balance as a fact beside the controls that move it: sold is what happened, the cap is what the user decides. The two must never share a field.
options.cost: Three figures plus a field for one decision, and the derived Left line must update as the cap is typed. It is the most screen per field in this item.

compact.behaviour: The recommended option reflows: one column, header actions under the title, and a table scrolls inside its own region.

patterns.assessment: The number with the warehouse ceiling restated is the pick: one field, the stock it draws from, and what is left, all on the same screen. The split across tiers is the runner-up for the product page, where the question is the whole stock rather than one tier. Never ship a capacity with no ceiling stated: a number without its stock is a number that oversells.

patterns.title: A colour field for the storefront accent
patterns.question: The company brands its storefront with one accent colour: a #RRGGBB value dark enough for white button text to read on it. The field takes the value and proves the contrast before it is refused.

options.name: Hex field with a swatch and a contrast readout
options.rationale: Shopify theme editor pairs a hex field with a swatch and the rule it must pass, because a colour value means nothing until it is seen. The readout repeats the validation rule, so the user is told before the request rather than after it.
options.cost: The ratio must recompute as the user types, and an unfinished value has no ratio to state. Six characters that are not yet a colour need patience, not a refusal.

options.name: Preset swatches plus a custom value
options.rationale: Slack and Notion offer a row of presets that all satisfy the rule, with a custom field for the user who knows better. One tap covers the common case and cannot produce a failing colour.
options.cost: Six presets cannot hold a brand colour, so the custom field carries the real work anyway. And a preset row that never changes starts to look like the whole choice.

options.name: The accent previewed on a customer button
options.rationale: Mailchimp previews a brand colour on the button the customer presses, because a ratio is believed once it is seen. The user reads white on #1F2937 instead of reading 14.7:1.
options.cost: A preview is a second surface to keep honest: it must show the typed value, not the saved one, and it must update as the user types. A stale preview proves nothing.

options.name: The browser colour well beside the hex
options.rationale: The browser native colour well is the only picker that costs no code: one input, the platform dialog, and a hex the user can still type. MDN documents it as the accessible default.
options.cost: The well draws the browser chrome instead of the back-office control and renders differently everywhere, which is the same charge the native date input faces. It also offers colours that fail 4.5:1 without saying so.

options.name: A pale colour refused with the ratio that failed
options.rationale: The validation rule worded on screen in the GOV.UK template: the message names the value, states both ratios, and says what to do. The user learns the rule from the refusal, not from documentation.
options.cost: A refusal that only says darker leaves the user guessing how much darker. It earns its place fully only beside presets that all pass.

options.name: An inherited accent with an override command
options.rationale: Figma variables inherit down the tree and override at one level with the source still named, so a product can differ without hiding where its value came from. The company default stays the decider.
options.cost: An inherited value with an override is two values and a rule about which wins. A reader who never opens this screen cannot tell which products differ.

compact.behaviour: The recommended option reflows: one column, header actions under the title, and a table scrolls inside its own region.

patterns.assessment: The hex field with a swatch and a contrast readout is the pick: it takes any colour, shows it, and states the ratio the validation enforces. The customer-button preview is the runner-up beside it, because a ratio is believed once it is seen. Never ship a free colour with no contrast check: a pale accent ships white text nobody can read.

patterns.title: A repeatable group for price tiers
patterns.question: The Oak desk lamp sells in Standard, Trade and Bulk: three groups of the same fields, each with its own name, price and allocation. The group repeats, and the stock counts every repetition.

options.name: Stacked cards, one per type
options.rationale: Shopify draws product variants as one row per variant with its price readable at once, because the user compares repetitions before editing one. Sold tiers stay visible but lose their Remove.
options.cost: A row shows the price but hides the dates, the discount rule and the description, so editing still opens each tier. The list answers what, never why.

options.name: A table with inline editing
options.rationale: Airtable edits values where they sit, so changing three prices costs three fields and no navigation. One row in edit state at a time keeps the table readable while it is also a form.
options.cost: A table that is also a form validates cell by cell, and a refused cell must hold its row open. At phone width the columns scroll sideways, which hides the price behind a swipe.

options.name: One section per type with add another
options.rationale: GOV.UK add-another repeats the full group once per entry with its own remove, because each repetition deserves the same labels, help and errors as the first. Nothing about tier 2 is abbreviated.
options.cost: Three full groups is a very long page, and the stock total has nowhere to sit. It fits creation, where each tier is new; it drags for review, where each tier is known.

options.name: Dated price steps for the launch
options.rationale: A launch tiers its prices by date, because early customers pay less for committing first. The dates are part of each step, so the price on any day is answered by reading one row.
options.cost: Dated steps plus per-tier allocations is two ways to divide one stock, and they can disagree: a step can close with units left, or sell out with days left. One of the two has to win.

options.name: Drag to reorder with the customer order shown
options.rationale: Linear and Trello order by dragging with button equivalents beside each row, because drag alone strands keyboard users. The customer order is numbered, so the back-office order and the storefront order cannot drift apart silently.
options.cost: Order is one more field per tier with its own conflicts: two users reordering at once, and a tier added in the middle. It needs the same version check as every shared write.

options.name: The group refused, naming the type that breaks the ceiling
options.rationale: The refusal above the group plus the offending row named below it: GOV.UK puts the summary first and the message on the field, and here the field is a row. Standard carries the overage because Standard grew last.
options.cost: Blaming one row for a stock total is a guess the page makes about intent: the user may sooner cut Bulk than Standard. The message must offer both, not decide.

compact.behaviour: At phone width the table keeps its columns and scrolls sideways; the tier column stays first.

patterns.assessment: The stacked cards are the pick: one card per tier with its price and allocation readable at once, and one command to add another. The dated price steps are the runner-up for launches, where time decides the price rather than the customer choice. Never ship a group whose repetitions cannot be removed: a tier added by mistake must leave without taking its sold units with it.

patterns.title: A tag input
patterns.question: Products and customers carry short labels: oak, home, trade. Tags are typed freely but read everywhere, so the input must take new words and still keep old ones spelled one way.

options.name: Chips with type-to-add and suggestions
options.rationale: GitHub and Linear offer existing labels as the user types and accept a new word on Enter, so the old spelling wins without forbidding the new one. The count beside each suggestion says how shared it is.
options.cost: Suggestions must search across every product on every keystroke pause, and a slow search answers after the user has already pressed Enter. The new word wins by timing, not by choice.

options.name: A checkbox list in a popover with a count
options.rationale: Shopify and Jira draw a closed tag set as checkboxes with a count on the button, because ticking is faster than typing when the words already exist. Managing the list is a separate task with its own dialog.
options.cost: A closed set cannot take a new word where it is needed, so the user leaves the form to make one. It fits a governed vocabulary; it fights a growing one.

options.name: Free text split on commas
options.rationale: Stack Overflow and WordPress take tags as one comma-separated line with the parsed chips read back below, so pasting a list from elsewhere just works. The readout is what makes the parsing honest.
options.cost: No suggestions means no shared spelling: oak and Oak become two tags and nobody is told. The readout shows the split but cannot judge the words.

options.name: Colour-coded tags for audience segments
options.rationale: Mailchimp and Klaviyo colour segments by meaning, because a segment is read in lists where its word is small. The tone repeats the signal instead of decorating it.
options.cost: Five tones cover five meanings and no more; a sixth segment reuses a tone and the code breaks. Colour must never be the only signal, so the word stays anyway.

options.name: A tag refused with the rule
options.rationale: The GOV.UK error template on the tag being added: the good chips stay and the bad word carries the message. The rule is stated with the value that broke it.
options.cost: The message judges one word while the field holds a list, so the user must tell which word failed. The chips above carry that by staying put.

options.name: Inherited tags with their source named
options.rationale: HubSpot shows inherited properties with their source beside the local ones, so a tier page answers the whole label set without hiding where each word came from. Removing an inherited word is refused by pointing at its source.
options.cost: Two lists where one was expected, and the inherited one cannot be edited here. A reader who wants the tier untagged must walk up the tree.

compact.behaviour: The recommended option reflows: one column, header actions under the title, and a table scrolls inside its own region.

patterns.assessment: The chips with type-to-add and suggestions are the pick: new words are allowed and old ones are offered, so oak is spelled once. The checkbox list is the runner-up where the tag set is closed and counted. Never ship free text with no suggestions: it grows oak, Oak and oak-desk side by side.

patterns.title: An address field
patterns.question: Acme Supply answers for its orders with a name, an address and a telephone number on every customer message. The address field takes the street the law asks for and the postcode the mail needs.

options.name: Postcode lookup that fills the street
options.rationale: Postcode.nl and GOV.UK ask for postcode plus number first because the user knows both by heart, then fill the street the user would mistype. Two short fields beat one long one.
options.cost: The lookup covers the Netherlands and nowhere else, so every other country falls back to manual entry. Two paths through one field is two paths to test.

options.name: One search that fills the address
options.rationale: Google Places resolves a half-typed street to a full address, because the user knows where they are but not how the database spells it. One field holds the whole search.
options.cost: An address search is a read against a provider the back office pays per keystroke, and a wrong first result is chosen without reading. The manual fallback must stay one tap away.

options.name: Country first, then the local shape
options.rationale: Stripe Checkout asks for the country first because the shape of an address follows it: a Dutch postcode is nothing like a German one. The labels and the validation change with the country.
options.cost: Every supported country needs its own shape, its own labels and its own validation. Three countries fit this pattern; thirty need a library.

options.name: Warehouse address with a map pin
options.rationale: The warehouse is pinned on a map beside its address, because drivers navigate to a pin, not to a street name. The pin is placed by the company, not guessed from the postcode.
options.cost: A map is a third-party surface with its own terms and its own load time. A static pin box proves the pattern; the live map is a dependency, not a field.

options.name: The postcode refused with the expected shape
options.rationale: The GOV.UK error template on a postcode: the message states the shape and gives the example, so the user repairs 1011 without opening a second page. The example is the company's own postcode.
options.cost: The shape differs per country, so the message must follow the country field. A Dutch message under a Belgian address refuses a value that was right.

options.name: A verified address with a change command
options.rationale: Banks and company registers show a verified address as a fact with a change command, because a verified value is depended upon by payouts and invoices. The badge states what the last check found.
options.cost: Verification is a check against a register the back office does not hold, so the badge can only age. A move the company forgets to report leaves a true badge on a false address.

compact.behaviour: The recommended option reflows: one column, header actions under the title, and a table scrolls inside its own region.

patterns.assessment: The postcode lookup is the pick: two short values the user knows produce the street they would mistype. The country-first manual entry is the runner-up for companies outside the lookup coverage. Never ship a single free-text address box: one line cannot be split into street, postcode and city again.

patterns.title: An email body editor
patterns.question: Acme Supply mails every customer when goods are dispatched, and the message carries the customer name, the order number and the delivery window. The editor takes the company words once and fills the customer facts per order.

options.name: Subject plus body with variable chips
options.rationale: Klaviyo and Mailchimp draw template variables as chips inside the sentence, because a variable is a word with a value, not code. The user reads the message as the customer will, with the facts marked.
options.cost: Chips inside an editable body are a small rich-text editor, not a textarea: backspace across a chip, paste with chips, and undo all need answers. The plain-text option exists for that reason.

options.name: Side-by-side preview of the customer message
options.rationale: Postmark and SendGrid preview a template beside the editor with a real record filled in, because a variable is only proven by its value. Maria Garcia's order fills every variable this template holds.
options.cost: Two columns collapse to one on a phone, so the preview sits below the editor and the user scrolls between them. A long template makes a long round trip.

options.name: Plain text with a variable list beside it
options.rationale: GOV.UK Notify writes templates as plain text with ((double bracket)) variables and lists each one beside the editor with an example value. Nothing about the message can break in a mail client that reads text.
options.cost: Double brackets are learned, not guessed: ((delivery window)) with one bracket fails silently or loudly depending on the parser. The editor must highlight what it recognises as you type.

options.name: One tab per language
options.rationale: Contentful and Shopify Translate keep one tab per locale with the missing ones badged, because a customer reads exactly one language and the user must know which ones exist. The badge names the gap instead of hiding it.
options.cost: Two tabs is two templates to keep in step: a variable added to one must be added to the other, and the Dutch sentence grows while the English one waits. Tabs hide the drift they also cause.

options.name: The send refused with the missing variable named
options.rationale: GOV.UK Notify refuses a send whose personalisation is missing and names the variable, because a blank where the order number belongs is worse than no mail. The message offers the fallback shape, not just the complaint.
options.cost: The refusal can only name what the test record lacks; a variable filled on the test order but empty on a real one still sends blank. Every variable needs a fallback, not just a test.

options.name: A sent copy with the values filled in
options.rationale: Postmark activity keeps the sent copy with every variable filled, because a dispute about what the customer was told is settled by reading what was sent. The record is read-only: history does not take edits.
options.cost: A copy per sending is storage that grows with every order, and each copy holds personal data under retention rules. The record must expire with the order, not live beside it.

compact.behaviour: The preview sits below the editor; the user scrolls between writing and reading.

patterns.assessment: The subject plus body with variable chips is the pick: the user writes the sentence and places the facts where they belong. The side-by-side customer preview is the runner-up beside it, because a template is believed once it is seen filled. Never ship a template with no preview: variables are spelled in one place and filled in another, and only the filled copy proves they meet.

patterns.title: Confirming a command that cannot be taken back
patterns.question: The evidence is unusually blunt. NN/g: a confirmation is worth its cost only when the action is rare, consequential and irreversible, and used routinely it becomes a reflex click. GOV.UK does not require typing; Cloudscape and GitHub do, for one object each.

options.name: Name the object, state the consequence, offer the alternative
options.rationale: The MOJ pattern: title asks, body states what it is and what happens, and the safe way out is in the same dialog. The commit button repeats the verb, as Carbon asks.
options.cost: Three pieces of copy per destructive command, in two languages, all of which have to stay true as the domain changes. The words are a second copy of the domain rules.

options.name: Type the launch name to confirm
options.rationale: Cloudscape's pattern, restricted to the most dangerous object: type the name, with the expected string selectable on screen, and the commit button disabled until it matches.
options.cost: NN/g's objection is exact: a product that asks people to type names all day trains them to copy and paste without reading, which is the reflex the pattern existed to break. One object per deployment is the ceiling, not one per record type.

options.name: No dialog at all: act, then offer an undo
options.rationale: The command runs and a toast names what happened with an Undo that stays until it is dismissed. Carbon keeps an action-bearing toast on screen for exactly that reason.
options.cost: On money this trains the reflex the confirmation exists to prevent, and an Undo on a refund is a second refund command rather than a reversal of the first.

options.name: An interruption page, not a dialog
options.rationale: GOV.UK's own answer for the most serious, irreversible action: leave the page entirely for one that says what will be lost and offers the way back as a link.
options.cost: A full page for one command means leaving the record and coming back, and it loses the page context that makes the consequence understandable.

options.name: A dialog with the consequence as numbers
options.rationale: Where a command changes money, the dialog shows the money. This is the strongest form of the pattern: the reader reads the figure before committing to it.
options.cost: The figure has to be read at the moment of the click, which means a read between the button and the command. On a slow connection the dialog waits.

options.name: A dialog that says it cannot act yet
options.rationale: The command is forbidden by a dependency, so the dialog names the dependency and the command that clears it, and the commit button is disabled with the reason on it.
options.cost: A dialog that cannot be completed is a dead end. Cloudscape handles this by disabling the commit control, which is honest but leaves the reader needing another surface.

options.name: Confirm by ticking each consequence
options.rationale: Safer destructive action. The commit button stays disabled until the reader ticks every consequence line. Unlike typing one name, ticking forces the eye across each line, so the refund route and the record-keeping are each acknowledged.
options.cost: Three checkboxes for one command is the heaviest confirmation in this set. Past one object per deployment it becomes the reflex click the pattern exists to break.

options.name: An alert dialog with the safe action first
