options.rationale: The way GitHub Primer draws an AlertDialog: one consequence in plain words, a danger icon, and focus on the safe action so Enter keeps the launch. Less copy than the first option, the same protection.
options.cost: One consequence means the other two move to the page or disappear. Where the money figure matters, the dialog with the consequence as numbers still wins because the reader never sees the amount here.

compact.behaviour: The recommended option reflows: one column, header actions under the title, and a table scrolls inside its own region.

patterns.assessment: Ship A: it names the object, states the consequence in figures, and offers the alternative in the same surface. E is the runner-up wherever money moves, because the figure is read at the click. Never ship C: an undo on an irreversible cancellation is a second command rather than a reversal, and on money it trains the reflex the confirmation exists to break.

patterns.title: A short task in a dialog
patterns.question: The composition rules are explicit: one to four inputs, nothing to consult and infrequent is a form dialog; more than four inputs, sections, steps or a need for a linkable result is a full page. The check is input count, and it is checked.

options.name: Two or three inputs, one dialog
options.rationale: One dialog shape for short commands: title, two fields, Cancel and the commit verb. This is where most short commands belong.
options.cost: A dialog is a separate surface from the page, so a refusal has to be worded in the dialog rather than on the page it came from.

options.name: Five inputs, so it becomes a page
options.rationale: The same command once it carries five inputs. The composition rule sends it to a full page, with a linkable result that can be returned to later.
options.cost: Losing the page the reader was on, and a linkable result that can be returned to later. Worth it when the command has that many parts.

options.name: Four inputs with a list to choose from
options.rationale: The large dialog size. Carbon's rule is that a modal is for a short non-frequent task and not for anything repeated; four inputs with a list is still on the right side of that line if it is rare.
options.cost: A 560-pixel dialog holding a table is close to a page with worse navigation, and the size has to be argued case by case rather than by a rule.

options.name: A dialog whose second step is another dialog
options.rationale: Refusing a file needs its own question, and the second dialog opens over the first. Base UI supports it and suppresses the child backdrop.
options.cost: Atlassian states it plainly: do not use dialogs to trigger other dialogs, as it is inaccessible and confusing, and do not place a modal over a panel. This is the pattern the project forbids.

options.name: The task on the page, not in a dialog
options.rationale: Where the command repeats, Carbon says make it completable on the main page rather than in a modal. An inline row becomes an editing row, which is where a repeatable task belongs.
options.cost: Inline editing works only on a narrow table, and NN/g warns the row must look visibly different or people edit it by accident.

options.name: A dialog whose command needs a second thing done first
options.rationale: The task cannot proceed until a dependency is cleared, so the dialog shows the dependency as a step of its own rather than opening a second dialog over itself.
options.cost: Now the dialog is two surfaces, which Carbon says should be a page. The line between a two-step dialog and a wizard is a matter of degree.

options.name: Stay open for the next note
options.rationale: The way Linear draws Create another: a checkbox in the dialog keeps it open for repeat entry, so five notes cost five dialogs and zero navigation. Suited to warehouse logging, where notes arrive in bursts.
options.cost: A dialog that stays open hides the list it appends to, so the reader cannot see the note land. Past three repeats in a row, the task on the page is still the honest surface.

options.name: Run the task from the command palette
options.rationale: The way Raycast runs a scoped command: one input, results grouped by record, Enter runs without leaving the page. Staff who know the palette reuse a surface they already have.
options.cost: Invisible until opened: a reader who never presses the shortcut never learns the task exists. It suits frequent staff and fails new ones, who still need the button on the page.

compact.behaviour: The recommended option reflows: one column, header actions under the title, and a table scrolls inside its own region.

patterns.assessment: Ship A for any command with one to four inputs: title, fields, one verb, no navigation. E is the runner-up for commands that repeat all day, where leaving the page costs more than the dialog saves. Never ship D: a dialog over a dialog is the nesting the project forbids, and a helper supporting it does not make it readable.

patterns.title: A drawer beside the list
patterns.question: A drawer opens from a list action so a reader can see a record without leaving the list. Atlassian's panel rules say the panel is for contextual information that complements the workflow, default 365 wide, and it becomes an overlay at 1024 and below.

options.name: Read-only record beside the list
options.rationale: The recommended shape. The list is untouched and narrowed, the record holds facts, and the way out is back to the full record. Nothing in the drawer is editable, so it cannot become a task.
options.cost: A 420-pixel drawer against a 1440 screen leaves the list about 900 wide, which is five columns and not eight. Two nested navigations on one screen.

options.name: The drawer over the list, with a scrim
options.rationale: The drawer slides over the table rather than beside it, so it can be wider and holds more without squeezing the table to five columns.
options.cost: The row the reader is comparing against is hidden. Atlassian puts the panel beside the main area and only over it at 1024 and below, so this breaks the source rule at 1440.

options.name: The drawer holding a small edit, list behind
options.rationale: A record and a two-field edit together, which is the one case where a drawer beats a dialog: the reader can see the row and the record at the same time.
options.cost: Two nested sets of controls and one narrow column. Carbon says a modal is not for repeatable work, and this is repeatable work.

options.name: The drawer as a filter, list results behind
options.rationale: A drawer that holds the filters rather than a record. The list updates behind it as each control changes, so the reader never leaves the results.
options.cost: Carbon asks that several filter categories never live inside a menu; a drawer is not a menu, but it is the same discovery problem. And it covers the toolbar the reader would use to search.

options.name: The drawer as a preview, opening over a row
options.rationale: The row's second line opens in a drawer rather than navigating. Cheap for a reader comparing two orders, and it keeps the scroll position and the filters.
options.cost: PatternFly's own guidance reserves primary-detail for comparing a short list of the same type, and requires a selected state and a close control. On 268 orders the comparison is rarer than the navigation.

options.name: The drawer at phone width, as a page with a Back
options.rationale: At 390 pixels there is no beside, so the drawer takes the screen and Back returns to the list at the same scroll position. The behaviour is honest about having no room.
options.cost: Keeping the list alive behind a full-screen view is a navigation model rather than a layout, and it has to hold filters and scroll in memory or the return is a different list.

options.name: A tabbed drawer: the record, its history, its messages
options.rationale: The way Linear layers its peek view: the row stays selected behind while tabs divide facts from history. Three views in one drawer beat three navigations when support compares refunds.
options.cost: Tabs inside a drawer are two navigations deep on one screen. Readers lose track of which tab held the fact they half-read, and the Back control has two jobs.

options.name: A drawer with a drag edge
options.rationale: The way VS Code sizes its side bar: a drag edge lets the reader trade list width for record width per task. A wide lines table gets room without a navigation, and a narrow read keeps the list.
options.cost: A width the reader sets is a width the layout must remember and repair. Every stored pixel is state that follows the reader to a narrower screen, where it has to be clamped.

compact.behaviour: At phone width there is no beside: the drawer takes the screen and Back returns to the list at the same scroll position, with its filters intact.

patterns.assessment: Ship A: the list keeps its scroll and its filters while the record reads beside it, and nothing in the drawer is editable. F is the required shape below 768 px, where beside becomes a full screen with a Back. Never ship D: filters belong in the toolbar, and a drawer over the results hides the list the filters describe.

patterns.title: A toast at the edge of the screen
patterns.question: A short message after a command. The constraints are firm: Material allows one action per snackbar and neither may be Dismiss, Carbon keeps an action-bearing toast until dismissed, and nothing critical may go in something that disappears on a timer.

options.name: A confirmation that closes by itself
options.rationale: No action on it, so it can leave on its own. Base UI's default timeout is 5,000 milliseconds, and nothing is lost by it going.
options.cost: NN/g's own example: a reader missed an error that faded after five seconds and waited five minutes. Fine for a success, wrong for anything else.

options.name: A confirmation carrying an undo, which stays
options.rationale: The toast carries one action and persists until it is dismissed, which is Carbon's rule for an actionable notification. Undo is the action, and nothing else competes for it.
options.cost: A toast that stays is on screen until the reader deals with it, so a page where the reader moves on accumulates one. Android's own guidance warns a snackbar's timer can take the action away.

options.name: A refusal, which is not a toast
options.rationale: The same slot filled with a refusal, to show why a failure must not be transient. An alert sits on the page and stays until the command succeeds.
options.cost: The visual difference between a success toast and an error alert has to be learned, and Carbon's guidance is that a tone never paints a full-width band on a page about other work.

options.name: A toast carrying two actions
options.rationale: The toast offering Undo and Dismiss together, which is the shape most people reach for first.
options.cost: Material forbids it: one action per snackbar, and it may not be Dismiss. Two buttons turn a transient message into a small panel with a timer.

options.name: A toast that is the only route to the result
options.rationale: The toast says the export finished and offers Download, which is the only way to get the file. A message that vanishes takes the result with it.
options.cost: Carbon states it directly: because toasts can dismiss automatically, users must be able to access the result elsewhere. This violates that on purpose, to show what it costs.

options.name: A stacked notification area
options.rationale: Three toasts stacked at the bottom edge, so several commands in quick succession each say what they did. Base UI caps the viewport at three.
options.cost: A stack on a page the reader is working through covers the bottom-right of the table, which is where the pagination and the bulk bar live.

options.name: A toast that links to the result
options.rationale: The way Vercel ends a deployment toast: the message links to the result, and the result also waits on the page. The toast going away costs nothing because the file does not go with it.
options.cost: Two routes to one result need the same name in both places. Where the names drift, the reader stops trusting the link and opens the page instead.

options.name: A progress toast while a slow command runs
options.rationale: The way Shopify reports a bulk export: a persistent notice with a bar and a count, dismissible only by cancelling. The reader keeps working while the count climbs.
options.cost: A toast that cannot be dismissed is a band with a timer that never fires. Past five minutes it is clutter rather than feedback, and it still covers the pagination.

compact.behaviour: The recommended option reflows: one column, header actions under the title, and a table scrolls inside its own region.

patterns.assessment: Ship A for success and B where an undo exists, with the undo toast staying until dismissed. The toast that links to the result is the runner-up for commands whose result lives elsewhere, because the link going away costs nothing. Never ship D or E: two actions turn a transient message into a panel with a timer, and a toast must never be the only route to a result.

patterns.title: A menu of a row's commands
patterns.question: The row's other commands sit behind an overflow. The first command draws inline and the rest sit behind a menu; the rule is that a row's other commands go in its row menu.

options.name: A menu with groups and a destructive item last
options.rationale: The recommended shape. The items are grouped under small headings and the destructive one sits at the end, after a separator, in the destructive tone. Nothing is disabled without a reason.
options.cost: A menu item that is disabled gives no reason in the menu itself, so the reader has to hover or press it to learn why. An explained action solves that on the page, not here.

options.name: A menu that says why an item is disabled
options.rationale: The disabled item carries its reason in place, so the reader learns it without pressing it. This is the fix for a menu whose commands are conditionally absent.
options.cost: A reason inside a menu is a paragraph among one-word items, so the menu becomes taller than the row that opened it.

options.name: A menu with a confirmation inside it
options.rationale: A destructive item opens its confirmation from inside the menu, so the menu stays and the question appears beside the row it applies to.
options.cost: That is a dialog opening over a menu, which is a menu opening a dialog. Atlassian forbids a dialog triggering another dialog; the same reasoning applies to a menu.

options.name: A menu as a split button: the first command and the rest
options.rationale: One button carries the first command and its own half carries the menu, so both are reachable without the reader ever opening anything to find the first one.
options.cost: Two targets in one shape, and the second half is a chevron that a reader may read as 'open' rather than 'the rest'. It also breaks where a button would wrap.

options.name: No menu: the row's commands are all on the row
options.rationale: One or two commands inline and nothing hidden, for a row whose whole set is small. NN/g's ceiling for inline placement is two.
options.cost: Two buttons plus a checkbox plus five columns is a wide row, and it stops fitting at 24-pixel density. And it breaks the moment a third command arrives.

options.name: A menu on the page rather than the row
options.rationale: A page-level overflow holding every command for the record, rather than a menu per row. One menu instead of twenty-five.
options.cost: A command that applies to one record cannot live in a page-level menu, and the row-menu rule says a row's commands go in its row menu. This inverts that rule.

options.name: A menu with a search field at the top
options.rationale: The way Linear filters its command menu: typing narrows twenty commands to one without submenus. Suited to rows whose command set keeps growing past what a scan can hold.
options.cost: A search field in a menu needs focus on open, which steals the keys a reader uses to move. With six commands it is furniture around a list nobody filters.

options.name: Grouped commands behind submenus
options.rationale: The way Radix UI nests submenus, which is what the shadcn menu is built on: Refund opens sideways into its three routes. Groups stay visible while the choice stays one hover away.
options.cost: Sideways menus punish every reader on touch, where hover does not exist. Three routes fit; a fourth means the submenu needs its own scroll, and then it is a panel.

compact.behaviour: The recommended option reflows: one column, header actions under the title, and a table scrolls inside its own region.

patterns.assessment: Ship A: grouped items, the destructive one last after a separator, nothing disabled without a reason. B is the runner-up where a command is often disabled, because the reason in place beats a hover. Never ship C: a confirmation inside a menu is a dialog over a menu, the same nesting the project forbids for dialogs.

patterns.title: A short panel that opens beside a control
patterns.question: Not a dialog and not a toast: something anchored to a control, closing when the reader looks away. The question is what earns one, given the rule that a reference to another record is chosen from a picker and nothing else floats.

options.name: A row preview popover on hover and focus
options.rationale: Hovering a parcel code shows the parcel's facts. It gives context without leaving the list and costs one read.
options.cost: A hover affordance is invisible on touch and undiscoverable at all. It needs focus as well as hover, and then it is two renders of every row.

options.name: A popover that explains what a term means
options.rationale: A word somebody may not know carries its glossary entry beside it. It answers the question where it is asked.
options.cost: Only for a term the application has defined. A hint on every unfamiliar word becomes noise, and the glossary has to stay in step with the hint.

options.name: A popover carrying the whole picker
options.rationale: The record picker's list opens in a popover rather than a dialog, anchored to the field, so the rest of the form stays visible behind it.
options.cost: This is what the picker in the forms category already is. It only works while the list is short enough to sit under the field without leaving the viewport.

options.name: A popover for the calendar
options.rationale: The date field opens a month grid in a popover rather than a dialog, so the form and the calendar are both visible and Escape closes the calendar alone.
options.cost: APG's date-picker combobox example puts the grid in a dialog, not a popover, because a popover can be clipped by an overflow container and the calendar is essential rather than advisory.

options.name: A popover on the copy button, saying what was copied
options.rationale: Copying an identifier is a command with no visible result otherwise, so the control confirms in place rather than opening anything.
options.cost: A confirmation for a copy is easy to miss and the value is already on screen. It is politeness rather than information.

options.name: A menu and a popover used for the same thing
options.rationale: The row menu for commands and a popover for context, side by side, so a reviewer can see the two floating shapes in this item next to each other.
options.cost: A page with both on it has three floating layers counting the dialog, and a reader has to learn which is which. This is the reason the one-overlay rule wants one overlay at a time.

options.name: A customer hover card with recent orders
options.rationale: The way GitHub Primer draws a Hovercard: identity, facts, and one link, on hover and on focus. Support reads the customer without leaving the refunds queue.
options.cost: A card that fetches on hover fires a read per row skimmed. Without focus support it is invisible on touch, where support increasingly works.

options.name: A coach mark pinned to the control
options.rationale: The way Atlassian spotlights a new control: one anchored card, one fact, one dismissal. An application that already tours new staff extends a surface they know.
options.cost: A coach mark interrupts the task it annotates. Past the first week it is dismissed unread, and every new control cannot have one or none is read.

compact.behaviour: The recommended option reflows: one column, header actions under the title, and a table scrolls inside its own region.

patterns.assessment: Ship B: a defined term carries its glossary entry where it is read, and only for terms the application has defined. A is the runner-up for dense lists where a hover card saves a navigation, on focus as well as hover. Never ship F: a menu and a popover open together teach that floating layers stack, which the one-overlay rule refuses.

patterns.title: A bar that stays while the reader works
patterns.question: Not an overlay in the dialog sense: a band the page keeps. It has to be worded as a fact about the page, because a tone may not paint a full-width band on a page about other work.

options.name: A neutral band for what this page is
options.rationale: A band across the back office that holds on every page, such as which deployment this is. Neutral, never a tone, because it is about the page rather than about work.
options.cost: A band on every page is chrome the reader cannot remove, and it competes with the heading for the top of the screen. It has to earn its height.

options.name: A bar for unsaved work, pinned to the foot
options.rationale: A bar across the bottom saying what is not saved and offering Save and Discard. It answers a question the editor currently leaves open.
options.cost: It covers the bottom of the page, which on a table is where the pagination lives. And a neutral band over a form is still a full-width band.

options.name: A bar naming a deadline that is closing
options.rationale: A band on the disputes page naming the date the bank charges back, so the work on that page has a clock the page states.
options.cost: A full-width caution band on a page about disputes is exactly the case the tone rule forbids: the tone paints the whole page rather than the thing in that state.

options.name: A bar saying what is read-only and why
options.rationale: Where a whole area is read-only for this role, one band names the reason and the grant, and the page below is drawn as it would be for a reader who could act.
options.cost: Every page of the area repeats the band, so the reader's eye skips it after the first and then misses the one place it changes.

options.name: A bar on the record page, not the console
options.rationale: The band is scoped to one record rather than the whole console, so it appears only where the fact is true and disappears everywhere else.
options.cost: The reader learns the band on one page and then has to learn that another page does not have one. A scoped band is not a deployment marker, it is a per-record notice.

options.name: No bar: the fact goes in the heading instead
options.rationale: The sandbox is named in the heading and the switcher, rather than in a band. Nothing is lost and one element is removed from every page.
options.cost: A reader who has seen four pages without the word 'sandbox' may not notice it. And the heading is already carrying the record or the page job.

options.name: A save bar pinned under the header
options.rationale: The way Shopify Polaris draws its ContextualSaveBar: a dark bar under the header with Discard and Save, appearing only while the form is dirty. The actions stay in view on a long form.
options.cost: A bar that appears and disappears moves the page it sits over. Readers learn to distrust the top of every form, dirty or not.

options.name: A band the reader dismisses for the session
options.rationale: The way GitHub Primer draws a dismissible Banner: the fact shows once per session and the close is remembered. Suited to announcements, where the second reading has no value.
options.cost: A dismissed band cannot carry anything the reader must see. The first dismissal teaches that every band can go, including the next one that matters.

compact.behaviour: The recommended option reflows: one column, header actions under the title, and a table scrolls inside its own region.

patterns.assessment: Ship A: a neutral band stating a fact about the deployment, the same on every page. E is the runner-up for facts true of one record only, drawn as a notice on that record. Never ship C: a full-width caution band paints the whole page in a tone about other work, which is the case the tone rule forbids.

patterns.title: A bottom sheet on a phone
patterns.question: On a phone there is no beside and no centre: a dialog becomes a sheet from the bottom edge. Material keeps a modal bottom sheet one swipe from dismissed, with a handle, a title, and actions stacked full width.

options.name: Order actions in a bottom sheet
options.rationale: The way Material Design draws a modal bottom sheet: a handle, a title naming the record, thumb-sized rows, one full-width dismissal. The sheet is one swipe from gone, so the list behind stays the surface.
options.cost: One record per sheet. Bulk commands need the list rather than this, and past five rows the sheet needs its own scroll.

options.name: Filters with a sticky apply bar
options.rationale: The way Shopify filters a mobile list: chips for what is set, controls for the rest, and an apply bar pinned to the foot with the match count. The reader never loses the results behind.
options.cost: Chips wrap tall. Past six filters the sheet needs its own scroll, and the match count has to be live or it lies.

options.name: A sheet that opens half and expands full
options.rationale: The way Apple Maps stages detents: half height answers the glance, full height answers the read, and the handle invites the pull. The list behind stays visible at half.
options.cost: Two heights are two layouts to keep true. Content must read sensibly cut at half, which means the fact at the cut cannot be the one that matters.

options.name: A sheet with a destructive section
options.rationale: The way an Apple action sheet seats the destructive row apart and last: the danger is separated, red, and below the fold of safe rows. The thumb meets safe actions first.
options.cost: Destructive at thumb reach still needs its confirm step, which this sheet cannot hold without nesting. The tap must open the full dialog, so the sheet is a detour rather than a shortcut.

options.name: A full-screen sheet takeover
options.rationale: The way Material draws a full-screen dialog on a phone: the sheet takes the screen while keeping the scrim behind, so dismissal still reads as dismissal rather than navigation.
options.cost: A full screen with a handle is a page that cannot link. Deep tasks deserve the route with its Back, not this.

options.name: A sheet with no handle and no dismissal
options.rationale: Some banking apps block the screen until a choice is made. This shows what that costs here: the reader is stuck until they pick a refund route.
options.cost: It traps the reader on the smallest screen, where every trap costs the most. Only a command that cannot wait earns this, and a refund route can always wait.

compact.behaviour: Every option in this item is the phone behaviour: a dialog becomes a sheet from the bottom edge with a handle, a title naming the record, and a full-width footer.

patterns.assessment: Ship A for commands and B for filters: both keep a handle, a title, and a full-width footer above the home indicator. C is the runner-up where the content is genuinely long, because detents let the reader choose half or full. Never ship F: a sheet with no dismissal traps the reader on the smallest screen, where every trap costs the most.

patterns.title: A dialog with a long body and a sticky footer
patterns.question: Some commands need more words than a dialog holds: terms, line items, per-audience consequences. The footer must stay where the thumb is while the body scrolls, or the reader agrees to what they cannot see.

options.name: A scrolling body with a pinned footer
options.rationale: The way the Stripe Dashboard pins actions on a long refund dialog: the body scrolls under a footer that never moves, so the commit stays in reach and the terms stay above it.
options.cost: A scrolling region inside a dialog is two scrolls on one screen. Keyboard readers must land in the body rather than behind it, or the terms are decoration.

options.name: A pinned header and footer with a section read
options.rationale: The way Atlassian pins modal headers on long content: the record and the amount stay named while the sections scroll. The reader never wonders which order the terms belong to.
options.cost: Pinned chrome eats a third of a phone dialog, and the body shows two lines at a time. On a short dialog the pinned header is furniture.

options.name: Sections that collapse
options.rationale: The way Shopify collapses modal sections: one open at a time, the rest one tap away. Four sections read as four lines until the reader wants one.
options.cost: Collapsed sections hide the term the reader most needed. The dialog must open the section that matters for this order, which means it must know which one that is.

options.name: A summary pinned above the footer
options.rationale: The way Stripe pins the total above Pay: the figure the click commits to stays visible while the terms scroll. The reader signs the number, not the scroll position.
options.cost: The pinned summary duplicates the body. Where the two disagree the reader trusts the pin, and the body becomes decoration nobody checks.

options.name: A wide dialog for dense facts
options.rationale: The way Vercel widens a modal for dense settings: two columns of facts read side by side instead of stacked. Four sections fit without scrolling on a laptop.
options.cost: Wide on desktop is full-width on a phone, where the columns stack and the dialog doubles in height. The no-scroll promise holds at exactly one width.

options.name: No pinned footer: the buttons scroll away
options.rationale: Included to refuse it: without a scroll cap the dialog grows past the viewport and the footer sits below the fold. The reader agrees first and finds how after.
options.cost: On a phone the footer is two screens down, past terms nobody scrolled to. This is the shape every other option in this item exists to replace.

compact.behaviour: The recommended option reflows: one column, header actions under the title, and a table scrolls inside its own region.

patterns.assessment: Ship A: one scrolling body, one pinned footer, nothing else. D is the runner-up wherever money moves, because the totals pinned above the footer are read at the click. Never ship F: buttons that scroll away ask the reader to agree first and find how after.

patterns.title: A keyboard shortcut help overlay
patterns.question: Staff who live in lists learn keys faster than clicks. Linear and GitHub both answer ? with an overlay, grouped by where the keys work, closable with the same key.

options.name: A grouped grid of shortcuts
options.rationale: The way Linear answers ?: groups by where the keys work, each key in its own cap, the same key closes. Staff learn the catalogue in one reading.
options.cost: A catalogue dialog lists keys the reader has no reason to press yet. Past twenty keys it is reference rather than learning, and reference belongs on a page.

options.name: A single-column list
options.rationale: The way Superhuman lists every key in one column: no groups to learn, scanning top to bottom, each row one fact. Shorter to build and shorter to read.
options.cost: One column grows long. Groups would shorten the search for a key the reader half-remembers, and this list has none.

options.name: Shortcuts inside the command palette
options.rationale: The way Raycast teaches keys in its footer: the hints sit where the keys work, so every palette visit is a lesson. No separate catalogue to keep true.
options.cost: Hints teach three keys. The rest stay hidden until the full dialog opens, so this is a reminder rather than a catalogue.

options.name: Shortcuts for this page only
options.rationale: The way Figma scopes its shortcuts panel to the tool at hand: only the keys that work here, so the list stays short enough to learn. The global keys live one link away.
options.cost: Page-scoped lists repeat the global keys on every page or omit them. Either way the reader meets two lists where one catalogue would do.

options.name: A printable cheat sheet page
options.rationale: The way GitHub Docs prints its cheat sheet: one page, two columns, made for paper pinned beside a screen. Counter staff learn from paper faster than from a dialog.
options.cost: A page for keys is a destination nobody bookmarks. The keys are needed where the work is, and this page is never there.

options.name: No overlay: hints only on tooltips
options.rationale: Included to refuse it: the catalogue hides one hover at a time, and touch readers never meet it at all. A reader who would learn ten keys learns none.
options.cost: Each hint is accurate and each is undiscoverable. The tooltip teaches the key for a control already found, which is the one key that reader needed least.

compact.behaviour: The recommended option reflows: one column, header actions under the title, and a table scrolls inside its own region.

patterns.assessment: Ship A: three groups, one grid, every key the application honours, closed by the same key. D is the runner-up on dense pages, where a This page section answers the only keys that work there. Never ship F: tooltips alone hide the catalogue from the reader who would learn it fastest.

patterns.title: A context menu where the pointer is
patterns.question: A right click asks what this thing can do. Linear and VS Code answer at the pointer, with the same commands the row menu holds, so the menu is a shortcut rather than a second set.

options.name: A right-click menu on a row
options.rationale: The way Linear answers a right click: the row's own commands at the pointer, nothing added, nothing missing. The menu is a shortcut to the row menu rather than a second set.
options.cost: Right click is invisible. Staff who never try it keep the row menu, and both menus must hold the same commands or one of them lies.

options.name: A context menu with icons and shortcuts
options.rationale: The way VS Code pairs icons with keys in its context menus: the icon scans, the key teaches, and the pair stays the same everywhere the command appears.
options.cost: Icons for Refund and Report read as decoration. A wrong icon teaches faster than no icon, and every icon is a second name to keep true in two languages.

options.name: A context menu for a bulk selection
options.rationale: The way Figma rewrites its right-click menu for a multi-selection: the count in every label, single-record commands gone. The reader cannot ask three rows to open one record.
options.cost: The menu rewrites per count, so muscle memory for one row breaks at three. And the count must be exact at the click, not at the render.

options.name: A long-press menu on touch
options.rationale: The way iOS answers a long press: the same menu, opened by time rather than button. Touch staff get the shortcut without a second design to learn.
options.cost: Long press has no hover state, so discovery is zero and the delay punishes every use. It is a courtesy for those who know, not a route for those who do not.

options.name: A context menu on empty space
options.rationale: The way VS Code menus its explorer background: page commands where the pointer is, so Refresh and Export do not need a trip to the toolbar.
options.cost: Page commands in a hidden menu compete with the toolbar that already holds them. Two homes for Export means two places to keep true.

options.name: No menu: the browser default answers
options.rationale: Included to refuse it: silence hands the gesture to the browser, whose commands act on the page rather than the record. Staff learn the gesture does nothing for them and stop trying.
options.cost: Inspect element beside Reload, on a row about money. The absence is not neutral; it teaches that right click is not part of the application.

compact.behaviour: Touch has no right click: a long press opens the same menu, with the same commands and the same order, positioned above the row.

patterns.assessment: Ship A: the row's own commands at the pointer, nothing added, nothing missing, closed by the same click elsewhere. C is the runner-up for bulk work, where the menu rewrites itself for the selection count. Never ship F: silence hands the gesture to the browser, whose commands act on the page rather than the record.

patterns.title: Creating one record
patterns.question: The rule is explicit: a create stays a dialog or a page, never a drawer. One to four inputs is a dialog; more is a page. The open question is what a create looks like before the reader has entered anything.

options.name: A dialog for two or three inputs
options.rationale: A dialog with three inputs, one verb on the commit button, Cancel beside it. This is where most creates belong and where they usually end up.
options.cost: A create that grows past four inputs has to leave the dialog, and the reader's typed values have to come with it or be lost.

options.name: A full page for the ones that grow
options.rationale: The form pages with sections, steps or more than four inputs. A page gives the fields room and gives the result a link.
options.cost: Leaving the list to create one record, and coming back to the list afterwards, is two navigations for every single creation. It only pays when the form is long.

options.name: Create from a template, chosen before the form
options.rationale: One shape offers 'A blank delivery' or 'A template' at the top of the form. Choosing first means the form below already knows what it is for.
options.cost: A control inside a form that is not part of the form. Once a template is chosen the toggle is meaningless but stays visible, because nothing knows the create is already under way.

options.name: Create from a copy of an existing record
options.rationale: Duplicate a delivery that worked, then change what is different. The copy carries products and a plan and starts as a draft with nothing committed.
options.cost: A duplicate of a shipped delivery is nearly meaningless: the orders and the money all belong to the original. It only works for a template-like record with no history.

options.name: Create inline in the table, as an empty first row
options.rationale: The table grows a form row at the top. Nothing opens, nothing closes, and the reader sees what they are adding in the context of what is already there.
options.cost: Carbon says a modal is for tasks that are not repeated, and this is the most repeated create in the back office. It also puts a form inside a table, which the layout rules do not cover.

options.name: Create many at once from a file
options.rationale: A bulk create: a file, a check of what it made, and a report. This is the shape for a season of products or a list of customers, where one dialog per record would be absurd.
options.cost: An import writes across many records at once. A partial failure has to be reportable and undoable while nothing is charged.

options.name: One question per step, kept as a draft
options.rationale: A long create split into one question per step with a progress bar and an already-answered recap. Nothing is lost between steps because every answer saves a draft.
options.cost: Steps hide the whole form, so a reader who knows every answer types slower than on one page. Drafts also need a list, an expiry, and a rule for who can see them.

options.name: A split button that names the starting point
options.rationale: The way Shopify Polaris draws a split button: the main face creates a blank delivery, the chevron names the other ways to start. Three starting points already exist on this list, and this is the control that holds them without a toggle inside the form.
options.cost: The chevron hides the template and the duplicate from anyone who never opens it. A first-time user still lands on the blank form and never learns the faster start exists.

options.name: A command menu create, from anywhere
options.rationale: The way Linear opens creation: one shortcut, one input, and the record type is chosen by typing. A manager who lives in the back office creates without travelling to the list first.
options.cost: Invisible until learned, and it only starts the create: the form still opens afterwards. It needs the shortcut taught on the page, or nobody finds it.

compact.behaviour: The recommended option reflows: one column, header actions under the title, and a table scrolls inside its own region.

patterns.assessment: The dialog stays the pick for one to four inputs: it keeps the list behind it and commits with one verb. The full page is the runner-up and the right one past four inputs or with sections. The inline table row is the one to refuse, because a form inside a table breaks the layout rules and hides validation. Of the further options, the split button earns its place on the deliveries list, where three starting points already exist.

patterns.title: Changing a record that already exists
patterns.question: A record page with two sections can carry one Save per section. A reader who edits the first and saves the second believes they saved both.

options.name: One Save per page
options.rationale: The whole page is one form and one Save. A reader who has changed three things saves once, and nothing on the page disagrees about what is pending.
options.cost: A partial failure loses the lot, and a reader who wants to save the name and leave the dates cannot. The page has to say what changed while it is dirty.

options.name: One Save per section, and each says what it saves
options.rationale: Each section's button repeats its own verb: Save the name, Save the labelling. Nothing is ambiguous about what a click will commit.
options.cost: Still two commits on one screen. It works only because each button names what it commits, which is two things a reader can forget to do.

options.name: Editing in place in the list row
options.rationale: One cell becomes an input, the row looks different while it does, and Save and Cancel sit in the row. NN/g's rule: the row must visibly change or people edit by accident.
options.cost: It works only on a narrow table. This table has five columns, which is past the width NN/g means by narrow.

options.name: Editing with the impact stated before the save
options.rationale: Where a change breaks something, the page says what before the reader commits: who is affected, what stops working, what cannot be changed back.
options.cost: It needs a read that answers the hypothetical, which is not a command and not the record as it stands.

options.name: Editing in a dialog, for two fields
options.rationale: Two fields do not need a page. A dialog holds them, the list stays behind, and the reader sees the change in context as soon as it lands.
options.cost: Carbon says a modal is not for repeatable work. Renaming a product happens a dozen times a season, which is repeatable enough to matter.

options.name: Editing blocked, with the reason and the way out
options.rationale: A change that the record's own state forbids. The field is read-only, the reason is stated on the field, and the command that would unblock it is named.
options.cost: The reader has to leave to unblock and come back, and whatever they typed is only kept if the page holds it. Read-only plus a link is the compromise.

options.name: Autosave, with the saved state always visible
options.rationale: The way Notion saves: there is no Save button, every keystroke lands, and the header always says when. A description edited over an afternoon cannot be lost to a closed tab.
options.cost: Two people typing at once overwrite each other without noticing, and every keystroke is an audit entry unless the trail groups them. It fits free text, not prices or counts.

options.name: Edit in a side panel, the list still visible
options.rationale: The way HubSpot edits a record: the list stays on screen and the form opens beside it. Renaming twelve deliveries in a row means twelve saves without twelve page loads.
options.cost: It breaks the rule that a form is a dialog or a page, never a drawer, so create and edit would disagree about where a form lives. The panel is also too narrow for sections or steps.

compact.behaviour: The recommended option reflows: one column, header actions under the title, and a table scrolls inside its own region.

patterns.assessment: One Save per page is the pick: a reader who changed three things saves once, and the dirty banner says what is pending. The impact statement is the runner-up for any change that breaks something, where the page must say what before the commit. The inline list-row edit is the one to refuse on this wide table. Autosave earns its place only for free text where two people cannot collide; the version history in the after-the-fact item is its required companion.

patterns.title: Removing something
patterns.question: The evidence points one way: prefer archive over delete. Shopify says product deletion is irreversible and suggests archiving instead; Google Drive's trash empties after 30 days; GitHub's repository deletion is recoverable for 90 days. No cited system publishes a pattern for deletion blocked by dependent records.

options.name: Archive, with what archiving means
options.rationale: Archive is the default removal. The dialog says what stops being visible and what is kept, and the record keeps its place with a state that says it is archived.
options.cost: The reader now has two ways to hide something, archive and delete, and a list that shows both needs a view or a filter separating them.

options.name: Delete, where nothing may be archived
options.rationale: Some records must go rather than be hidden. The dialog says the record is gone for good, and it names what is kept because a record of the decision outlives the record.
options.cost: Everything the company holds has to stay reconstructable for an audit, which means 'delete' removes the operational record and keeps the evidence. Two different things under one verb.

options.name: Removal blocked, naming what blocks it
options.rationale: The command cannot run because something depends on the record. The dialog names the dependency and the command that deals with it, rather than refusing with a bare code.
options.cost: No cited design system publishes this pattern, so it is an inference from the two cases that exist: Cloudscape's prerequisite-disabled button and the product page's explained refusal.

options.name: Reversal rather than removal, for money
options.rationale: A refund does not remove an order, it reverses it and leaves the record. The customer is shown the order before and after, so the reversal is visible as a fact rather than an absence.
options.cost: The record grows rather than shrinks, and a list of orders has to be able to show an order that has been fully reversed without it looking empty.

options.name: Void, where the record must stay but stop counting
options.rationale: A code that was issued and is being withdrawn. The code stops working, the code stays on the order, and the record says why.
options.cost: Void and refund are different verbs for different effects and a reader has to know which is which. Voiding a code that was already used is refused outright, because the order log holds that.

options.name: Suspend, for something that must keep running
options.rationale: Pause rather than remove: the record keeps every property, it stops accepting what it accepts, and the page says what is still possible while it is paused.
options.cost: A pause is invisible to a customer unless something tells them, so 'what happens to somebody who tries to order while this is paused' has to be answered by the same page.

options.name: Trash with thirty days to change your mind
options.rationale: The way Google Drive removes: delete moves the record to a trash that empties itself after thirty days. The verb stays delete, which is what the reader reaches for, and the reversibility stays too.
options.cost: There is still a day when the record goes for good, and the trash needs its own view, its own emptying rule, and an answer for records with placed orders. Those cannot sit in a trash the same way.

options.name: No confirmation, one Undo in a toast
options.rationale: The way Gmail removes mail: the command applies at once and the toast carries the way back for eight seconds. Removing a plan entry is too small for a dialog and exactly the size of an Undo.
options.cost: It only fits what is cheap to reverse. Money, orders and anything the audit trail must hold still need the dialog that says what happens, because an Undo that expires is not a record.

compact.behaviour: The recommended option reflows: one column, header actions under the title, and a table scrolls inside its own region.

patterns.assessment: Archive stays the pick: it is reversible, it keeps the audit trail, and the Archived view is the way back. The thirty-day trash is the runner-up where delete is the verb the reader reaches for, because it keeps the reversibility without keeping two hiding verbs. Never ship a bare delete for anything with history; the delete dialog is only for records that must go, and it must say what is kept. The Undo toast earns its place for small reversible removes such as a plan entry.

patterns.title: Removing several at once
patterns.question: A bulk removal is the case where a confirmation stops being a speed bump and starts being a safety net, because the count itself is the risk.

options.name: A dialog naming the count and the money
options.rationale: A bulk refund confirmation, which lists the records and totals the money before the commit button. The count and the amount are the two things a reader must check.
options.cost: Twenty-five rows in a dialog is a scroll inside a dialog. Past about five, the total carries the meaning and the list is a detail the reader cannot afford to read.

options.name: A dialog that names the scope it is about to use
options.rationale: Where the selection could be page-scoped or filter-scoped, the dialog says which. Gmail's banner exists for exactly this and Shopify documents the same escalation.
options.cost: Two sentences of scope in a dialog about money, and the reader has to check the number as well as the amount. Both are worth checking, and the dialog carries both.

options.name: Bulk removal as a bulk archive, then a dialog for the record
options.rationale: Archive is cheap and reversible, so a bulk archive needs only a count. The dialog appears once per record type rather than once per selection.
options.cost: Archiving 200 deliveries hides 200 deliveries, and the reader has no way back except an Archived view. The safety net is the view, not the dialog.

options.name: A partial bulk refusal: some rows will not do it
options.rationale: When some of the selection cannot take the command, the dialog says which and why before anything runs, and offers to do the rest.
options.cost: A partial result has to be reportable afterwards as well, so the reader ends up reading the same information twice. Better to refuse the whole batch and let them narrow it.

options.name: A typed confirmation for a bulk removal
options.rationale: Where a bulk removal is genuinely dangerous, type the count. The number is the thing being confirmed, not the name of one record.
options.cost: Typing 200 trains copy and paste, which is the reflex the pattern exists to break. Cloudscape's own restriction is to the most dangerous object, and this is many objects.

options.name: A bulk removal that is a cancellation, with consequences per row
options.rationale: Cancelling a plan of deliveries is one command with several effects, and the dialog lists them per row rather than as a total. What the reader needs is not the sum but which deliveries have customers.
options.cost: A dialog that varies per row is a table in a dialog, which is a page. Past a handful of rows, the consequence list belongs on a page of its own.

options.name: A background job with a report, for the large ones
options.rationale: The way Shopify runs bulk operations: past a size no dialog can carry, the selection runs as a job and a report lands afterwards. Refunding 1,204 orders cannot be checked on screen, so it is checked in the report instead.
options.cost: The reader walks away and comes back, so the job needs progress, a cancel, and a report that names every row it refused. A job that fails halfway also needs a rule for what already ran.

options.name: A dry run first, the way a migration previews
options.rationale: The way Terraform plans before it applies: a page that says what each row will do, so the refusals are read before anything runs rather than after. Three rows fit; three hundred still fit, because it is a page.
options.cost: The plan can go stale between reading and applying: a payment can settle, a window can close. The apply step must recheck every row and say which answer changed.

compact.behaviour: The recommended option reflows: one column, header actions under the title, and a table scrolls inside its own region.

patterns.assessment: The dialog naming the count and the money stays the pick up to about twenty-five rows: the two figures are what the reader must check. The background job is the runner-up past that, where a dialog cannot carry the list and a report must land afterwards. Never ship the typed count for an ordinary bulk remove; it trains copy and paste, and it belongs only to the irreversible import undo. The dry-run plan earns its place where rows can refuse, because it shows the refusals before anything runs.

patterns.title: Creating a record and then filling it in
patterns.question: One answer is a setup section on the home page and a getting-started page. The alternative is to require everything at creation.

options.name: Create with a name, fill the rest later
options.rationale: The name is the only required field, and the record exists as a draft. Every later addition is its own command, each audited, each reconstructable.
options.cost: A draft delivery is nearly useless on its own, and if nothing ever prompts the reader to finish it, it sits unfinished on a list. The setup section is the counterweight.

options.name: Everything required before the record exists
options.rationale: The record is not created until it is whole: name, date, warehouse, one product, one channel. Nothing half-made is ever in a list.
options.cost: A five-part form before anything exists, and a reader who only wants to pencil in a date has to do all of it.

options.name: Create from a series, where the series holds the parts
options.rationale: The plan carries the warehouse, the delivery plan and the products, and each delivery is created already holding them. One create, many records, no repetition.
options.cost: A delivery created from a plan can be edited away from it, and then the two disagree. The plan has to state which fields are shared and what diverging means.

options.name: A checklist that closes itself
options.rationale: After creation, the page is a checklist and each item is a command. Finishing the last item removes the checklist rather than leaving a ticked list.
options.cost: A checklist on every draft is a page of work before anything is usable, and it is one more place that has to know which commands are already done.

options.name: Create inside a wizard that ends at publish
options.rationale: One flow from nothing to on sale: the delivery, its products, its channel and the publish step. The reader never lands on a draft they have to finish by hand.
options.cost: Carbon says simplify before you wizard, and a stepper is only for a linear flow of three or more steps. Going on sale really is linear, so this is the case a stepper exists for.

options.name: Nothing created until the reader says publish
options.rationale: The form holds everything in the browser and nothing is written until the last click. One command, one audit entry, one record per creation.
options.cost: Losing the browser loses the work, and a five-step form held in memory is a lot to lose. The record's state during the form does not exist, so nothing else can read it.

options.name: A setup guide on the home page, with progress
options.rationale: The way Stripe onboards: the home page carries the setup as a guide with a progress bar, not as one more list. A reader who finished three of five sees two left every time they sign in.
options.cost: It sits at the top of the home page until it is done, and a guide nobody dismisses becomes a banner nobody reads. It needs a dismiss that stays dismissed per company, not per person.

options.name: Nudges at the point of use, not a checklist
options.rationale: The way Webflow gates publish: no checklist page, just the missing piece named where it is missing. The publish button says what it needs, and the section that needs it says so too.
options.cost: Five missing pieces mean five separate discoveries, and nothing tells the reader how much is left. It fits one gap, not a new company with five.

compact.behaviour: The recommended option reflows: one column, header actions under the title, and a table scrolls inside its own region.

patterns.assessment: Create with a name and fill the rest later stays the pick: the record exists as a draft and every later addition is its own audited command. The home-page setup guide is the runner-up and the required companion, because a draft nobody is prompted to finish is a dead record. Never ship everything-required-before-the-record-exists, which blocks pencilling in a date, or nothing-until-publish, which loses the work with the browser. The point-of-use nudge earns its place beside the checklist for readers who skip guides.

patterns.title: Changing something that has already happened
patterns.question: A record of what is true now cannot always be edited. A charge already priced must stay reconstructable, which makes several edits structurally different rather than merely harder.

options.name: The old value stays on the record beside the new
options.rationale: A rename shows what it was and when. The record never loses the earlier name, because an order placed last month must still resolve to the delivery it was placed for.
options.cost: Every edit grows the record, and a reader looking for 'what is this called' has to skip past what it used to be called.

options.name: The edit is refused, with the newer way named
options.rationale: Some edits cannot happen at all after the fact. The command is not disabled silently: it says what cannot change, and names the command that achieves what the reader was trying to do.
options.cost: A reader who wants a price change on a sold unit is told no and given a different thing. That is the honest answer, but it is also the most likely source of support cases.

options.name: A correction, dated and attributed
options.rationale: Where a figure was entered wrong and the correction is a statement about the past, the record carries the correction as its own dated fact rather than overwriting the wrong one.
options.cost: Two figures for the same thing is confusing on any page that shows only one of them, so every read has to choose which to show and the choice is a rule rather than a display decision.

options.name: A change with a window, before it takes effect
options.rationale: A scheduled change: what it will be, when it takes effect, and how to stop it before then. The record shows both the current value and the one coming.
options.cost: Two values on one record is a rule every read has to honour, and 'what is this worth' has a date attached that a reader has to notice.

options.name: A change that only reaches what has not shipped
options.rationale: The edit page says which population the change reaches, and which it cannot. Editing a delivery plan changes this delivery; editing the warehouse does not.
options.cost: It needs a read that counts the affected population, and that count is a fact the API has to be able to answer rather than a number typed into the copy.

options.name: A reverse, keeping both figures and the reason
options.rationale: A charge that turns out to be wrong is reversed with a reason, and both figures stay on the record. This is the shape every financial correction takes.
options.cost: The record holds two values for one thing, and every statement has to decide which one to print. That decision is a rule, not a display preference.

options.name: A version history with restore
options.rationale: The way Notion keeps versions: every save is a version with a who and a when, and restoring writes a new version rather than rewriting the old. A name changed in October can be read in June as what it was then.
options.cost: Versions multiply: a description edited fifty times has fifty rows, and only the last few matter. The list needs grouping by day, or it hides the one version anyone wants.

options.name: Two people for a change to the past
options.rationale: The way GitHub guards a protected branch: a change to what is settled needs a second person. A correction to money that one person could type alone is the case this exists for.
options.cost: Every correction waits on someone else, and a team of one cannot use it at all. It fits corrections to money and the dispatch log, not names and text.

compact.behaviour: The recommended option reflows: one column, header actions under the title, and a table scrolls inside its own region.

patterns.assessment: Keeping the old value beside the new stays the pick: an order placed last month must still resolve to the delivery it was placed for. The dated correction is the runner-up where a fact was entered wrong, and the reversal is the only shape for money. Never ship a silent overwrite of anything priced or shipped; where no honest edit exists, the refusal with the newer way named is the option. The version history earns its place for names and text, and two-person approval for corrections to money.

patterns.title: Duplicating a record
patterns.question: A duplicate is a create that starts from something. The copy carries the setup and never the history: prices and a delivery plan travel, orders and money stay with the original.

options.name: A dialog that says what the copy carries
options.rationale: The way Shopify duplicates a product: the dialog names what the copy carries before it exists. The copy starts as a draft, so nothing about it is on sale until the reader says so.
options.cost: A long carried list makes a long dialog, and most of it is read once. Past about six parts the checklist option carries the meaning better.

options.name: One click from the row menu, then a toast
options.rationale: The way Mailchimp duplicates a campaign: one menu item, no questions, and the copy lands as a draft with a toast confirming it. A discount code carries no customers, so there is nothing to check first.
options.cost: No moment to rename or to choose what travels. It fits records with no customers and no money; a delivery duplicated this way would surprise everyone in June.

options.name: Copy of, renamed where it lands
options.rationale: The way Figma duplicates a layer: the copy appears beside the original as Copy of, already selected for rename. Duplicating a price tier is renaming plus a price check, and both happen in the list.
options.cost: The copy exists before it is named, so a list can fill with Copy of Standard rows that nobody renamed. It needs the draft state to say the copy is not on sale yet.

options.name: Choose what the copy carries
options.rationale: The way Notion duplicates a page with its subpages offered as toggles: every part is a checkbox with its size beside it. A reader who wants the prices but not the team says so here.
options.cost: Six checkboxes for a routine duplicate is five too many on the tenth use. It fits the first duplicate of a season, not the weekly one.

options.name: Duplication refused where there is nothing to carry
options.rationale: The way Stripe treats a paid invoice as a fact: it can be credited, never copied. An order is one customer payment for one set of products, so duplicating it would invent a payment that never happened.
options.cost: The reader who wants a second order like this one must build it by hand. The manual order is the way out, and this page must name it or the refusal leaves the reader with nowhere to go.

options.name: Duplicate a session inside its series
options.rationale: The series holds what every delivery shares, so the duplicate only asks for the date. The shared parts are named, not chosen, because the series owns them.
options.cost: Anything the delivery changed away from the series raises the question of which version travels. The page must say the series version wins, or the copy silently keeps the divergence.

compact.behaviour: The recommended option reflows: one column, header actions under the title, and a table scrolls inside its own region.

patterns.assessment: The dialog that says what the copy carries is the pick: a duplicate that silently drops the prices is worse than no duplicate. The carry checklist is the runner-up where the parts vary per company. Never ship one-click duplication for a delivery; it earns its place for discount codes and plan entries, which carry no customers. An order is never duplicated, because it is one customer's payment.

patterns.title: Putting a list in order by hand
patterns.question: Products, plan entries and storefront sections all have an order the reader sets. The customer reads the order the reader left, so the control must work for a mouse, a keyboard and a finger.

options.name: Drag handles in the list
options.rationale: The way Notion reorders blocks: a grip on every row, the dragged row lifted, and a line where it will land. The order saves on drop, so there is nothing to forget.
options.cost: A grip cannot be used from a keyboard or announced by a screen reader, and on a phone it conflicts with scrolling. The menu move is not an alternative; it is the other half of this option.

options.name: Move up and Move down in the row menu
options.rationale: The way Linear moves an issue with the keyboard: the same move drag performs, as a named command. A screen reader announces Moved to position 2, and nothing about it needs a pointer.
options.cost: Moving one row past twenty others is twenty menu opens. It is the accessible half of drag, not a replacement for it on long lists.

options.name: A position number typed on each row
options.rationale: The way WordPress orders menu items: a number on each row, one save for the whole list. Jumping a row from 14 to 1 is one keystroke where dragging would cross the whole list.
options.cost: Two rows numbered 3 are a question the page cannot answer, and renumbering fourteen rows by hand is slower than dragging one. Numbers suit a jump across a long list and nothing else.

options.name: Automatic order, with pinned rows on top
options.rationale: The way Shopify sorts products: the list follows a rule such as price or date, and pinned rows stay above it. Ninety-three deliveries need no hand ordering; the two that matter stay first by hand.
options.cost: Two orders on one list is a rule every reader must learn: pinned first, then the rule. A reader who sorts by name and finds two rows out of place has to be told why.

options.name: Order the storefront sections on the preview
options.rationale: The way Squarespace orders page sections: the list and the preview sit side by side, and moving a row moves the preview with it. The order is the design, so it is judged as one.
options.cost: Two panes need a wide screen; below 768 px the preview stacks under the list and the judgement breaks. It also fits sections, not products, which customers read as a list either way.

options.name: Move to top and Move to bottom for long lists
options.rationale: The way Trello positions a card: a position menu with top and bottom jumps beside the step moves. On a plan of forty entries the jump is the only move anyone uses.
options.cost: Top and bottom move without aim: everything important ends up first and the top becomes its own unordered list. It needs the step moves beside it for the ordering that follows.

compact.behaviour: The recommended option reflows: one column, header actions under the title, and a table scrolls inside its own region.

patterns.assessment: Drag handles in the list are the pick: direct, visible, and the order saves as it changes. Move up and Move down in the row menu are the required companion, because drag alone leaves keyboard and screen-reader users behind. Never ship typed position numbers alone; two rows both numbered 3 are a question the page cannot answer. The storefront preview earns its place for sections, where the order is the design.

patterns.title: Restoring an archived record
patterns.question: Archive is only honest if restore works. A restore returns the record to where it was, with its history, and says so when something changed while it was away.

options.name: Restore from the archived view
options.rationale: The way Shopify restores an archived product: the Archived view lists what is hidden, and each row carries its own Restore. The record returns to the state it held, not to a draft.
options.cost: Nobody opens the Archived view unless they remember it exists. Anything restored from here must say where it went, or the record vanishes from this list into another nobody is reading.

options.name: Undo in the seconds after archiving
options.rationale: The way Gmail keeps an Undo on every archive: the toast is the way back in the seconds after the click. Archiving the wrong delivery is fixed where it happened, without a visit to another view.
options.cost: Eight seconds and it is gone, so this is a correction for slips, not the way back. Anyone restoring a day later still needs the archived view.

options.name: Restore from the record page
options.rationale: The way GitHub reopens a closed issue from the issue itself: the archived banner sits on the record, with Restore beside it. Anyone arriving by link or search restores without finding the archived view first.
options.cost: The page must work while archived: read-only where it matters, with every command saying it needs a restore first. A banner on a broken page is worse than no banner.

options.name: Restore refused: the parent is still archived
options.rationale: The way Jira refuses to reopen a subtask whose parent is closed: the restore names the blocker and offers the way out. A price tier cannot return while its delivery stays archived.
options.cost: Two dialogs for one restore, and the offer to restore both at once is a second command hiding inside the first. It must say both are restored, not just the row that was clicked.

options.name: Restore with a name taken since
options.rationale: The way Notion renames a restored page when the title is taken: the restore keeps both records by renaming the restored record. Two tiers called Standard would disagree on the invoice, so only one keeps the name.
options.cost: The restored record comes back under a name nobody chose, and renaming it again is a second command. The dialog must show the name it will hold, not just the clash.

options.name: Restore several at once
options.rationale: The way Google Drive restores a selection: the count is the confirmation, and every record returns to where it was. Archiving a whole season by mistake is fixed in the same gesture it was made with.
options.cost: A bulk restore can return records to states the reader forgot, including one that clashes. The report afterwards must name each record and where it landed.

compact.behaviour: The recommended option reflows: one column, header actions under the title, and a table scrolls inside its own region.

patterns.assessment: Restore from the archived view is the pick: the view is the way back, and the row says where the record returns to. The record-page banner is the runner-up for anyone arriving by link. Never ship a restore that silently un-archives parents or overwrites a newer name; both need their own dialog. The Undo toast earns its place in the seconds after archiving, not as the way back days later.

patterns.title: Inviting a team member
patterns.question: Warehouse crew join per delivery and staff join per company. An invitation names the person, the role and the scope before it is sent, because access granted by accident must be found and removed later.

options.name: Invite by email, with the role chosen first
options.rationale: The way Slack invites: one dialog, the email, then the role with what it can do beside it. The scope line says whether Noa joins the company or one delivery, before the invitation exists.
options.cost: One invitation per person, typed by hand. Assigning forty pickers for a season needs the link option beside it.

options.name: An invite link anyone with it can use
options.rationale: The way Discord invites: a link with an expiry and a use count, for the forty pickers nobody wants to type by hand. The link joins one delivery in one role, and nothing else.
options.cost: Anyone with the link joins, including anyone it was forwarded to. It fits warehouse crew on one delivery and is refused for owner, finance and manager roles.

options.name: Invite to one delivery, not the company
options.rationale: The way Linear invites to one team rather than the workspace: the scope is chosen up front and printed on the invitation. Noa works the loading bay on 14 Mar and sees nothing else afterwards.
options.cost: Scopes multiply: sixty deliveries a year is sixty small grants to read later. The team page must group by person as well as by delivery, or nobody can answer what Noa can do.

options.name: Pending invitations, with resend and revoke
options.rationale: The way GitHub lists organization invitations: every waiting invitation shows its age, its expiry and its way out. An invitation is read far more often than it is sent, so the list is the pattern.
options.cost: A list of the waiting is a list of the neglected: half of it expired quietly. Expired rows must say they expired and offer reissue, or the list fills with rows that can no longer be used.

options.name: An expired invitation, reissued
options.rationale: The way Google Workspace reissues an expired invite: the old link stays dead and a new one goes out with a fresh expiry. Reissuing is a new invitation with the old role, not the old link made live again.
options.cost: Two emails for one join, and the first still reads as live to anyone who kept it. The expired link must land on a page that says it expired, not on a bare refusal.

options.name: A request to join, approved by an owner
options.rationale: The way Slack handles join requests: the asker waits in a queue and an owner approves with the role. It is drawn here to be refused, because the back office has no join request and adding one would invite strangers to ask.
options.cost: A queue nobody asked for, and every request is a stranger asking for access to money. The company invites its team; nobody applies. This option stays in the library as the refused shape.

compact.behaviour: The recommended option reflows: one column, header actions under the title, and a table scrolls inside its own region.

patterns.assessment: Invite by email with the role chosen first is the pick: the person, the role and the scope are all named on one dialog. The pending list with resend and revoke is the runner-up and the required companion, because an invitation waits far longer than it takes to send. Never ship an open invite link for staff roles; it earns its place only for warehouse crew on one delivery. A request to join is refused: the company invites, nobody applies.

patterns.title: Publishing and unpublishing a listing
patterns.question: A draft is private until customers can see it. Publishing says what customers will find, and unpublishing says what happens to what they found, because placed orders outlive either command.

options.name: Publish with the readiness check beside it
options.rationale: The way Webflow publishes: the dialog lists what is ready and the button commits only when all of it is. Publishing is the one create the reader cannot undo quietly, so the check is the dialog.
options.cost: A check that reads five systems can disagree with the page behind it by the time the button lands. The publish command must recheck and refuse with the missing piece named.

options.name: Unpublish with the customer consequences stated
options.rationale: The way Shopify unpublishes a sales channel: the dialog says what stops and what stays, because placed orders are a commitment that outlives the listing. Unpublishing stops sales; it touches nothing sold.
options.cost: Two truths on one dialog, and the second is the one customers will ask about. The page behind it must keep answering for the sold units after the listing is gone.

options.name: Publish on a date, set in advance
options.rationale: The way WordPress schedules a post: the date is set on the draft and the publish happens without anyone present. A sale starting at 10:00 on a Tuesday should not need Sam Rivera at the desk at 10:00.
options.cost: A scheduled publish can land on a draft that changed since: the price moved, the stock moved. The scheduler must recheck at the hour and hold the publish with the reason named.

options.name: Publish blocked, with the missing pieces listed
options.rationale: The way Squarespace blocks publish on an unfinished site: the button stays, the missing pieces are listed with links, and each link lands on the field. A disabled button alone would read as broken.
options.cost: Every missing piece is a link away, and fixing one can reveal the next. The list must be complete on first read or the reader learns of them one publish attempt at a time.

options.name: Pause sales without unpublishing
options.rationale: The way Shopify pauses a store: the page stays up and says so, sales stop, and everything sold stays valid. A product that may restock needs the pause, not the unpublish.
options.cost: Paused reads as broken to a customer who does not read the message. The customer message must say when sales return, or customers stop trusting the pause.

options.name: Publish per channel, one at a time
options.rationale: The way Shopify publishes per sales channel: each channel holds its own state, so phone orders can sell while the storefront waits. One publish button per channel, each with its own check.
options.cost: Three channels in three states is a matrix the reader must hold in mind. The product page must show every channel at once, or one sells what another promised not to.

compact.behaviour: The recommended option reflows: one column, header actions under the title, and a table scrolls inside its own region.

patterns.assessment: Publish with the readiness check beside it is the pick: the reader reads what customers will find before they find it. Per-channel publish is the runner-up for companies that sell in more than one place. Never ship a silent unpublish; placed orders stay valid and the page must say so. Pause earns its place where the listing stays visible but nothing may sell.

patterns.title: Scheduling a change for later
