patterns.question: Prices, fees and sale windows change on dates, not at clicks. A scheduled change names the value, the date and the way to stop it, and the record shows both values until the date arrives.

options.name: A change with a date, listed with the record
options.rationale: The way WordPress lists a scheduled post beside its drafts: the coming change is a row with a date and a cancel, not a hidden timer. The fee page shows now and next together.
options.cost: Two values on one record is a rule every read must honour: orders placed before the date keep the old fee. Any page that prints the fee must print its date too.

options.name: A tier ends on its date
options.rationale: Each price holds its own dates, and the timeline shows what sells when. Standard at three prices is three rows, not one price edited twice.
options.cost: Three rows for one product is three records to read on every invoice and in every report. A customer who finds the old price can ask for the difference back, and the page must not hide that.

options.name: A scheduled change cancelled before it runs
options.rationale: The way Stripe voids a scheduled subscription change: cancelling is one dialog that says what stays. The EUR 6.00 fee never happens, and the record says it was cancelled rather than forgetting it.
options.cost: A cancelled schedule leaves a row that did nothing, and a year of those is noise. Cancelled rows must collapse into the history, not sit beside the value.

options.name: Two changes on one date, refused
options.rationale: The way Google Calendar refuses a second booking in a locked room: the clash names both changes and offers the move. One record cannot become two fees on the same morning.
options.cost: The second change waits on the first being moved or cancelled, which means leaving and coming back. It must offer the move inline or the refusal sends the reader hunting.

options.name: The sale window, set at creation
options.rationale: Opens and closes are two dates on the record, and the state follows them. Standard sells from 12 Jan to 14 Mar without anyone present at either end.
options.cost: A window set at creation is rarely rechecked: it opens on an unfinished product or closes on a selling one. The product page must show the window beside the state, always.

options.name: What the customer sees, before and after
options.rationale: The way Squarespace previews a scheduled site change: the reader reads the customer page twice, now and after. A fee change is judged by its customer line, not by its row on a settings page.
options.cost: A preview is a second rendering of the storefront and can drift from it. It must render from the same listing read the customer gets, or it shows a page the customer never sees.

compact.behaviour: The recommended option reflows: one column, header actions under the title, and a table scrolls inside its own region.

patterns.assessment: A change with a date, listed with the record, is the pick: the current value and the coming one sit side by side with a cancel. The tier timeline is the runner-up where prices change on fixed dates. Never ship overlapping schedules on one record, and never a change without its customer preview where customers read the value. The sale window earns its place at creation, where open and close are set together.

patterns.title: Nothing has ever existed
patterns.question: Carbon's first empty state: first use, nothing yet. The title should be a positive statement, the body says the next action, and one primary button fills the space. A setup section uses exactly this.

options.name: Positive title, one action
options.rationale: One positive title, one line saying what a product is for, and one button that creates the first one.
options.cost: The reader cannot see what a row will look like, so every column is undiscoverable until there is data. Carbon accepts this.

options.name: The empty state beside the thing it fills
options.rationale: The list holds nothing, and beside it the page says what the first product needs to be sellable. The empty state is a checklist rather than a sentence.
options.cost: A list page whose job is finding becomes a setup page while empty, and a reader with no products has no reason to want a list at all.

options.name: Empty with the first record's shape shown
options.rationale: The table's headers and a single dashed row showing what a row will contain, so the columns are known before there is data.
options.cost: Carbon says an empty state should replace the table, headers included, because a screen reader otherwise reads six empty headers before the message. This deliberately breaks that.

options.name: Empty inside a section, beside the sections that do have things
options.rationale: One section of a page is empty while its neighbours are not. The empty state is scoped to its section and takes no page-level action.
options.cost: A section with an empty state is taller than a section with three rows, which breaks the rhythm of a page of sections. It also invites a per-section action bar.

options.name: Empty with a reason and a way to fix it
options.rationale: The page is empty for a reason the reader cannot guess: the month has not closed. The empty state names the reason and the date it changes, and shows the figures that do exist.
options.cost: A page whose empty state depends on why it is empty needs a read that answers why, which is a second thing the API has to be able to say.

options.name: Empty because a permission hides everything
options.rationale: The list is not empty, it is withheld. Carbon's third empty state is permissions, and this one names the grant rather than saying nothing is there.
options.cost: It confirms that records exist, which some deployments would rather not do. Naming the grant makes the record count a secret the page reveals.

options.name: A sample the reader can open, keep, or remove
options.rationale: Real sample rows instead of an empty illustration, fenced with a Sample state and a notice. The reader learns the page by using it rather than by reading about it: faster first value than any of the six.
options.cost: Samples must be fenced out of every export, total, and customer surface, and a sample left in place at go-live ships fake data as the company's own.

options.name: One primary action and two quieter ways to start
options.rationale: Shopify Polaris's EmptyState: one primary action, one secondary, and a link to learn more. The reader can start blank, copy the shape of a standard gift box, or read what a product needs first.
options.cost: Three ways in is one decision more than one way in. A template only helps if the templates are good, so this needs at least one template that is worth copying.

options.name: A setup guide on Home, plain empty states elsewhere
options.rationale: Shopify's and Stripe's onboarding: the steps to a first order live once, on Home, with progress, and each list page keeps a plain one-line empty state. Setup is a journey across pages, so it gets one place rather than seven.
options.cost: The guide has to know what is done, which is a read across several modules. It also needs a way to be dismissed, or it stays on Home after the company has shipped 10,000 orders.

compact.behaviour: The recommended option reflows: one column, header actions under the title, and a table scrolls inside its own region.

patterns.assessment: The pick stays on A: one positive title, one line about what a product is for, and one button. It is the simplest shape and the only option that asks nothing of a reader who has nothing yet. Runner-up is the setup guide on Home, which suits a company whose first order needs five steps across five pages rather than one. Never ship the table with a dashed sample row: it teaches the columns by showing a record that does not exist, and a reader who tries to open it meets a dead end.

patterns.title: Nothing matches what was asked for
patterns.question: Carbon's second empty state, and the one most products get wrong: no results for a search is not the same as nothing yet, and the copy must not be the same.

options.name: Different copy, and it names the term
options.rationale: The title quotes the term that found nothing, the line says how many records exist so the reader knows the search failed rather than the data, and two actions separate clearing the search from clearing the filters.
options.cost: Two actions, and Carbon says an empty state should offer one primary action. The secondary one is a ghost link, which is the compromise.

options.name: The controls stay editable above the empty state
options.rationale: The search box and the filters keep their values so the reader can adjust rather than start again. The empty state sits below them, not instead of them.
options.cost: An empty state with live controls above it is taller than one alone, and the reader has to know which control to change.

options.name: Suggesting what does match
options.rationale: The empty state offers the nearest thing the reader probably meant: a similar customer name, or the same order without the filters. A search that helps is a search that proposes.
options.cost: Every suggestion is a read the API has to be able to answer, and a wrong suggestion is worse than none because it sends the reader further away.

options.name: A filters panel instead of an empty state
options.rationale: When a filter has narrowed the list to nothing, the panel itself becomes the message. The reader sees which of their own choices did it.
options.cost: The list is gone, so the reader cannot see how many records the unfiltered list holds unless the panel says so.

options.name: The same empty state with no actions at all
options.rationale: Where nothing can be done about it, the state says so and stops. An empty search with no results and nothing to adjust is a fact, not a failure.
options.cost: Carbon says an empty state should offer the verb that fills it. A page that violates that is telling the reader they are stuck, which may be the truth.

options.name: An empty state that carries the count it should have
options.rationale: Where a filter is the only thing between the reader and the records, the empty state names the filter and the number behind it. The reader can go back one step.
options.cost: The count is a second read, and it is a number on a page that was about to show none. Two numbers where one would do.

options.name: One line in place of the rows, with one link that clears everything
options.rationale: GitHub's issue list: 'No results matched your search', and a single link that clears the query, the filters and the sort together. The toolbar keeps its values, so a reader who wants to change one thing still can.
options.cost: It does not say how many records exist without the filters, so the reader cannot tell a narrow search from an empty list. Adding the count is the only change it needs.

options.name: The table header stays, with the message as its only row
options.rationale: Stripe's payments list keeps the column headers when a filter finds nothing, because the filters name columns and the reader is still reading the same table. The message sits in one full-width row.
options.cost: Carbon replaces the table for a first-use empty state, and this differs from it on purpose. It is right for a filter result and wrong for first use, so the two states need two components.

compact.behaviour: The recommended option reflows: one column, header actions under the title, and a table scrolls inside its own region.

patterns.assessment: The pick stays on A: copy that names the term, the count that proves the data exists, and two ways out. It answers both questions a reader has, what failed and what to change. Runner-up is the table that keeps its headers with the message as its only row, which suits a reader who filters a table all day and wants the columns to stay put. Never ship the empty state with no actions: a search that names its term always has one thing to offer, which is clearing it.

patterns.title: Loading
patterns.question: Carbon is explicit: use skeleton states instead of spinners where extra load time is expected. The narrower rule beside it: a spinner sits in the control that waits, and a skeleton is for the page's first read.

options.name: Skeletons at the real row height
options.rationale: Carbon's answer, and the page-frames shape. Each skeleton row is shaped like the row it will become, so nothing moves when the data lands.
options.cost: Carbon also requires the header, toolbar and pagination to match the row size, so a skeleton page has to get four heights right or the page jumps.

options.name: A spinner in the control that is waiting
options.rationale: A control-level rule: a search that is running shows a spinner inside the search field, not over the page. The table stays as it was.
options.cost: On the first load of a page there is no control to put it in, which is exactly why Carbon asks for a skeleton there and a spinner for a re-read.

options.name: A spinner in the submit button while it sends
options.rationale: A submit is disabled only while it sends. The spinner lives in the button, so the reader's eye is already there and nothing else on the page changes.
options.cost: A button whose label is replaced by a spinner loses its width, so the layout shifts unless the button holds its size. It also says nothing about how long it will be.

options.name: Progress for work that takes a while
options.rationale: Where the read is genuinely slow, a bar with a percentage and what is happening. This is the case Carbon's skeleton does not cover, because it is not a read.
options.cost: A percentage is a claim. If the server cannot estimate the remaining work, the bar is theatre, and a bar that stalls at 40% is worse than a spinner.

options.name: A dimmed page with the spinner centred
options.rationale: A scrim over the whole page with a spinner and a sentence. Unambiguous, and the page underneath is deliberately not readable.
options.cost: A scrim over the page is neither a shared component nor a page slot, and it hides the page a reader may want to scroll.

options.name: Nothing at all, briefly
options.rationale: No placeholder. The page renders as it will, and the content appears when it does. Correct only where the load is under about 200 milliseconds.
options.cost: Anything slower reads as a page that failed. Every read needs a loading state, so this is the shape the rule refuses.

options.name: The last rows stay, a thin bar says a new read is running
options.rationale: Linear and Vercel keep what was on screen and show a thin bar while the next read runs. A reader changing a filter keeps their place, and nothing jumps when the rows arrive.
options.cost: The rows on screen are briefly the old answer. A reader who acts on a row during that second acts on the old answer, so commands on a list that is reading must wait or say so.

options.name: A skeleton that admits a slow read after a few seconds
options.rationale: Polaris and Material both time loading states: nothing for the first few hundred milliseconds, a skeleton after that, and words once the wait is long. After five seconds this one says what it is reading and offers to stop.
options.cost: Three timed states per page is more to build and to test, and the five-second line only helps if the read can really be cancelled.

compact.behaviour: The recommended option reflows: one column, header actions under the title, and a table scrolls inside its own region.

patterns.assessment: The pick stays on A: skeletons at the real row height, so nothing moves when the data lands. It is the simplest shape and the only option that survives a slow first read on a phone. Runner-up is the thin bar over the old rows, which suits a re-read where the reader keeps their place, such as changing a filter. Never ship nothing at all: any read slower than a blink reads as a page that failed, and every read needs a loading state.

patterns.title: A command the API refused
patterns.question: A refusal alert words a refusal by its code, from a dictionary keyed on the code. WCAG 3.3.1 requires the error to be identified in text and 3.3.3 requires it to say how to fix it.

options.name: The refusal sentence, its code and a way to fix it
options.rationale: One refusal shape: a title saying what is wrong, the detail saying why, and a Why link where the application can explain the refusal. The refusal sentence comes from the dictionary, not the component.
options.cost: Three pieces per refusal code in two languages, and every new command that can be refused adds a code. The dictionary is the second copy of the domain rules.

options.name: The refusal beside the button that caused it
options.rationale: The same refusal, placed under the control that sent it. On a page with one form, the reader is already looking there and the connection is obvious.
options.cost: On a page with several forms, a refusal above the form and one under a button are two placements for one kind of message, and the reader has to know which is which.

options.name: The refusal with a code, for support
options.rationale: The refusal plus the code and a copy control, for the reader who needs to quote it. This is what a support conversation needs and what a normal reader does not.
options.cost: A code on screen breaks the usual rule: do not show a raw code. Shown deliberately, it has to be labelled and copyable rather than bare.

options.name: A refusal that changed nothing, stated plainly
options.rationale: Not every refusal is a problem. Some commands are refused because nothing needed doing, and saying so is more honest than an error tone.
options.cost: The reader cannot tell a no-op from a failure unless the tone differs, and the tone is the only signal. A refusal that was correct should not be red.

options.name: A refusal with nothing lost, said first
options.rationale: The refusal leads with what is intact, then what is wrong. NN/g's rule is that a message must not need reading twice; naming the damage first is the difference between a refusal and a dead end.
options.cost: The sentence order matters and has to be right per code, which is why the dictionary is the right place for it and a component is not.

options.name: The refusal on the record it happened to, not a banner
options.rationale: One command on one record refused. It goes into the record's own timeline, where the reader goes looking for what happened, rather than at the top of a page they are passing through.
options.cost: Invisible. A reader who sent the command from somewhere else will not come back to this page to find out why it did not happen.

options.name: The refusal inside the dialog that sent it
options.rationale: Stripe's refund dialog keeps a refusal inside the dialog, above the amount, and leaves the dialog open so the reader can change what was refused. Focus moves to the message, and the alternative is one button away.
options.cost: The dialog grows by the height of the message, and a long refusal pushes the buttons down. On a phone the dialog may need to scroll.

options.name: Refused before it is sent: the button explains
options.rationale: GitHub's merge box disables Merge and says which check blocks it. Where the page already knows the refund window has closed, it says so beside the button, and the refusal never has to happen.
options.cost: Only works for refusals the page can predict from what it already read. The API still refuses, so the dictionary sentence and the button sentence must say the same thing.

compact.behaviour: The recommended option reflows: one column, header actions under the title, and a table scrolls inside its own region.

patterns.assessment: The pick stays on A: the refusal with the dictionary sentence, the code behind Why, and the two things that can be done instead. It meets WCAG 3.3.1 and 3.3.3 in one place. Runner-up is the refusal inside the dialog that sent it, which suits a dialog flow where closing it would lose the amount the reader typed. Never ship the refusal only on the record timeline: a reader who sent the command from anywhere else never comes back to find out why it did not happen.

patterns.title: A command that worked
patterns.question: The catalog rule is precise: a success message follows only a command that succeeded, and a command that changes money, access or stock leaves evidence on the page it ran from.

options.name: Evidence on the page, not only a toast
options.rationale: The record changes and the page says what changed: the state becomes Refunded, the money section shows the reversal, and the timeline gains an entry. That is evidence a toast cannot be.
options.cost: The reader has to find the evidence. A toast is faster and leaves nothing once it goes, so a toast alone is not evidence.

options.name: A toast, for a change with no evidence to leave
options.rationale: Where the command changed nothing visible, a toast is the whole answer. Copying a reference is the clearest case: the value was already on screen.
options.cost: Material allows one action and no Dismiss, and Android warns the timer can take the action away. It is fine for a message with no action.

options.name: A success notice that persists, for a change in progress
options.rationale: Where the command succeeded and the effect is still arriving, the notice says so and stays until it does. A toast that goes would leave the reader unsure.
options.cost: A success message that waits is a status, not an alert, so it must not take a tone. And a notice that persists has to resolve into something else.

options.name: A success with a count, when a batch partly worked
options.rationale: A bulk command's success says what succeeded and what did not, in the same breath. '3 of 5 sent' is more useful than 'Sent'.
options.cost: A count that is not expected raises a question the message then has to answer, so a partial success needs its own copy per command.

options.name: No message, because the record says it
options.rationale: The lightest answer: the command runs and the thing it changed is visibly different. Nothing announces anything, so there is nothing to read twice.
options.cost: Fails WCAG 4.1.3 unless the change is exposed as a status. A screen reader user gets no signal that the command worked.

options.name: A success and a next step, where the flow is not finished
options.rationale: Where a command succeeded and the work is not done, the success names what is left rather than pretending it is finished. The listed product that still has no dispatch plan is the case.
options.cost: It sits between a success and a checklist, so it needs its own place. The outcome page is the shape that already claims this.

options.name: A toast with Undo, for a change that can be taken back
options.rationale: Gmail and Linear confirm a reversible change with a toast that carries Undo. The list already shows the change; the toast adds the one thing the page cannot, a way back for a few seconds.
options.cost: Never for money, access or stock, which cannot be taken back quietly. Undo also needs the command to be truly reversible on the server, not hidden on the client.

options.name: Saved, said quietly beside the button
options.rationale: Stripe's settings and Notion's pages say 'Saved' beside the control, with the time, and nothing else moves. A settings form is the case: the values on screen are already the evidence.
options.cost: Easy to miss, and a screen reader hears it only if it is a live status. It suits settings and not a command that changes money.

compact.behaviour: The recommended option reflows: one column, header actions under the title, and a table scrolls inside its own region.

patterns.assessment: The pick stays on A: evidence on the page, with the state, the money, and the timeline all saying what changed. A toast alone is never evidence for money, access, or stock. Runner-up is the toast with Undo, which suits a reversible change such as hiding a product from the store. Never ship no message at all: it fails WCAG 4.1.3, because a screen reader user gets no signal that the command worked.

patterns.title: A fact somebody has to read before acting
patterns.question: The content rule: a static notice is a status; only a command result is an alert. A tone may paint the object in that state and never a full-width band on a page about other work.

options.name: A neutral notice above the page
options.rationale: One neutral sentence about this page, above the sections: not a band and not a tone. It says why the page is what it is.
options.cost: It sits above the sections, so it is the first thing and the last thing read. A long notice pushes the work down on every visit.

options.name: The notice inside the section it is about
options.rationale: A fact about one section goes in that section, not at the top of the page. The reader only meets it where it changes what they do.
options.cost: The reader has to open the section to learn something that may change whether they should be in the section at all.

options.name: A callout inside a form, about what the form will do
options.rationale: A callout inside the field group, in words, before the command runs. This is the position-neutral form of the same rule and it is the one that keeps a tone off a page.
options.cost: A callout inside a form is a paragraph among fields, and it is the least visible of the alert shapes. It is also the one a reader reads before committing rather than after.

options.name: A hint under the field, with no tone at all
options.rationale: Some facts are not worth interrupting for. A hint under the field says the same thing in a quieter register, and the reader reads it because it is where they are looking.
options.cost: A hint has no visual weight, so it is the first thing a reader skips. It works for a definition and not for a consequence.

options.name: A tool tip on the word that carries the fact
options.rationale: A term hint beside a heading or a table note, where the term is the product's and the glossary entry explains it. Nothing is interrupted.
options.cost: Only for a term that is genuinely the product's and genuinely unclear. On any other word it is noise, and every term needs a glossary entry to keep in step.

options.name: The fact as the heading, instead of an alert
options.rationale: Where the fact is what the page is for, it is the heading and description rather than an alert. No second thing to read, and the page title says the same thing.
options.cost: The heading cannot carry a tone, so severity has nowhere to go. And the description is one line, which is not much room for a consequence.

options.name: The shipped Banner, for a fact about the whole console
options.rationale: A banner in GitHub's and Stripe's test-mode shape: one centred sentence across the top of every page, for a fact that holds on all of them. Sandbox is the case it exists for, in the info tone.
options.cost: A band is the loudest place on the screen. Used for a fact about one product it breaks the rule above, so it needs a short list of what may go there.

options.name: The fact beside the record, in its side column
options.rationale: Stripe's payment page puts risk and dispute facts in a right-hand column beside the payment, and GitHub does the same for a pull request. The fact is next to the record it is about, and the main column stays for the work.
options.cost: A side column drops below the record on a phone, so the fact is read last there. It needs a heading that says why it is there.

compact.behaviour: The recommended option reflows: one column, header actions under the title, and a table scrolls inside its own region.

patterns.assessment: The pick stays on A: one neutral sentence above the page, with no tone and no band. It says why the page is what it is and stays out of the work. Runner-up is the fact beside the record in its side column, which suits an order page where the refund window changes what the reader does next. Never ship a full-width toned band for a fact about one record: the rule refuses it, and a banner stays for facts that hold on every page, such as Sandbox.

patterns.title: The reader may not do this
patterns.question: A page its role cannot use shows it with the reason and the grant that helps. A back office with several roles meets this state on most pages, so it needs one shape.

options.name: The commands are refused, each with its grant named
options.rationale: The explained action: the button is refused and the reason is visible text beside it, naming the role that can. The record stays readable, which at the counter is the point.
options.cost: A page of refused commands looks broken to somebody who does not know their role. The role's name in the reason is what makes it legible.

options.name: The page itself is refused
options.rationale: The whole page is out of reach. A not-permitted state replaces the body with the reason and the grant, and nothing of the record is shown.
options.cost: Nothing at all is shown, so a warehouse lead cannot read a customer name to answer a question at the counter. That is a real cost on the surface where names matter.

options.name: The tab is absent, so the reader never sees the gap
options.rationale: A tab, sidebar entry or link appears only for a viewer who may open its page. Invoices, Reports and the money pages are simply not in a warehouse lead's sidebar.
options.cost: The reader cannot find out the capability exists. On a surface where someone is guessing at what the product can do, that is a real cost.

options.name: A banner naming what this role cannot do, once
options.rationale: One neutral band on the area says what the role may not do there, rather than a refused button beside every command. Stated once, in words, at the top.
options.cost: It repeats on every page of the area, and the reader's eye skips it after the first. A tone may not paint a full-width band on a page about other work.

options.name: The names are hidden, the figures are not
options.rationale: Where the record itself is sensitive but its shape is not, the customer is withheld and the money is shown. A finance reader gets the reconciliation without the personal data.
options.cost: A screen reader reads whatever is in the DOM, so anything hidden this way has to actually be absent rather than blurred. Blur alone is not a boundary.

options.name: The role is named in the refusal, and the way to change it
options.rationale: The refusal says which role the reader has, which role would be needed, and offers the command that asks for it. Everything a reader can be told without a support call.
options.cost: A request that reaches an owner is a message somebody reads, and a busy owner ignores it. It should not be the only route, so the page has to stay useful read-only.

options.name: The page refused, with a request sent to a named person
options.rationale: Google Drive's 'You need access' page: the reader asks for access in place, with a short message, and the request goes to a named person rather than to 'an administrator'.
options.cost: A request is a message an owner must answer, so it needs a place in the owner's queue. Without that it is a button that leads nowhere.

options.name: A read-only section: values as text, one line saying why
options.rationale: Stripe's settings for a role that may read but not change them: the fields become plain values, and one line at the top of the section names the role that can edit. Nothing looks like a form that fails on Save.
options.cost: The page looks different for different roles, so a support call about it has to start with which role the caller has.

compact.behaviour: The recommended option reflows: one column, header actions under the title, and a table scrolls inside its own region.

patterns.assessment: The pick stays on A: the explained action, with each refused command naming the role that can do it and the record staying readable. At the pickup counter, reading the record is the point. Runner-up is the read-only section with values as text, which suits a settings page where a form that fails on Save would be worse. Never ship the whole page refused for a warehouse lead: hiding a customer name they need to answer a question at the counter costs more than the secrecy is worth.

patterns.title: The connection is gone
patterns.question: The warehouse desk has to work without a connection, which means the back office's counterpart is a stale page. Nothing here shows how fresh its data is, so these options decide what a stale page says.

options.name: A banner saying what is stale and what still works
options.rationale: A neutral band naming when the page last read and which commands are refused while it is offline. The reader can still read, and knows it.
options.cost: Every page needs a last-read time and a notion of which commands are safe offline. Commands that change money almost never are.

options.name: Read-only, with every command refused and why
options.rationale: Every command refused with the same reason in words. Unambiguous, and a page of refusals that all say the same thing is noisy.
options.cost: A reader on a train sees a page they cannot use. It is honest and it is still frustrating, and the frustration is not information the page can carry.

options.name: A queued command, so the reader does not lose the work
options.rationale: A command the reader wants is held and shown as pending, with what it will do when the connection returns and a way to drop it. Nothing is lost, and nothing is claimed to have happened.
options.cost: A queued refund is a refund nobody has confirmed, and a queue of them is a liability. The page has to say plainly that the money has not moved.

options.name: A connection control in the header, always present
options.rationale: The connection is a fact about the session rather than about a page, so it lives in the header and holds on every page. A refresh control already exists for the queue's version of this.
options.cost: A second status in a header that already carries the theme and the language. And a header-level indicator is easy to learn and then ignore.

options.name: Nothing shown, because a stale page is a dangerous one
options.rationale: Where the reader is about to act on money, a stale page is refused outright. The page says so and offers one thing: try again.
options.cost: A reader who needs to answer a question at the counter gets nothing. The printed pick list exists precisely because the counter cannot refuse, which is why the two surfaces answer this differently.

options.name: The staleness stated on the values themselves
options.rationale: Each figure that could have moved carries when it was last true, so a reader comparing two rows sees which is fresher rather than assuming both are current.
options.cost: A timestamp on every money cell makes a table unreadable. It works on a page with two or three figures and not on a list.

options.name: The read fails in place: the server could not be reached
options.rationale: The problem state for status 0: where a read fails because nothing answered, the section says the server could not be reached and offers Try again. Nothing claims to be current, because nothing is shown.
options.cost: It only appears when a read is tried. A page that loaded before the connection dropped looks normal until the reader does something.

options.name: A small bar that retries by itself and says when
options.rationale: Gmail's 'Not connected. Trying again in 8s. Try now': the page stays readable, one quiet line says it is retrying and when, and the reader can retry at once.
options.cost: A countdown is movement on a page the reader is trying to read. It must stop once it gives up, and it must not count down forever on a laptop that has gone to sleep.

compact.behaviour: The recommended option reflows: one column, header actions under the title, and a table scrolls inside its own region.

patterns.assessment: The pick stays on A: one band saying what is stale, when it was read, and what still works. A stale page the reader can read beats a page that refuses to show anything. Runner-up is the problem state for a failed read, which suits a page that has nothing to show because the read itself failed. Never ship a queued refund as a quiet default: a refund nobody has confirmed is a liability, and the page must say plainly that the money has not moved.

patterns.title: The sign-in ran out
patterns.question: A session ends while the reader is working. Sign-in runs on the application's own origin, and a refused or ended session lands on /signed-out. The reader's unsent work is what this state must not lose.

options.name: Signed out, on its own page
options.rationale: A refused or ended session lands on /signed-out, worded by one sentence: 'Your sign-in has expired. Sign in again.' No back-office frame, because there is no session to show it to.
options.cost: The reader leaves their work to sign in again. Whether anything typed survives depends on the browser keeping the page, which is exactly what the other options make explicit.

options.name: A dialog over the work, which stays where it is
options.rationale: Stripe's dashboard re-authentication and Linear's session dialog: the work stays on screen behind a dialog, signing in again returns to it, and nothing typed is lost.
options.cost: A dialog over a form the reader cannot touch until they sign in. On a phone it fills the screen, which is acceptable because there is exactly one thing to do.

options.name: The form says so where Save was
options.rationale: Notion keeps an unsent change in place and says what blocks it beside the control. The Save button becomes the way back, so the reader's eye is already where the answer is.
options.cost: Only the form knows. A reader on a list page, with no Save button, meets the expiry somewhere else, so this needs a page-level sibling.

options.name: Warned before it ends
options.rationale: Dutch banks and DigiD warn before a session ends, with one button to stay. The reader who is still there never meets the expired state at all.
options.cost: A countdown on a page the reader is trying to use. It must only appear when the reader is idle enough to need it and active enough to answer it.

options.name: Refused as a command, worded by its code
options.rationale: The refused-command answer applied to a session: the save is refused with the session sentence, in the same alert shape as every other refusal. One component, one dictionary, no special case.
options.cost: The reader learns it only when they save. An expiry discovered at Save is later than one discovered at reading, and the typed work waits longer.

options.name: A toast, and the typed work goes with it
options.rationale: What happens with no design: the save fails, a toast says the session expired, and the toast goes in seconds. Drawn here to be refused on purpose.
options.cost: The message leaves and the typed notes leave with it. A reader who looked away loses work they cannot reconstruct.

compact.behaviour: The recommended option reflows: one column, header actions under the title, and a table scrolls inside its own region.

patterns.assessment: The pick is B: a dialog over the work, which stays where it is. It is the only option that keeps unsent work on screen and names the one thing to do. Runner-up is D, the warning before it ends, which suits a reader who is still at their desk and should never meet the expired state. Never ship F, the toast alone: the message leaves in seconds and the typed work leaves with it.

patterns.title: Somebody else saved first
patterns.question: Two people edit one record. The API refuses the second save with concurrency/record.changed-elsewhere, worded as 'Someone else changed this'. The reader's unsent edits are still on the page.

options.name: The refusal above Save, with her value under the field
options.rationale: Linear's conflict handling: the save is refused in words, the other person's value appears under the field it beats, and each field offers one button to take hers. The reader fixes exactly what collided.
options.cost: Works field by field. Where both people rewrote the same long notes, one button per field is not enough and the dialog in C takes over.

options.name: Field by field: keep mine or use hers
options.rationale: Contentful and Airtable resolve a conflict per field: each row shows both values and takes one. Nothing is reloaded wholesale, so nothing Alex typed is lost.
options.cost: A row per field is a second form to build and to read. Past three fields it is longer than the form it argues about.

options.name: A dialog with three ways out
options.rationale: Dropbox and Office ask on a conflict: keep mine, take theirs, or look at both. Three buttons, no field surgery, and the dialog says whose version is whose.
options.cost: Whole-record choice. Alex's arrival time and his notes travel together, so he cannot keep one and take the other.

options.name: Presence first, so the conflict never happens
options.rationale: Figma and Google Docs show who else is on the record before anyone saves. Alex sees Priya's avatar on the arrival field and waits or talks, and the refusal never has to happen.
options.cost: Presence is a live subscription per open record, and it only helps readers who look. The API still refuses, so this is early warning, not handling.

options.name: Merged where you did not overlap
options.rationale: Git merges what does not overlap and asks only about the rest. The dock Priya Shah fixed at 09:34 lands in Alex's form silently; only the arrival time needs a choice.
options.cost: Silent changes to a form the reader is editing. If Priya's dock fix surprises Alex at Save, the merge reads as tampering.

options.name: Read-only until reload
options.rationale: The banking answer: the form locks, one button reloads Priya's version, and Alex's edits are dropped. Drawn to be refused: nothing on this form is worth deleting notes over.
options.cost: Alex's notes are gone. A lock that deletes work teaches the reader to type notes somewhere else first.

compact.behaviour: The recommended option reflows: one column, header actions under the title, and a table scrolls inside its own region.

patterns.assessment: The pick is A: the refusal above Save, with her value under the field. It refuses in the dictionary's words and fixes exactly what collided, without a dialog and without losing a keystroke. Runner-up is B, the field-by-field choice, which suits a record where both people changed several fields and each choice differs. Never ship F, read-only until reload: it deletes Alex's notes to resolve an arrival time.

patterns.title: Work that runs without you
patterns.question: An import or a bulk refund runs longer than a page. The reader starts it and does other work. The job must be visible while it runs and answerable when it is done.

options.name: An activity tray, like an upload panel
options.rationale: Vercel, Linear, and Figma run uploads in a tray at the corner: progress while it runs, a line when it is done, and the page behind stays usable.
options.cost: A corner tray holds two jobs well and five badly. Past that it needs the jobs section in B, and the tray becomes its summary.

options.name: A jobs section on the page that started it
options.rationale: Shopify's bulk operations and Stripe's dashboard keep jobs on the page that started them, each with its state and a way to stop it. The reader who started the import finds it where they stood.
options.cost: The jobs live on one page. A reader who started an export and moved to refunds has to go back to find it.

options.name: Told when it is done, not while it runs
options.rationale: GitHub Actions tells the reader when a run finishes; while it runs there is nothing to decide. A toast plus a timeline entry answers the only two questions: did it work, and where is the evidence.
options.cost: Silence while it runs. A reader who waits for 850 records with no progress bar waits less patiently than one who watches 70%.

options.name: Progress on the rows it changes
options.rationale: Mailchimp and Intercom show a bulk send on the rows it touches: each row gains its result as the job reaches it. The reader watches 31 refunds land one by one.
options.cost: Thirty-one rows updating under the reader's eye. It needs the reader to stay on the page, which is exactly what background work should not need.

options.name: A job page with the failures listed
options.rationale: Stripe's bulk runs and Shopify's imports end on a page that lists what failed and why, each with its retry. The 29 that worked need no attention; the 2 that did not get all of it.
options.cost: A page per job is a place readers bookmark and support must explain. It earns its keep only for jobs that can partly fail.

options.name: A dialog that holds the reader until it is done
options.rationale: The old desktop answer: a progress dialog with nothing behind it clickable. Drawn to be refused: 850 records take minutes, and minutes of a held reader are the cost this whole item exists to remove.
options.cost: The reader cannot do other work while the job runs. Stop is the only choice, and it wastes the minutes already spent.

compact.behaviour: The recommended option reflows: one column, header actions under the title, and a table scrolls inside its own region.

patterns.assessment: The pick is A: an activity tray, like an upload panel. It stays visible on every page, it never holds the reader, and it answers progress without being asked. Runner-up is E, the job page with the failures listed, which suits a bulk refund where 2 of 31 need a person and the rest do not. Never ship F, the dialog that holds the reader: minutes of a blocked page are the cost this pattern exists to remove.

patterns.title: This record does not exist
patterns.question: A link names a record that is gone, mistyped, or at another company. A problem state words it as 'Not found'. The reader needs a way back, not a code.

options.name: The shipped record state
options.rationale: The problem state for a missing record: 'Not found' and the line that covers gone, mistyped, and another company's. It offers no retry, because the read answered correctly. Nothing claims the record exists.
options.cost: No retry and no way back: the record is not there, so there is nothing to retry. The way back in B is what the reader actually needs.

options.name: Not found, with the way back
options.rationale: Stripe's dashboard and Linear name the missing record, say what may have happened, and offer the list and the search. The reader typed one character wrong; the fix is one look away.
options.cost: The suggestions are guesses. Where the record belongs to another company, no suggestion helps, and the copy must say so rather than keep guessing.

options.name: The section says so, the page stays
options.rationale: GitHub shows a missing comment inside an intact thread. The order exists; one line on it does not. Only the lines section says so.
options.cost: Only for a child that is missing from a parent that exists. Where the whole record is gone, a surviving page is a lie.

options.name: Gone, and when
options.rationale: Linear and Notion name who removed a page and when, because 'does not exist' for something the reader saw yesterday reads as a fault. The audit trail already knows; the page says it.
options.cost: It confirms the record existed, which leaks across companies if the reader should not know. For another company's record this must fall back to B.

options.name: Search from the dead end
options.rationale: GitHub's 404 offers search where the reader stands. The reader who mistyped an order number searches without going back to the list first.
options.cost: A search box on an error page is a second search to keep in step with the list's. It earns its keep only where mistyped codes are common, which pickup codes are.

options.name: The big code
options.rationale: Vercel and Next.js draw a bare 404. It is honest about the status and silent about everything a reader needs: what is missing, why, and where to go.
options.cost: A code means nothing to a reader. Left bare it is a dead end with a number on it.

compact.behaviour: The recommended option reflows: one column, header actions under the title, and a table scrolls inside its own region.

patterns.assessment: The pick is B: not found, with the way back. It names the record, covers the three ways a record goes missing, and offers the list and the search. Runner-up is A, the record state, which suits a section whose read failed rather than a page whose record is gone. Never ship F bare: a code means nothing to a reader, and a dead end with a number on it is still a dead end.

patterns.title: Something went wrong on our side
patterns.question: The server fails a read or a command. A problem state words it as 'That did not go through', with a reference the reader can quote. The reader must know what did not happen.

options.name: The shipped failure with its reference
options.rationale: The problem state for a failed command: the title, the caller-safe detail, Try again, and a reference the reader can quote to support. The money sentence is the point: what did not move.
options.cost: A reference is only useful if support can read it back. Without that lookup it is a number that comforts nobody.

options.name: An outcome page that says what did not happen
options.rationale: Stripe's dashboard failure page leads with what did not happen, because after a failed refund that is the reader's first question. The money sentence comes before the retry.
options.cost: A page per failure is heavier than a state in place. It suits a failed command and not a failed read, where A stays.

options.name: Tried again by itself, and says when
options.rationale: Gmail retries a failed send and says when, with Try now for the impatient. A failure that clears on its own should not need a reader to clear it.
options.cost: Retrying a refund doubles it unless the command is idempotent. This suits reads and sends, and must never retry money blindly.

options.name: A toast for a background command that failed
options.rationale: Gmail's failed send and Linear's failed sync: the reader moved on, so the failure comes to them as a toast with its retry. The page behind is whatever they do now.
options.cost: A toast goes. A failed refund must also land in the record's timeline, or the evidence leaves with the message.

options.name: The section fails, the page stays
options.rationale: React error boundaries and Vercel's per-section recovery: the money section fails into its retry while the customer section stays readable. One failed read does not take the page.
options.cost: Two sections can fail two different ways on one page. Past one failure the page is a list of retries, and B takes over.

options.name: The old data with a quiet line
options.rationale: What happens when a failed re-read is swallowed: the old figures stay with a quiet line. Drawn to be refused: a refund total that may be wrong is worse than none.
options.cost: The reader acts on figures the server could not confirm. For money this is not a degradation, it is misinformation.

compact.behaviour: The recommended option reflows: one column, header actions under the title, and a table scrolls inside its own region.

patterns.assessment: The pick is A: the failure with its reference. It words the failure once, says what did not move, and gives support something to read back. Runner-up is B, the outcome page, which suits a failed command where the money sentence deserves a page of its own. Never ship F: figures the server could not confirm are misinformation, and a quiet line does not make them honest.

patterns.title: The back office is down for a short while
patterns.question: A planned window stops the back office. The warehouse keeps its printed pick lists, but the dispatch desk checks every parcel against the system, so dispatch waits too. The reader needs the window, what still works, and when to come back.

options.name: Told ahead of time, on every page
options.rationale: Stripe's status banner and Linear's scheduled maintenance: one sentence on every page from days before, with the window and what still works. Nobody meets maintenance by surprise.
options.cost: A band on every page for days is days of noise for a 30-minute window. It must appear late enough to matter and early enough to plan the warehouse around.

options.name: The maintenance page itself
options.rationale: GitHub and Vercel draw the window as a page: what is happening, when it ends, and what still works. During the window this is every page.
options.cost: Nothing can be read behind it, including the pick lists. Anything the warehouse needs must be printed before 02:00.

options.name: Read-only while it lasts
options.rationale: Shopify and Notion degrade to reading when writing is unsafe. Orders can be read for the counter; nothing that changes money is offered.
options.cost: Read-only needs every command to know it is refused and why. A page that forgets one offers a refund that fails at 02:15.

options.name: A countdown with what still works
options.rationale: Cloudflare's waiting room counts down with the facts beside it. The reader watches one number fall instead of wondering whether to keep waiting.
options.cost: A countdown that passes 02:30 with the system still down breaks trust faster than no countdown. It must switch to words the moment the window does.

options.name: The window as a calendar fact on Home
options.rationale: Incident.io and Linear put a planned window on Home days ahead, next to the work it touches. The dispatch plan for the day carries the note, not a banner.
options.cost: Home is one page. A reader who lives in Orders never sees it, which is why this pairs with A and never replaces it.

options.name: A message beforehand, nothing on screen
options.rationale: What happens when maintenance is announced by message only: owners get the mail on Thursday and the warehouse meets the window on Sunday. Drawn to be refused as the only signal.
options.cost: Nobody reads a Thursday message on Sunday at 02:00. A message tells; only the back office can remind.

compact.behaviour: The recommended option reflows: one column, header actions under the title, and a table scrolls inside its own region.

patterns.assessment: The pick is A: told ahead of time, on every page. A window nobody meets by surprise is a window the warehouse can plan around, and the printed pick lists are the plan. Runner-up is B, the maintenance page itself, which is what every page becomes while the window runs. Never ship F alone: a Thursday message tells, and only the back office reminds on Sunday at 02:00.

patterns.title: Too many tries
patterns.question: The reader hits a limit: too many exports, too many sign-in tries, too many sends. The API answers 429 with when to try again. The reader needs the wait, not a lecture.

options.name: The button waits, and says how long
options.rationale: GitHub and Stripe answer 429 with Retry-After, and the button counts it down. The reader waits 40 seconds knowing why, instead of clicking a button that keeps refusing.
options.cost: A countdown on a button is a timer the page must keep honestly. If the reader reloads, the count must survive or start over truthfully.

options.name: Sign-in tries, counted down
options.rationale: DigiD and Dutch banks count sign-in tries down and name the wait at zero. The reader who mistyped twice knows exactly where they stand.
options.cost: Counting tries tells an attacker the same thing. The wait at zero must be real, and the count must not leak whether the account exists.

options.name: Queued behind the others
options.rationale: Cloudflare's waiting room queues rather than refuses: the export is 3rd in line with its wait stated. The reader's work is held, not lost.
options.cost: A queue is a promise of order. If an export jumps it, or the wait restarts, the queue reads as a trick.

options.name: The limit stated before it hits
options.rationale: Stripe's API dashboard and Linear's limits page show usage against the ceiling before anything refuses. The reader who sees 9 of 12 plans the last 3.
options.cost: Usage figures are a read of their own, and a stale one refuses a reader it told there was room. The figure and the enforcement must agree.

options.name: The 429 page
options.rationale: Cloudflare answers a hard stop with a page: too many tries, when to come back, and a reference. No retry button, because retrying is what caused this.
options.cost: A page with nothing to do but wait. It suits a stop measured in minutes and insults one measured in seconds, which A handles.

options.name: A spinner that never says why
options.rationale: What happens when the 429 is swallowed into a loading state: the search spins with no message. Drawn to be refused: a wait the reader cannot name reads as a page that broke.
options.cost: Indistinguishable from a hang. Every second past the first is a second the reader spends deciding whether to reload, which restarts the wait.

compact.behaviour: The recommended option reflows: one column, header actions under the title, and a table scrolls inside its own region.

patterns.assessment: The pick is A: the button waits, and says how long. It turns the limit into a 40-second wait with its reason attached, which is all a reader who hit 12 exports needs. Runner-up is D, the limit stated before it hits, which suits a reader planning a month of exports rather than one too many. Never ship F: a wait the reader cannot name reads as a page that broke, and reloading restarts it.

patterns.title: The sidebar
patterns.question: A back-office console holds seven top-level areas and thirty routes under Settings alone. Fluent allows two levels and calls a group an accordion rather than a link; GOV.UK wants current and active distinguished.

options.name: Grouped areas with expandable sub-items
options.rationale: Seven areas, each expandable, with the current item marked and the sub-item indented under its area. The account sits at the foot.
options.cost: Thirty settings routes in one group means a group longer than the screen, and Settings is open on every settings page so it never collapses.

options.name: Two levels, with the group showing a live count
options.rationale: The groups carry the number a reader would otherwise have to go and get: 10 under Refunds, 3 team invitations, 5 disputes. The count is the group's whole job.
options.cost: A count beside every area is a claim on every read, and an area whose count is zero is an area that looks finished rather than empty.

options.name: A flat list with a search box
options.rationale: Thirty settings routes plus six areas is a tree. A flat list of every page with a search box collapses the tree into one index, and the reader types what they want.
options.cost: Thirty settings routes is the reason a tree exists at all. A flat list of over a hundred entries is a wall, and the sidebar stops being a map.

options.name: A command palette for the whole product
options.rationale: The sidebar holds the seven areas and a palette holds everything else. Cmd-K is the shape most consoles now use for a large route count.
options.cost: It only works if the reader knows a key exists, so it cannot be the only way to anything: WCAG 2.1.1 requires every function to be available from the keyboard, and a hidden palette is a discoverability problem rather than an accessibility one.

options.name: The sidebar as a page, opened over the content
options.rationale: At 390 pixels there is no beside, so the navigation is a page of its own with a Back. Every entry is visible at once rather than behind a hamburger.
options.cost: One more navigation level on the surface where a warehouse lead is holding a phone on the warehouse floor, which is the worst possible time for an extra tap.

options.name: The sidebar as an accordion with only one open
options.rationale: One group open at a time keeps the sidebar short regardless of how many routes each group holds. Seven areas become seven lines plus two.
options.cost: Fluent's guidance is the opposite: the indicator must stay visible on a collapsed parent when a child is current, so a reader has to look at a closed group to see where they are.

options.name: Recent pages pinned above the areas
options.rationale: The three most recent pages sit above the seven areas, so resuming work is one click instead of re-walking the tree. None of the other variants remembers where the reader was: clearer navigation by recency rather than by structure.
options.cost: Recents are per person, so a shared screen shows another person's trail. A recent that was archived or renamed also needs a rule for what its row says.

options.name: Collapsed to an icon rail on a narrow screen
options.rationale: Linear collapses its sidebar to an icon rail rather than hiding it, so the seven areas stay one click away on a narrow laptop. The rail keeps the current item marked and the account visible as an avatar.
options.cost: Labels are gone, so a new reader has to hover all seven glyphs to learn them. Counts beside groups have nowhere to go either.

options.name: The sidebar as an off-canvas sheet on a phone
options.rationale: The sidebar turns into a sheet below the md breakpoint: the same entries slide in over a scrim and dismiss with a close control. Nothing about the tree changes between desktop and phone.
options.cost: The sheet covers the page it came from, so comparing the navigation with the content means opening and closing it. A warehouse lead looking up one order costs one extra tap.

compact.behaviour: Below the md breakpoint the sidebar becomes an off-canvas sheet: the same entries slide in over a scrim and dismiss with a close control.

patterns.assessment: Keep the grouped areas with expandable sub-items: seven areas with two levels is what Fluent allows, and the expandable group is the shape sidebar components ship. The counts beside groups are the runner-up for areas that hold a queue, such as refunds, but a count beside every area reports status the reader did not ask for. Never ship the flat list of every page: over a hundred entries is an index, not a map, and it belongs in the command palette.

patterns.title: The breadcrumb
patterns.question: Fluent's rules are that a breadcrumb never wraps, may scroll horizontally, and that aria-current goes on the last item. The trail runs four levels deep on a product variant and sometimes shows Dutch strings in an English frame.

options.name: The trail as the parent chain
options.rationale: Every level is a link except the last, which carries the current item. It is the only place the record's place in the tree is stated.
options.cost: Four levels on a price tier, and Fluent's no-wrap rule pushes the last item off a phone unless the trail scrolls.

options.name: A trail that truncates from the left
options.rationale: Fluent truncates after 80 characters with a tooltip and collapses the overflow into a menu starting from the second item, so a long product name never pushes the current page off.
options.cost: A menu in the trail is a third kind of menu on a page that already has row menus and header menus, and the reader has to open it to see where they are.

options.name: No trail, because the sidebar already says it
options.rationale: The expanded sidebar entry is the trail. One navigation element instead of two, and the heading starts at the top of the page.
options.cost: Fails WCAG 2.4.8 in the practical sense on a phone where the sidebar is closed, and there is no evidence of where a record sits in the tree. GOV.UK's own rule is that the trail appears when a parent page exists.

options.name: A trail with the state on the parent link
options.rationale: The trail carries the parent's state, so a reader knows whether the product they are inside is still live before they read anything else. The trail becomes informative rather than structural.
options.cost: Fluent truncates a trail item at 80 characters, and a product name plus a state badge plus an ellipsis is three things in eighty characters. The breadcrumb stops being a navigation control.

options.name: A trail with the area's other pages beside it
options.rationale: The trail, then the sibling pages of this area as tabs. The reader can move sideways without going back to the sidebar.
options.cost: Two navigation mechanisms for the same tree: sibling pages of one area already have their own navigation, and this adds a second beside it.

options.name: A trail that scrolls sideways rather than truncating
options.rationale: Fluent allows a breadcrumb to scroll horizontally rather than wrap, so every level stays readable and the current item is reached by scrolling rather than by being cut off.
options.cost: The current item is off screen on arrival, which is the opposite of what a breadcrumb is for, and a horizontal scroll inside a page is easy to miss.

options.name: Back to the parent on a phone
options.rationale: GitHub collapses its trail to a single back link on narrow screens: the parent name with a chevron, above the heading. One line replaces four levels and the heading keeps its place.
options.cost: Grandparents are unreachable from the record, so a reader three levels deep walks up one level at a time. The full chain remains only on desktop.

options.name: The current title as a sibling menu
options.rationale: Notion turns the current page title into a menu of its siblings: opening it lists the other price tiers beside Standard. Moving sideways costs one click instead of up and back down.
options.cost: A heading that opens a menu is a heading that does not behave like one, and the menu repeats the sidebar section the reader just left. It is justified only where siblings are visited together.

compact.behaviour: On a phone the trail collapses to a single back link to the parent, above the heading.

patterns.assessment: Keep the parent chain with the last item marked current: it is the only place a record states its place in the tree. The left-truncating trail with an overflow menu is the runner-up for four-level chains on narrow screens, since it keeps the current page visible where sideways scrolling hides it. Never ship no trail at all: on a phone the sidebar is closed, so the trail is the only statement of where a record sits.

patterns.title: The header bar
patterns.question: The bar carries the page title, a sidebar toggle, a help control and the theme. It does not carry the company name, who is acting, or where they are beyond the page title.

options.name: The bar with the company name
options.rationale: The page title on the left, then the things that are true everywhere: which company, who is acting, help and theme. The sidebar toggle stays because a phone needs it.
options.cost: Four things in a bar above the content on every page, and a brand mark that repeats what the sidebar already says.

options.name: The bar as the breadcrumb, replacing the trail
options.rationale: The chain moves into the bar, where the page title already is. One place states where the reader is rather than two.
options.cost: The bar is present on every page including the list pages where there is no chain, so the bar has two different shapes. Fluent treats the breadcrumb as a page-level element below the header.

options.name: A bar that carries nothing but the frame
options.rationale: The bar holds only the sidebar toggle and the theme. Everything else is in the sidebar or the page, so the bar never competes with the content.
options.cost: The reader loses the company name and who they are acting as, which are the two facts a support conversation needs before anything else.

options.name: The bar with a persona switcher, which is the same as being somebody else
options.rationale: The foot switcher, moved into the bar and made explicit. Acting as somebody changes what the session can do, so it belongs where a reader looks for who they are.
options.cost: On a production deployment with one real account there is nothing to switch to, and a switcher that always lists one person is a control that cannot do anything.

options.name: The bar with the deployment identity
options.rationale: Where a deployment is a sandbox, the bar says so on every page. Naming the deployment is the one job of an identity band.
options.cost: A deployment identity in the bar competes with the page title for the same horizontal space, and a reader who has seen it fifty times stops seeing it.

options.name: No bar at all, with the theme and language in the sidebar foot
options.rationale: The controls that change nothing about the data live with the account they belong to. The top of the page is then entirely the page's own.
options.cost: Three global controls become three taps on every visit, and removing the header landmark is a structural change rather than a preference.

options.name: Search, inbox and account in the bar
options.rationale: GitHub keeps one global bar: a search trigger that opens the palette, a bell with the unread count, and the account avatar. Everything true on every page sits in one row and the page starts below it.
options.cost: Three global controls compete with the page title for the same row, and on a phone the bar keeps only the menu glyph and the bell. The account moves to the sheet.

options.name: The record name and state in the bar on a record page
options.rationale: Linear keeps the record identifier and state in the header once a record is open, so a reader who scrolled past the heading still knows which record is on screen. The bar names the record; the page carries the detail.
options.cost: The bar then has two shapes, one for lists and one for records, and the record shape repeats the heading word for word. It is worth the height only on long records.

compact.behaviour: The recommended option reflows: one column, header actions under the title, and a table scrolls inside its own region.

patterns.assessment: Keep the bar with the company name and the acting person added: a support conversation needs both facts before anything else, and the sidebar toggle is what opens the phone sheet. The deployment identity band is the runner-up for sandbox deployments only, where naming the deployment on every page avoids confusion with production. Never ship no bar at all: burying the theme and language in the sidebar foot turns a visible control into three taps.

patterns.title: Tabs within a page
patterns.question: Sibling pages of one area sit in a sub-page navigation; a second tab row uses a subordinate level. Tabs are capped at about six, and the active tab belongs in the URL.

options.name: The shipped tab row, with the tab in the URL
options.rationale: The tab row under the header on a price tier, with the active tab as a URL parameter, so a pasted link carries it.
options.cost: A reader cannot compare two facets, and every new backend facet adds a tab. Carbon and GOV.UK both cap tabs at about six for this reason.

options.name: Tabs carrying counts
options.rationale: Each tab carries how many things are in it, so a reader knows whether a facet is worth opening. Four tabs where one holds 9,412 and another holds 0.
options.cost: A count of 0 invites a click that leads to an empty state, and a count has to be a read per tab rather than a number in a template.

options.name: Tabs below the summary, as a sub-page navigation
options.rationale: The summary stays on screen, and the sibling pages of this area become a tab row at a subordinate level beneath it.
options.cost: The tab row is lower on the page and a reader has to scroll to reach it, so on a long record the facets are below the fold.

options.name: Tabs as links, so a middle click works
options.rationale: The tab labels are real links to sibling routes rather than buttons that swap a panel. Middle click, open in a new tab, and the back button all behave the way a reader expects.
options.cost: GOV.UK's own tabs implementation is exactly this, anchor links with a URL fragment, so this is the most defensible option available rather than an alternative.

options.name: A segmented control instead of tabs
options.rationale: Where the choice is between two or three views of the same data rather than different pages, a segmented control is the right control. Carbon names the content switcher for exactly this.
options.cost: A segmented control cannot hold a count, cannot overflow, and says nothing about being on a different page. Three segments is its ceiling.

options.name: No tabs, because the facets are a checklist
options.rationale: Where a record has a handful of facets and they all fit, headed sections on one page. GOV.UK names this as the first-class alternative to tabs and it is the right answer for most records.
options.cost: A long page. It stays honest only while the sections stay few, and it is why a record with eight facets carries tabs rather than eight sections.

options.name: Overflow tabs in a More menu
options.rationale: GitHub Primer moves overflowing tabs into a menu rather than scrolling the row, so the first five facets stay visible and the rest sit one click away. Eight delivery sections fit a row built for five.
options.cost: A reader cannot see which facet is current when it sits inside the menu, so the More control has to carry the current label too. The menu also needs the same counts the row would have shown.

options.name: Vertical tabs on a settings page
options.rationale: Stripe settings put the sections in a vertical list beside the content, so six sections read as a short index rather than a wide row. The current section stays visible while its fields scroll.
options.cost: The list spends horizontal space on every section page, and on a phone it stacks above the content where it reads as a second heading. It fits settings, not records.

compact.behaviour: The recommended option reflows: one column, header actions under the title, and a table scrolls inside its own region.

patterns.assessment: Keep the tab row with the active tab in the URL: a pasted link carries the facet, and the row sits where every tab implementation puts it. Tabs as real links are the runner-up and the most defensible alternative, since middle click and the back button then behave as expected; prefer them where each facet is its own route. Never ship the segmented control for facets: three segments is its ceiling and it cannot carry counts or overflow.

patterns.title: The icons in the frame
patterns.question: Seven area icons, a sidebar toggle, a help mark and the theme. A page never writes a raw interactive element, so every one of these is a component with a name and an accessible label.

options.name: An icon beside every label
options.rationale: Every area carries an icon and its name, so the icon is reinforcement rather than the only label. It is what makes seven areas easy to read at a glance.
options.cost: Seven icons is seven drawings to keep consistent and to give a name to. Carbon's tab guidance refuses icons in tab labels for the same reason.

options.name: Words only, no icons
options.rationale: The labels are the navigation. Nothing to draw, nothing to name, and nothing that fails when a reader cannot distinguish the icons.
options.cost: Seven areas of the same weight in the same style is a wall of text, and the eye has nothing to catch on. This is the shape that needs a bold current item to work.

options.name: Icons with labels, and the label hidden on a phone
options.rationale: On a phone the sidebar is a page of words; inside the collapsed frame the icons carry the seven areas and the labels are gone. The same component, two densities.
options.cost: An icon-only sidebar on a phone is seven drawings with no labels, which is the case Carbon refuses in tab labels. It works only if the phone also keeps the labels somewhere.

options.name: A section of the sidebar with a heading
options.rationale: Seven areas become two or three headed groups: what you sell, what it makes, how it is set up. The grouping is about the job rather than the object.
options.cost: Grouping an area tree by job means a reader has to decide which group an area is in, and grouping by object is the convention everywhere else in the product.

options.name: Icons only for the actions, words only for the areas
options.rationale: The split the evidence supports: an icon reinforces a labelled area, but an icon alone is never the label for a place. An action with one obvious meaning can be an icon with a tooltip and an accessible name.
options.cost: An action that has to be learned has to be hovered, and Material's rule is one action per notification and no Dismiss, which is the same economy applied to a button.

options.name: Icons that carry a state as well as a meaning
options.rationale: The theme and the language are icons because they have one obvious meaning and no label worth the width. The company name is not an icon because it has to be read.
options.cost: Theme and language are two icons whose meaning is only conventional, and a reader who has not used one cannot tell them apart without hovering both.

options.name: The current item with a left indicator bar
options.rationale: VS Code marks the current view with a border beside the label rather than an icon, so the eye finds it without reading. The bar sits outside the label, which keeps words-only areas easy to read at a glance.
options.cost: A two-pixel bar is easy to miss on a long sidebar, and it says nothing on a phone where the sidebar is closed. The trail still has to carry the current page.

options.name: Lucide icons at one size, from one set
options.rationale: Icons from the Lucide set at 16 px with a 2 px stroke, so every area icon comes from one set at one size and no two disagree on weight. One set is what keeps seven drawings consistent.
options.cost: Fourteen pixels leaves no room for detail, so each glyph has to read as a silhouette. A new area needs a new drawing that fits the set.

compact.behaviour: The recommended option reflows: one column, header actions under the title, and a table scrolls inside its own region.

patterns.assessment: Keep an icon beside every label, drawn from one icon set: seven areas need a visual catch, and the icon reinforces the label rather than replacing it. Words-only areas with icon-only actions are the runner-up where icon budget is short, with each action carrying a tooltip and an accessible name. Never ship state-carrying icons in the frame: theme and language as bare glyphs force the reader to hover both to tell them apart.

patterns.title: Language and theme
patterns.question: Two switches that change nothing about the data and are therefore the easiest things to get wrong: an explicit choice is preferred to the account's, which is correct, and a missing translation falls back to the other language on several pages.

options.name: Both switches in the header, each showing its value
options.rationale: Each control carries its current value rather than an icon, so the reader can see what is set without opening it.
options.cost: Two text buttons in a header of text, and a reader who wants to change the language twice a day reads 'EN' as decoration.

options.name: Both switches in the account menu
options.rationale: Everything about who you are and how the product looks sits in one place, and the header is left for the page title. Account, language, theme and sign-out are one decision.
options.cost: Two taps for a reader who only wants to switch to dark at the end of a shift, and the theme is not something a reader goes to an account menu to find.
