options.rationale: The shared code shape: monospaced, never wrapped, with a copy control. A code a person reads aloud on a support call is a fact, not decoration.
options.cost: A copy control on every row of a list is a control per row. And a code in a monospaced font is visibly different from a name, which is correct and slightly louder than the page around it.

options.name: The identifier labelled by what it is, not by its form
options.rationale: The label says Order number rather than Reference, because a reference could be anything. A reader who knows what a thing is can use it; a reader who does not can ask.
options.cost: Some identifiers have no natural name and end up labelled by their kind, which tells a reader nothing about where to use it.

options.name: The identifier behind a disclosure
options.rationale: A code a reader usually does not need is hidden behind a disclosure. It is there for a support case and out of the way otherwise.
options.cost: A hidden code is a code a reader does not know exists. On the record where a support case is likely, that is the wrong place to hide it.

options.name: No identifier, because the reader knows the record
options.rationale: Nothing technical is shown. A reader who arrived by clicking the record already knows which record it is, and a code is noise to them.
options.cost: It removes the one thing a reader needs to quote in a support conversation. And a reader who arrived by address, which happens, has no way to tell two records apart.

options.name: The identifier as the record's name
options.rationale: Where a record has no human name, the identifier is the heading: the code is what the record is called and it is never repeated as a field.
options.cost: A code as a heading is not readable aloud. It is the right shape for a system where the code is all there is and the wrong shape for one where a person named the thing.

options.name: Click the code to copy it
options.rationale: Vercel copies a deployment address on click and answers 'Copied', so the identifier is its own control with no button beside it. The code stays monospaced and labelled, and the confirmation is the feedback the click needs.
options.cost: There is no visible affordance until hover, so a reader may never try. Keyboard users need the code to be a real button, which it is, with its label read aloud.

options.name: A short code on the list, the full one on the record
options.rationale: Stripe's dashboard shortens a charge identifier in the list and shows it whole on the record, because a list is scanned and a record is quoted. Search accepts either form, so the short code is never a dead end.
options.cost: Shortened identifiers can collide on screen, and a reader quoting the short form in a support case forces a second question. The record must show the full reference above the fold, not behind a disclosure.

options.name: No bare identifier anywhere on a list
options.rationale: Where a record has no subject yet, the state says so and the code is behind a copy control. A list shows subjects, never raw codes.
options.cost: A draft with no subject reads as broken, and a subject is a thing the company has to write before the row is useful. That is the cost of not showing an identifier.

compact.behaviour: The recommended option reflows: one column, header actions under the title, and a table scrolls inside its own region.

patterns.assessment: Ship the labelled, monospaced, copyable code on the record: it is the rule's shape and the one thing a support case needs quoted. The runner-up is the identifier as the record's name, which is the better choice for records with no human name such as a serial number in the warehouse. Never ship the page with no identifier: a record nobody can quote is a record support cannot help with.

patterns.title: The team and what each person may do
patterns.question: The team is who works for the company, and a role is what each of them may do. The owner invites people, grants roles, limits some to one warehouse, and suspends or removes them, while everyone else sees the team by name and role and nothing more.

options.name: Members with the invitations below
options.rationale: Linear lists members with their role and state in line and pending invitations below, because joining and belonging are one list with two states. The owner acts on a row without opening it.
options.cost: Row commands for suspend, remove, change role and limit access cannot all fit, so most move into a menu per row.

options.name: Permission matrix per role
options.rationale: GitHub compares team roles in a capability matrix, which answers what a role may do without opening each one. The matrix is the honest shape for custom roles.
options.cost: Capabilities multiply past twenty, so the matrix needs grouping by area and is a reference rather than a page.

options.name: Inviting one member in a dialog
options.rationale: Clerk invites with address, role and scope in one dialog, because an invitation is one decision with three fields. The scope line limits warehouse staff to one building at the point of inviting.
options.cost: Inviting a whole seasonal crew means repeating the dialog per person, so bulk inviting needs a different shape.

options.name: Warehouse-scoped staff cards
options.rationale: Vercel scopes team access per project, which fits seasonal staff who work one warehouse and nothing else. The card names the building, the role and the end of the access.
options.cost: Staff cards separate from the member list split the team into two places, and the owner checks both.

options.name: Suspending a member with the reason
options.rationale: GitHub suspends with the reason recorded, because a suspension is reviewed later and the reason is the review. The dialog states what the member keeps and what stops.
options.cost: A dialog per member action means suspend, remove, reinstate and transfer ownership each carry their own copy to maintain.

options.name: The team as a member without controls sees it
options.rationale: Linear shows the member list without controls to members who cannot manage, because the names and roles are shared and the commands are not. The page is the same shape with the commands gone.
options.cost: A read-only page that looks like the managing page invites clicking where nothing happens, so the missing commands need no visible husk.

compact.behaviour: The recommended option reflows: one column, header actions under the title, and a table scrolls inside its own region.

patterns.assessment: The members table with the invitations below is the best option: it shows who is in, who is invited, and what each may do on one page. The permission matrix is the runner-up, and prefer it on the role page where capabilities are compared. Never ship the matrix as the team page, because the back office manages people, not capabilities.

patterns.title: API keys and webhooks
patterns.question: The company's own systems read the product through API keys and learn about orders through webhooks. A key's secret is shown once and never again, and each webhook delivery names whether it arrived, because a missed order update is money unaccounted for.

options.name: Keys table with the grants in line
options.rationale: The Stripe Dashboard lists API keys with their grants, creation and last use, because the back office asks what a key may do and whether it is still used. Revoke and rotate sit on the row.
options.cost: Grants in line fit only as short labels, so the full grant list lives on the key page one click down.

options.name: The secret, shown once
options.rationale: GitHub shows a new token once with copy front and centre, because the secret cannot be read again. The dialog states the grants so the back office stores the right secret against the right system.
options.cost: A secret shown once is lost when the owner closes the dialog too soon, and the only repair is revoking and creating again.

options.name: Webhook endpoints with their deliveries
options.rationale: Svix draws each endpoint with its recent deliveries and their states, because the back office asks whether an update arrived. A failed delivery carries its next retry and a replay command.
options.cost: Deliveries multiply into the thousands on a busy day, so the list needs the endpoint as a filter and aggressive paging.

options.name: Grant picker on a new key
options.rationale: GitHub scopes a new token with grouped checkboxes, because a key should hold the least it needs. The groups name the areas so the owner grants by area rather than by capability.
options.cost: Grouped grants hide the exact capabilities, so a careful owner opens each group and the dialog grows long.

options.name: Rotating a key that may have leaked
options.rationale: Vercel rotates with the old secret kept briefly, because the systems holding it need time to move. The dialog states the overlap and what happens to in-flight calls.
options.cost: An overlap keeps a leaked secret valid for its window, so the length of the overlap is a second decision with its own risk.

options.name: Embedding origins beside the keys
options.rationale: Clerk lists allowed origins beside the keys, because the checkout runs on the company's pages and nowhere else. Each origin names where it is used.
options.cost: Origins are a third concern on a developers page, and keys, webhooks and origins together crowd one set of tabs.

compact.behaviour: The recommended option reflows: one column, header actions under the title, and a table scrolls inside its own region.

patterns.assessment: The keys table with the shown-once dialog is the best option: the list states the grants and the dialog protects the secret. The endpoint with its delivery log is the runner-up, and prefer it on the webhooks tab where deliveries are the work. Never show the secret anywhere except the creation dialog, because a secret that can be read again is not a secret.

patterns.title: Bringing data from spreadsheets
patterns.question: Contacts, budget lines and newsletter consents arrive from the spreadsheets the company used before this product. Each import names what was brought in, what was refused and why, and the back office fixes the refused rows without importing the file twice.

options.name: Imports with the refused rows below
options.rationale: Shopify shows an import with its failed rows and the reason per row, because the file is never clean. The back office repairs the rows without touching what already imported.
options.cost: Refused rows from several imports pile up, so each import needs its refused rows grouped under it rather than in one list.

options.name: Matching columns to fields
options.rationale: Mailchimp matches spreadsheet columns to fields before importing, because the file's names never equal the system's. Each row pairs one column with one field and the back office corrects the guesses.
options.cost: A wide file means twenty mapping rows, so the page needs the unmatched columns first and the matched ones collapsed.

options.name: Dropzone with the template beside it
options.rationale: Intercom pairs the upload with the template download, because the file imports cleanly only when it starts from the template. The back office downloads, fills and drops in one loop.
options.cost: The template covers one kind of import, so contacts, budget lines and consents each need their own and the page lists three.

options.name: Dry run before the import
options.rationale: Stripe shows a dry run before a bulk change lands, because the back office should read the damage before it is done. The preview counts accepts, refusals and updates without writing anything.
options.cost: A dry run doubles the reads on a large file, so files over 5,000 rows are refused before the preview rather than during it.

options.name: Repairing one refused row
options.rationale: Shopify repairs a failed row where it lists it, because the fix is one field and the context is the row. The dialog shows the refusal reason above the fields.
options.cost: One dialog per row is slow when eighteen rows share one cause, so the common causes need bulk commands too.

options.name: Consent import refused outright
options.rationale: Customer.io refuses a consent file without proof, because consent cannot be assumed and the fine lands on the company. The page states the rule and the repair rather than a partial import.
options.cost: Refusing the whole file for some bad rows discards the good ones too, so the back office fixes and re-imports rather than continuing.

compact.behaviour: The recommended option reflows: one column, header actions under the title, and a table scrolls inside its own region.

patterns.assessment: The imports table with the refused rows below is the best option: the history and the repairs sit on one page. The column mapping is the runner-up, and prefer it at import time where the match is decided. Never ship the dropzone alone, because an import without its refused rows hides the work it creates.

patterns.title: Connecting the payment account
patterns.question: Every amount that reaches a customer comes from the company's connected payment account, as a reversal of a charge that customer made. The company connects that account once, chooses which methods customers may use, and reads what each method costs.

options.name: Connected account with the methods below
options.rationale: Stripe draws the connected account above the enabled methods, because methods depend on the connection. The card states the account, the payout bank, and when the capabilities were last refreshed.
options.cost: The account and the methods each want the top of the page, so on a phone the methods start below the fold.

options.name: Connecting a new account in steps
options.rationale: Stripe Connect onboards in named steps, because connecting means signing in at the provider, approving methods, and setting the payout bank. The steps name what is done and what is left.
options.cost: Steps imply an order the provider does not enforce, so a step can read as blocked when it is merely unordered.

options.name: Method capabilities as a checklist
options.rationale: Adyen shows each method with its capabilities and approval state, because a method can be connected but not yet live. The checklist names what works and what is still pending.
options.cost: Capabilities change at the provider without warning, so the checklist is a cached reading with a timestamp rather than the truth.

options.name: Method costs side by side
options.rationale: Mollie quotes each method with its fee in line, because the back office compares costs when choosing methods. The estimate grounds the percentages in last month's orders.
options.cost: An estimate from last month misleads when the next month sells differently, so the figures need their basis in the open.

options.name: Disconnecting with the consequences stated
options.rationale: GitHub states the blast radius before a destructive command, which disconnecting is: new orders stop at once. The dialog names what stops, what continues, and what happens to money already taken.
options.cost: A heavy dialog for a rare command is weight carried always and used once, but the cost of an accidental disconnect justifies it.

options.name: No account connected yet
options.rationale: Stripe shows an empty payments state with the single command that fixes it, because nothing can be sold until the account exists. The state names the step, not the product.
options.cost: The empty state cannot show methods or costs, so the back office connects without knowing what each method costs.

compact.behaviour: The recommended option reflows: one column, header actions under the title, and a table scrolls inside its own region.

patterns.assessment: The connected account card with the methods list is the best option: the connection state and the methods each have their place and the costs sit in line. The capability checklist is the runner-up, and prefer it while the connection is new and methods still need approval. Never show the methods without the account card, because a method means nothing while the account is disconnected.

patterns.title: The supplier invoice
patterns.question: The supplier invoices the company: the subscription for the plan, the fee per order handled, and the text-message cost. The company reads what each line charges, downloads the invoice for the books, and pays by direct debit under their mandate.

options.name: Invoice sheet with its lines
options.rationale: Stripe Billing draws the invoice as the document itself, because the company files it and pays it. The lines carry quantities and rates, and the totals add up top to bottom.
options.cost: A document-shaped page is read, not worked, so changing the plan or the mandate means leaving it.

options.name: Invoices newest first
options.rationale: Chargebee lists invoices with state and total in line, because the company asks which month is paid and which is open. The overdue row carries the retry date.
options.cost: The list shows totals without lines, so checking one figure means opening the invoice.

options.name: Plan with the mandate beside it
options.rationale: Stripe Billing shows the plan, the mandate and the next invoice together, because changing one affects the others. The company reads what they pay and how before changing either.
options.cost: Plan, mandate and next invoice each deserve the top, so the page orders three equals and one of them loses.

options.name: Usage lines with their rates
options.rationale: Vercel draws metered usage with the rate beside the meter, because a usage line without its rate is a figure the company cannot check. Each line names the plan allowance it counts against.
options.cost: Rates differ per plan and over time, so the page must state which rate version priced each line.

options.name: Overdue with the retry stated
options.rationale: Chargebee states the failed charge, the reason and the next retry, because an overdue invoice is a problem with a date. The company fixes the mandate rather than the invoice.
options.cost: Dunning copy on the invoice page alarms a reader who opened it to file, not to pay.

options.name: Text-message cost for the month
options.rationale: Resend breaks message cost down by kind, because delivery codes and reminders fail at different rates. The company reads what each kind cost before the invoice arrives.
options.cost: A cost page per channel multiplies: mail is free and text is metered, and the two need one page or two honest ones.

compact.behaviour: The recommended option reflows: one column, header actions under the title, and a table scrolls inside its own region.

patterns.assessment: The invoice sheet with its lines is the best option: it reads as the document the books need, with the mandate and the download beside it. The plan page with the mandate is the runner-up, and prefer it for changing the plan rather than reading a month. Never show the usage lines without their rates, because a metered figure without its rate cannot be checked.

patterns.title: Discount and promotion codes
patterns.question: A code takes money off an order, and each one has its own value, use limit and dates. The company watches what each code costs them, retires what leaks, and issues new ones for partners and campaigns.

options.name: Code table with use and state
options.rationale: Shopify lists discount codes with uses and limits in line, because the back office asks what each code costs and whether it leaked. The state badge names what the code does now.
options.cost: The conditions behind a code, such as which products it applies to, fit only as a second line and need the code page for the full rule.

options.name: Code editor with its conditions
options.rationale: Shopify edits a discount as named condition blocks, which fits a code that applies to some products, some channels and some dates. Each block reads as one sentence of the rule.
options.cost: The blocks take a long page, so the back office cannot check one code and move to the next without scrolling past every condition.

options.name: Vouchers with their balances
options.rationale: Shopify draws gift cards as balances that spend down, because a voucher is money held for a later order. The balance, not the code, is the figure the company watches.
options.cost: Vouchers and discount codes share little beyond the word code, so one list for both reads as two lists stapled together.

options.name: Redemptions, newest first
options.rationale: Shopify lists discount redemptions per order, which answers where a leaked code went. Each line ties one use to the order that used it.
options.cost: Redemptions multiply into the hundreds, so the list needs the code as a filter and is a report rather than the page.

options.name: Issuing one code in a dialog
options.rationale: Shopify issues a discount code from a short dialog, because a code for a partner is five fields and no conditions. The dialog keeps the list behind it for the names already taken.
options.cost: Conditions beyond value, limit and dates do not fit, so a code with channel or product rules needs the full editor anyway.

options.name: Retiring a leaked code
options.rationale: GitHub retires a leaked secret with the blast radius stated, which is what a leaked code needs. The dialog states the uses, the cost, and what happens to orders already placed.
options.cost: A confirm dialog for every retirement slows the back office who retires several codes after one leak.

compact.behaviour: The recommended option reflows: one column, header actions under the title, and a table scrolls inside its own region.

patterns.assessment: The code table with usage and state is the best option: it shows value, use and dates in one scan, and retiring a leaked code is one command on the row. The editor is the runner-up, and prefer it for creating a code with several conditions. Never ship the redemption-only list, because redemptions explain the past and the company manages the codes.
